caption: A, Fifth digit ulceration with raised, erythematous borders and drainage on initial dermatology visit. B, Poorly circumscribed infiltrate of atypical epithelioid cells within the dermis dissecting between collagen bundles with mixed inflammatory infiltrate. Epithelioid cells have round to oval, enlarged nuclei with vesicular chromatin, some pleomorphic, and abundant amphophilic cytoplasm.
scenario: A woman in her 30s presented with a chronic, painful, nonhealing ulcer on her fifth finger that developed after trauma 1 year earlier (Figure 1A). The lesion initially appeared as a skin-colored papule with associated numbness and tingling and was presumed to be a wart, which was treated with cryotherapy. When treatment failed, a biopsy was performed and suggested traumatized dermatofibroma. Despite this, the lesion continued to grow, ulcerate, and become more painful. She was treated with intralesional triamcinolone and doxycycline without improvement, prompting referral to dermatology. On examination, her PARACELSUS score was greater than 10, suggesting the possible diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Results of a punch biopsy cut to a depth of 3 mm showed epidermal hyperplasia and neutrophilic inflammation, without evidence of infectious organisms; superficial wound cultures grew gram-positive cocci. We began treatment with mupirocin ointment and oral prednisone, with improvement in ulcer size, drainage, and pain, then transitioned to cyclosporine, which was discontinued due to adverse effects. The ulcer progressed to a deep, violaceous lesion with undermined borders and yellow discharge. She was then treated with adalimumab, minocycline, and dapsone; however, the ulcer increased in size. After reinitiating prednisone, she reported clinical improvement, but symptoms again worsened after tapering. Radiology demonstrated soft tissue swelling but no bony necrosis. Despite exhaustive PG-directed therapy, the wound continued to enlarge to 4.5 × 3.0 cm, exposing tendon, with increased drainage and pain, prompting evaluation with point-of-care high-frequency ultrasonography (HFUS) and repeat biopsy (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathology results revealed an atypical epithelioid proliferation with positive staining for pancytokeratin, CD34, and ERG, with patchy CD31 positivity. There was negative staining for CD68, SOX10, S100 protein, human herpesvirus 8, calponin, p63, CK7, and CK20. Notably, there was loss of INI1 expression and no bacteria (Gram stain), fungi (periodic acid–Schiff stain), or acid-fast bacilli (Fite stain) were identified. Results of pathology, immunostaining, and imaging (Figure 2) confirmed the diagnosis of classic-type epithelioid sarcoma (ES). Immunosuppressants were discontinued, and the patient was referred to a multidisciplinary sarcoma team, ultimately requiring amputation. ES is a rare soft-tissue neoplasm most commonly affecting the distal extremities of young adults, with peak incidence around the age of 35 years.1It tends to grow along tendons, fascia, and nerves, with differentiation reflected in its varied immunohistochemical findings.2Histologically, ES appears as a dermal or subcutaneous nodule composed of epithelioid and spindle cells, which may be well circumscribed or irregularly lobulated, often with central necrosis. Immunohistochemistry typically shows positive results for cytokeratin and vimentin, with approximately 50% of cases with positive staining for CD34 and 40% showing ERG immunoreactivity.3,4ES is usually negative for S100, desmin, FLI-1, and CD31, although focal CD31 cytoplasmic expression has been described.2,5The highly sensitive diagnostic feature is loss of nuclear SMARCB1/INI1 protein expression.1 Prognosis remains poor due to diagnostic delays, high local recurrence rates, and distant metastasis. Five-year survival ranges from 25% to 70%.1The proximal subtype, typically involving the trunk, pelvis, or proximal limbs, is characterized by larger, pleomorphic cells and follows a more aggressive course.1The more common classic (distal) subtype typically affects the hands and forearms and may initially be less aggressive; however, it can metastasize, and the presence of high-grade histologic features, such as mitoses, necrosis, and atypia, results in behavior resembling the proximal variant. Importantly, ES is often chemoresistant, which explains why radical surgical approaches, including amputation in this case, may be required.1 Clinically, ES initially presents as a painless, firm dermal or subcutaneous nodule. It has been associated with prior trauma and may develop superficial bleeding or necrosis that can become painful.1Rarely, ES manifests as a nonhealing, ulcerative process with raised margins, mimicking conditions like perforating granuloma annulare,Mycobacterium ulcerans, or even PG, as in a case where diagnosis was delayed for 18 years.6Distinguishing features include the histologic absence of palisading granulomas, lack of organisms, and confirmatory immunohistochemical findings. Given the ambiguous presentation of ES, accurate diagnosis requires a high level of suspicion. HFUS has successfully identified ES even when tumors were not palpable or initially missed with magnetic resonance imaging, and it is increasingly used in skin oncology to assess lesion depth and vascularization.7,8Contrary to ES, findings of HFUS for perforating granuloma annulare typically appear as a poorly defined hypoechoic band in the dermis, while active PG demonstrates a heterogeneous, edematous process.9,10When used alongside clinical assessment and dermatopathology, HFUS can help differentiate lesions and assess involvement with nearby structures. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge in distinguishing ES from mimicking ulcers and emphasizes the importance of early imaging and repeat biopsy with immunohistochemical staining to reduce morbidity and guide appropriate treatment.

caption: A, Clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface on the left labia minora. B, Histopathologic examination reveals increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers within the dermis, arranged in a disorganized organoid pattern and lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
scenario: A 9-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of asymptomatic, irregular pigmented lesions on the vulva and was initially diagnosed with a nevus at a local clinic. Physical examination revealed clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface, located on the inferomedial aspect of the left labia minora (Figure 1A). The patient reported no pruritus, pain, abnormal discharge, or prior local trauma. Her personal and family history was unremarkable. No tenderness was elicited on palpation, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy or involvement of other mucosal sites. An excisional biopsy was performed for histopathological evaluation (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.

caption: A, Firm papules and nodules with seropurulent crusts on the dorsal hands, along with joint deformities. B, Diffuse dermal spindle cells with focal vaguely storiform architecture, along with sparse lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrates (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×100).
scenario: A woman in her 70s with rheumatoid arthritis who was receiving long-term immunosuppression (prednisolone and methotrexate) presented with a 6-month history of progressive papulonodules on her face and extremities. The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy specimens from the face and hand showed identical features (Figure 1B).
explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

B, Hematoxylin and eosin stain (original magnification ×400) of left forearm lesion biopsy shows clumps of basophilic material in the stroma and a superficial area of ulceration with lobular proliferation of vessels and central necrosis infiltrated by neutrophils. Fibrotic stroma with neutrophilic infiltration and red cell extravasation.
scenario: A man in his 60s with a medical history of end-stage kidney disease status after kidney transplant taking 750-mg mycophenolate mofetil twice daily, 1-mg tacrolimus twice daily, and 5-mg prednisone daily presented with 3 painless lesions on the left upper extremity. The lesions had been present and enlarging for months, bleeding easily when traumatized. The patient reported additional symptoms of fever, chills, night sweats, weakness, and unintentional weight loss spanning several months. Frequent scratches by multiple domesticated cats were noted. Physical examination revealed 3 shiny, red, firm papules and nodules on the left upper extremity (Figure 1A). Skin biopsies of the left forearm and upper arm were obtained for hematoxylin and eosin and tissue culture (Figure 1B). Elevated creatinine and hematuria with concerns for transplant rejection, malignancy of native kidney, or acute tubular necrosis prompted abdominal magnetic resonance imaging, demonstrating hepatosplenic hemangiomas. HIV testing was negative, and tissue cultures for bacteria, fungus and mycobacteria were negative.
explanation: Histopathology demonstrated a benign vascular proliferation and neutrophilic aggregate with positive Warthin-Starry stain suggestive of bacillary angiomatosis (Figure 2). Whole blood polymerase chain reaction (PCR) forBartonellaspecies was positive with positive serologic IgG (1:256) and negative IgMB quintanaantibodies and equivocalB henselaeIgG (1:64) with IgM negativity, confirming bacillary angiomatosis. Bacillary peliosis, characterized by blood-filled cystic spaces in the liver and spleen, was found on magnetic resonance imaging. An infectious disease physician prescribed doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily, for 3 months. Gastrointestinal symptoms resulted in self-discontinuation of treatment, despite the persistent hand lesion. Complete resolution occurred with a course of azithromycin, 500 mg daily, for 2 months. Bacillary angiomatosis is a disseminated disease caused by the small, pleomorphic, gram-negative rod,B henselaeorB quintana,most commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals and patients with advanced HIV disease.1,2Bacillary angiomatosis has been reported infrequently in adult solid organ transplant recipients with most presenting months after transplant, unlike the present patient presenting 11 years posttransplant.2Transmission occurs by direct contact with cats via scratches, fleas, or human body lice. Skin is most frequently involved, followed by bones and liver, and presents as single or multiple erythematous or violaceous papules or nodules.1,2Patients often experience constitutional symptoms of fever, anorexia, and weight loss.2 The diagnosis of cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis can be challenging, often requiring multiple diagnostic modalities, including skin biopsy and PCR.Bartonella, a fastidious organism, is difficult to isolate via culture and with a 20% sensitivity.3Serology can be useful in combination with whole blood PCR, but difficult to interpret due to high rates of cross-reactivity betweenBartonellaspecies.3TheBartonellaspecies could not be determined in this case due to serologic cross-reactivity, but genus-level identification guided effective treatment, which is similar across species. Tissue biopsy with PCR is a specific method for identification ofBartonellaspecies, making this molecular test crucial to diagnose cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis.4Histopathology is notable for neutrophilic infiltration and collections of organisms, identified with a Warthin-Starry stain.5Advanced imaging is necessary to exclude peliosis and to guide management in preventing complications such as liver failure and potential rupture.6 The differential diagnosis for bacillary angiomatosis includes Kaposi sarcoma, angiosarcoma, pyogenic granuloma, and mycobacterial and fungal infections. While Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HIV infection, iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma has been reported in patients on immunosuppressive therapies and in transplant recipients. Cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma presents as painless, well-defined, pink to purple patches, plaques, or nodules.7Kaposi sarcoma can be distinguished histopathologically from bacillary angiomatosis by spindle cell vascular proliferation in the dermis and immunohistochemistry staining positive for latent nuclear antigen-1 (LNA-1), a marker for human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8).8Pyogenic granulomas are extremely friable, benign vascular lesions that rapidly develop as a single red papule or polyp.5Pyogenic granulomas can share overlapping features with bacillary angiomatosis but have a lobular appearance and lack the clusters of neutrophils seen in bacillary angiomatosis.9Advanced angiosarcoma lesions can resemble bacillary angiomatosis with violaceous nodules that easily bleed. Histopathology reveals ill-defined vascular spaces with multilayering of hyperchromatic endothelial cells.5 Recommended treatment for bacillary angiomatosis includes erythromycin, 500 mg, 4 times daily or doxycycline, 100 mg, twice daily for 2 weeks to 2 months.10Longer therapy duration of at least 3 months may be necessary in immunocompromised states.2Preventive measures include eradication of body lice and strict flea-control measures for cats.1 Bacillary angiomatosis is critical to recognize in immunocompromised patients. Clinically, these lesions may appear similar to malignant and benign entities, making histopathology and laboratory testing essential for accurate diagnosis. It is critical to use multiple diagnostic modalities, including biopsy with Warthin-Starry stain, serology, and PCR testing. Comprehensive workup, including advanced imaging to exclude systemic involvement, is warranted to prevent potentially fatal outcomes.

caption: A, A firm, skin-toned oval plaque with localized hair loss was noted in the occipital area, consistent with the hair collar sign. B, Panoramic imaging of the biopsy is observed (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×4).
scenario: A 6-year-old boy with no relevant medical history presented to the pediatric dermatology clinic with a congenital scalp lesion. On physical exploration, an oval, indurated skin-colored plaque with overlying alopecia was observed on the occipital region (Figure 1A). A skin biopsy was performed for histopathological study (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathological examination revealed multiple dilated pseudovascular spaces in the mid and deep dermis, located between dermal collagen bundles. These were accompanied by an increased number of small, round cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, showing no atypia or mitotic activity (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that these cells were positive for epithelial membrane antigen and progesterone receptors, and negative for vascular markers such as CD31 and CD34. In view of the clinical stability of the lesion, the patient’s family opted against surgical intervention. Soft-tissue lesions of the scalp are common in clinical practice, with lipomas and trichilemmal cysts being among the most frequent. In children, common scalp lesions include dermoid cysts, infantile hemangiomas, and nevus sebaceous. Less common diagnoses are meningoceles, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, myofibromas, and hematologic neoplasms. Meningothelial hamartoma was first described in 1990 as a rare lesion, also known as a rudimentary meningocele.1Since then, 28 cases have been reported in the literature.2-8The presence of meningothelial cells outside of the central nervous system is an exceptional phenomenon. In meningothelial hamartomas, these cells are located in the skin, usually on the scalp, without extending beyond the subcutaneous tissue. The lesion contains multiple tissue types, including connective, vascular, and meningothelial components. In most patients, these lesions present as solitary, well-circumscribed nodules with overlying alopecia, exhibiting a skin-colored, reddish, or grayish hue. Although congenital, they are often detected in childhood or adulthood and may enlarge or cause pain. The hair collar sign should alert clinicians to the possible presence of ectopic neural tissue, with or without underlying central nervous system abnormalities.2,9 Since the clinical appearance of these lesions is nonspecific, diagnosis relies on histological analysis.1,9The differential diagnoses of meningothelial hamartomas include several mesenchymal neoplasms, such as angiosarcoma, spindle cell hemangioendothelioma, epithelioid hemangioma, giant cell fibroblastoma, and intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia. Meningothelial hamartomas arise in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue and are characterized histologically by connective tissue proliferation and small to medium caliber blood vessels intermixed with meningothelial elements. In histopathology, meningothelial elements refer to meningothelial cells, which are specialized cells that line the meninges, particularly the inner layer of the arachnoid and the arachnoid granulations. These cells appear oval to round with eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged in whorled patterns or surrounding pseudovascular spaces. Histological studies show no evidence of malignant transformation, such as nuclear atypia or increased mitotic activity. The epidermis overlying the lesion is usually histologically normal.5,10 Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically shows epidermal involvement with infiltration of Langerhans cells, which are S-100 and CD1a positive—findings not observed in this case. Aplasia cutis presents as an absence of skin at birth, usually ulcerated or scarlike, without dermal pseudovascular spaces or cellular proliferation. Spindle cell hemangioendothelioma is a vascular neoplasm characterized by spindle cells and vascular markers such as CD31, WT1, or GLUT1, all negative in this case. In contrast, the presence of uniform meningothelial-like cells arranged around pseudovascular spaces, along with positive staining for epithelial membrane antigen and progesterone receptors and absence of vascular, muscular, and neural markers, supports the diagnosis of meningothelial hamartoma. The negativity for S-100 aligns with the hypothesis that these lesions, despite a possible neural crest origin, do not express typical neural markers, helping to confirm the diagnosis of meningothelial hamartoma. While imaging such as magnetic resonance imaging can be useful to rule out deeper connections in suspected cases, in this patient, no neurological symptoms or bone abnormalities were observed clinically. Given the lesion’s confinement to the dermis and subcutis on histology, imaging was not deemed necessary, consistent with the approach reported in the literature. It is not necessary to perform additional complementary tests, as no associated pathologies have been described to date. Complete surgical excision of the meningothelial hamartoma is usually curative.1 Meningothelial hamartoma is an extremely rare, benign lesion that may be mistaken for a low-grade vascular neoplasm due to its unusual histological characteristics. Recognizing this lesion is crucial to avoid misclassification.

caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

caption: A. Clinical image of a well-demarcated, nodular lesion (arrowhead) measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter located on the left cheek and protruding into the oral cavity. B. Immunohistochemistry showing spindle-cell neoplasm located within the subcutaneous tissue, composed of medium-sized, basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern within a fibrous stroma containing thin-walled blood vessels, including larger branching staghorn vessels (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
scenario: A woman in her 50s was referred to our dermatology clinic due to a nodular lesion on her left cheek (Figure 1A). The lesion had been present for more than 5 years, with progressive slow growth. On examination, it measured 2.5 cm in diameter, was firm to palpation—lacking the typical consistency of a cyst or a lipoma—was nonmobile and apparently adherent to underlying structures, was asymptomatic with no reported pain or discomfort, and extended into the oral cavity. No additional lesions were observed on the head or neck. The patient had no relevant medical history and denied any prior facial injections. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined, hypervascular, solid tumor located within the subcutaneous tissue, measuring 2.1 × 2.5 × 2.3 cm, with no evidence of invasion into adjacent structures. A biopsy of the central portion of the lesion was performed (Figure 1B).
explanation: The biopsy revealed a neoplastic proliferation of medium-sized, spindle-shaped basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern on a fibrous stroma with small-caliber blood vessels (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for CD34, factor XIIIa, and STAT6. Given the histological findings and CD34 positivity, RNA sequencing was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue to detect sarcoma-associated gene fusions. The analysis revealed theNAB2::STAT6fusion, which confirmed the final diagnosis of solitary fibrous tumor (SFT). A full staging workup showed no lymphadenopathy or metastatic disease. Moreover, given that the tumor measured 2.5 cm in diameter, its mitotic count assessed over 10 high-power fields was 0, it exhibited less than 10% necrosis, and occurred in a patient in her 50s, it scores only 1 point on the risk of metastasis model for SFTs by Demicco et al.1The lesion was subsequently removed with wide surgical margins, with no recurrence 8 months after surgery. SFT is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm—with an estimated annual incidence of 0.35 per 100 000 individuals—first described in the pleura but now known to occur in various anatomical sites, including the abdominal cavity, orbit, retroperitoneum, and, less frequently, the skin.1-5Historically, hemangiopericytoma was considered a distinct entity, but molecular, immunohistochemical, and morphological studies have demonstrated that hemangiopericytomas and SFTs lie along the same tumor spectrum. They most commonly present as a slowly enlarging, painless mass that may produce different local mass effects depending on its location; pleural lesions may also cause cough or dyspnea. In cutaneous presentations, SFT arises from the dermis or subcutaneous tissue.2,3 The largest case series of cutaneous SFTs to date described a female predominance and preferential location on the head and neck, followed by the thigh and back, with a median age of 46.5 years at diagnosis.2Histologically, SFTs are composed of spindle cells arranged in a patternless architecture, often with alternating areas of hypocellularity and hypercellularity, variably collagenous stroma, and hemangiopericytomalike vessels. Variants such as lipomatous, fascicular, and storiform patterns have been reported.2-4 Immunohistochemical staining typically shows positivity for CD34, Bcl-2, and CD99, although expression can be variable. Nuclear expression of STAT6, due to theNAB2::STAT6gene fusion, has emerged as a highly specific and sensitive diagnostic marker.4,6Molecular confirmation via detection of this fusion gene provides additional diagnostic certainty.2-4,6 Differentiating SFT from other CD34-positive spindle-cell neoplasms can be difficult. Historically, many cases were misdiagnosed prior to the identification of theNAB2::STAT6fusion.2-4Fat-free or low-fat spindle-cell lipomas pose one of the most challenging differential diagnoses due to similar morphology and CD34 expression. However, spindle-cell lipomas typically display a school of fish arrangement, thicker collagen bundles, and loss of retinoblastoma protein expression.2-4 Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans must also be considered, particularly when the lesion is dermally based. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans exhibit a uniform storiform pattern and infiltrate subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern—features absent in SFT—and are characterized by the specificCOL1A1::PDGFBgene fusion.2,3Superficial CD34-positive fibroblastic tumors, while also expressing CD34, generally show greater cytologic atypia and focal cytokeratin positivity.2 The metastatic potential of SFTs can be stratified using the Demicco risk assessment model, which incorporates patient age, tumor size, mitotic rate, and necrosis.1Additionally, telomerase reverse transcriptase promoter andTP53variants have been associated with more aggressive clinical behavior.7,8 Management of cutaneous SFTs is challenging due to their unpredictable biological behavior; between 10% and 25% of SFTs recur, and 10-year survival rates range from 73% to 100%, even in tumors initially classified histologically as low risk.2,3Complete wide local excision is the treatment of choice. Mohs micrographic surgery has also been proposed to ensure clear margins, minimize recurrence, and preserve tissue—particularly in cosmetically sensitive areas.5 This case underscores the importance of recognizing the clinical, histopathological, and immunohistochemical features of cutaneous SFTs. Awareness of theNAB2::STAT6translocation is essential for accurate diagnosis, which in turn informs appropriate treatment and long-term follow-up.

caption: A, Clinical presentation displaying a collection of skin-colored papules with background hyperpigmentation. B, Punch biopsy revealing dilated infundibula, small, haphazardly placed follicular structures in the papillary dermis, and follicular hyperkeratosis.
scenario: A woman in her 20s presented with a 9-year history of an asymptomatic, erythematous eruption on her left cheek. Examination revealed a 4 × 3.5-cm collection of skin-colored papules with a background of hyperpigmentation (Figure 1A). She reported resting her left cheek on her hand while studying and sleeping on her left side. Before presentation, she had been treated with desonide, 0.05%, cream and ammonium lactate, 12%, lotion with minimal improvement. A punch biopsy was obtained from the left cheek for histopathologic evaluation (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathologic analysis revealed dilated infundibula, small, haphazardly placed follicular structures in the papillary dermis, and follicular hyperkeratosis (Figure 1B). On higher power, hyperkeratosis, a dilated follicular opening filled with keratin debris, and sparse superficial perivascular infiltrate were observed (Figure 2). Based on clinical history and pathology, a diagnosis of traumatic anserine folliculosis (TAF) was made. The patient was advised to use a doughnut pillow and avoid sleeping on her left side. Treatment with calcipotriene, 0.005%, cream and tretinoin, 0.025%, cream once daily was initiated. As the lesion improved with tretinoin, 0.025%, cream, the dosage was gradually increased to 0.1%. At 7-month follow-up, the patient reported a reduction in lesion size and hyperpigmentation, with minimal improvement in texture. TAF is a rare dermatologic disorder marked by closely grouped follicular papules, which may present on a background of hyperpigmentation or erythema.1,2Precipitated by repeated friction or pressure, TAF most commonly occurs on the chin, jaw, neck, and cheeks of children and teenagers.1,2TAF is also associated with a personal or familial atopic history.1The most common histopathologic features include hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, dilated infundibula with keratinaceous debris, and rudimentary follicles.3Additional features that have been reported include lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate and focal increase of stratum lucidum.4Management of TAF involves eliminating the source of pressure or friction via modification of causative postures.1,2Topical keratolytics, such as retinoids, may improve TAF by exfoliating the stratum corneum.1,5 Given this patient’s presentation, the differential diagnosis included acne mechanica, basaloid follicular hamartoma (BFH), and lichen simplex chronicus (LSC). Acne mechanica is a subtype of acne induced by repetitive friction or pressure. It primarily affects adolescents and young adults and has been linked to athletic equipment, tight clothing, and prolonged surface contact (eg, long-distance driving).6Clinically, it resembles acne vulgaris, presenting with inflammatory papules, pustules, nodules, cysts, and open comedones localized to areas of mechanical stress.6Histopathologic features include hyperkeratosis overlying an irregularly contoured epidermis with acanthosis, elongation of the rete ridges, and focal thinning of the suprapapillary plates.6The dermis shows a moderately dense, polymorphous inflammatory infiltrate, diffusely distributed and extending in a bandlike pattern to the dermoepidermal junction.6Although both acne mechanica and TAF arise from chronic friction, the absence of inflammatory papules, pustules, or comedones, together with histologic findings of dilated follicular openings filled with keratinous debris and a sparse superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, supports a diagnosis of TAF.1,6 BFH is a benign hair follicle neoplasm with multiple clinical variants; however, it typically presents as multiple 1-mm to 2-mm tan-to-brown papules on the face, scalp, neck, axilla, trunk, or pubic region.7,8When occurring on the face, it can resemble the papular eruption in this patient. If BFH is suspected, a biopsy is needed to distinguish it from basal cell carcinoma or other malignant epithelial neoplasms, preventing unnecessary surgical interventions for benign lesions.7-9Histologically, BFH is characterized by anastomosing strands and cords of basaloid cells confined to hair follicles, with hyperchromatic nuclei, sparse cytoplasm, and minimal mitotic figures.7,8In this case, a history of chronic friction, the presence of dilated follicles, and the absence of basaloid cell proliferation favor TAF over BFH. LSC presents as a well-demarcated, lichenified, scaly plaque resulting from repeated scratching or rubbing.10LSC most commonly involves the head, neck, arms, scalp, and genitals but can develop anywhere within hand’s reach, as it is self-induced.10Histopathologic findings include hyperkeratosis with focal parakeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis, elongation and irregular thickening of epidermal rete ridges, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, and papillary dermal fibrosis. Mild spongiosis and a superficial dermal infiltrate composed of histiocytes, lymphocytes, and occasional eosinophils are also observed.10Although both TAF and LSC result from chronic friction, the presence of closely grouped papules on a background of hyperpigmentation is more consistent with TAF.1,2Dilated follicular openings filled with keratin debris further support TAF over LSC.3 Due to its rarity and overlapping features with other follicular keratotic conditions, TAF is often underrecognized, leading to misdiagnosis and suboptimal management.1,2Greater clinical awareness and early recognition can improve diagnostic accuracy and prevent unnecessary interventions.

caption: A, Edematous, violaceous plaques on the forearms are shown. B, High-power magnification shows a dense upper to mid-dermal neutrophilic infiltrate admixed with vacuolated spherical structures.
scenario: A man in his 60s admitted for fluid overload was referred to the dermatology department for an acute eruption of painful rashes affecting his forehead, upper back, forearms, and dorsum hands. He had end-stage kidney failure, and at time of rash onset, he had not initiated dialysis. On examination, he had edematous violaceous papules and plaques on his forehead, forearms, and dorsal hands (Figure 1A). Prior to the eruption, he had received a computed tomography scan 3 days previously with 50 mL of iodinated contrast. A skin biopsy was performed from a violaceous plaque of the forearm (Figure 1B). Further diagnostic testing was performed to ascertain the diagnosis.
explanation: Histopathology revealed a diffuse interstitial dermal infiltrate of predominantly neutrophils admixed with occasional eosinophils with areas of upper dermal necrosis and hemorrhage. There were numerous round structures within the infiltrate each with a basophilic body surrounded by a clear space or halo resembling cryptococcus. Yet, results of Gömöri methenamine silver and periodic acid–Schiff stains were negative for fungal elements. Tissue sent for bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast bacilli cultures returned negative. Laboratory results revealed an elevated serum iodine level of 7392 µg/L (to convert to nmol/L, multiply by 7.88; reference range, 40-92 µg/L) and an elevated urinary iodine of 29 222 µg/L (reference range, 100-199 µg/L). These remained markedly high despite being sent off 2 weeks from the onset of rashes. Clinicopathological correlation was consistent with the diagnosis of acute iododerma. Complete resolution of skin lesions was achieved with the initiation of oral corticosteroids at 0.3 mg/kg/d tapered over 6 weeks. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodide-containing compounds including oral and intravenous iodinated contrast agents, amiodarone and potassium iodide, often in the setting of established risk factors. A major risk factor is impaired kidney function with the body’s relative inability to clear accumulated serum iodine.1Another risk factor is use of hydralazine2and topical and oral medications containing iodine, such as potassium iodide and amiodarone.3To support the diagnosis of iododerma, elevated serum and urinary iodine levels are essential. The normal half-life of iodine in a patient with normal creatinine clearance is 90 to 120 minutes, and high concentrations of iodine in the serum or urine beyond 2 days is pathological. Elevated levels can be detected in the order of weeks in patients with renal insufficiency.4 Lesions in iododerma often evolve rapidly, with a polymorphous appearance including vesicobullae, pustules, violaceous plaques, and vegetative lesions. It preferentially affects areas with high sebaceous activity, such as the face and upper trunk.5If left untreated, lesions can be disfiguring. The pathogenesis of iododerma remains unclear. An immunologic response is suggested in that iodides combine with serum proteins to incite a cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction.6Iododerma is not entirely benign as it can engender life-threatening complications including arrhythmias and pulmonary edema. Histopathological features of iododerma vary at different stages of evolution, with acute forms showing intense dermal neutrophilia and chronic stages exhibiting pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, epidermal microabscesses, and granulomas. An entity known as cryptococcoid neutrophilic dermatosis was first described in 2013, where skin biopsies showed numerous neutrophils in association with spherical vacuolated structures resembling cryptococcal yeast forms but were eventually proven not to be fungal elements,7like in the present case. Furthermore, clinical features of cryptococcosis include umbilicated papules, pustules, and ulcerovegetative plaques, which is different from the present case. Hence, cryptococcosis is the wrong diagnosis. On electron microscopy, the vacuolated structures represent apoptotic degenerate cells, likely neutrophils undergoing autolysis. With no underlying cause found, these were labeled as cryptococcoid Sweet syndrome until reports confirmed the presence of high levels of serum and/or urine iodine in some cases, establishing this histopathological entity as a unique manifestation of iododerma.2,5A case series relooked at reported cases of so-called cryptococcoid Sweet syndrome and found similar, if not identical, clinical and histopathological features to cryptococcoid iododerma.5In most cases, risk factors for iododerma were present, but iodine testing was not performed. It is probable that many cases of cryptococcoid Sweet syndrome in the literature were, in fact, cryptococcoid iododerma. Elevated urine and iodine levels in the present case makes Sweet syndrome the wrong diagnosis. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is inconsistently described in iododerma.2Distinctly, it presents with palpable petechiae and purpura on lower extremities. In this patient’s biopsy, fibrin exudation was seen around small vessels that were within areas of dermal necrosis, but these lacked features of a true leukocytoclastic vasculitis (Figure 2). It is probable that the vasculopathic changes and fibrin leakage seen in iododerma may be a response to the direct effects of iodine toxicity or neutrophilic cytokine release on vessel walls. Hence, leukocytoclastic vasculitis is the wrong diagnosis. This case demonstrates that cryptococcoid neutrophilic dermatosis should be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma, prompting the clinician to look for underlying iodine toxicity. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove exposure to iodinated agents and address risk factors. To treat the lesions, systemic corticosteroids and cyclosporine have been tried with success.

caption: A, Clinical image of the anterior trunk showing skin-colored papules, many with an umbilicated appearance and waterdrop or rose-petal papule morphology. B, Histopathological image showing absence of elastic fibers in the papillary dermis.
scenario: A teenage girl with atopic dermatitis presented with asymptomatic, skin-colored papules on her abdomen. She and her mother reported the appearance of multiple lesions on her chest and abdomen 2 months prior. Photographs from that time showed lesions compatible with molluscum contagiosum (MC), but the patient and her mother had not consulted her pediatrician or dermatologist. Clinical evaluation revealed nonfollicular skin-colored papules. Some of them had a central depression resembling umbilicated lesions, while others were flat (Figure 1A). A skin biopsy specimen was taken (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathological examination revealed fibrosis and vascular proliferation in the papillary dermis. Results of Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining demonstrated an absence of elastic fibers in the papillary dermis, whereas they were preserved in the remainder of the sample. No remnants of MC lesions were observed (Figure 1B). Dermoscopy results showed white circles with a central brown, structureless area, where no atypical vessels were observed (Figure 2). These findings, along with the history of possible MC infection in an adolescent patient with atopic dermatitis, suggest a diagnosis of secondary anetoderma due to MC. After 2 years of follow-up, the lesions showed no clinical improvement, and aesthetic treatment with laser therapy was recommended. The term anetoderma is derived from the Greek wordsanetos, meaning slack, andderma, for skin. Anetoderma is a benign condition included within the group of elastolytic skin disorders. Primary anetoderma arises in previously normal skin, while the secondary subtype develops at the site of previous skin lesions. However, some authors have classified anetoderma into 5 different subtypes, including primary anetoderma (associated with diseases of autoimmunity), secondary anetoderma from a preceding dermatosis (inflammatory, infectious, and traumatic, among others), drug-induced anetoderma, familial anetoderma, and prematurity-associated anetoderma.1 Anetoderma after MC infection is a rare complication. Four cases of clinically secondary anetoderma due to MC infection2-4and 1 case of histological anetoderma in a focal MC lesion have been described.5It has been suggested that complement-mediated recruitment of macrophages could be responsible for lysosomal enzyme release of elastases causing anetoderma.2,5 Monteagudo et al2reported a similar case of secondary anetoderma due to MC. Lesions were described as skin-colored areas with herniation of subcutaneous tissue. Dermoscopy findings were light erythema and wobbled lesions. We believe that MC lesions self-resolve and induce focal secondary anetoderma in the papillary dermis. Larger MC lesions leave pedunculated papules with a waterdrop or rose-petal morphology (Figure 1A), corresponding to the “wobble-sign” lesions described by Monteagudo et al.2On the other hand, smaller MC lesions may resolve as white macules or thin papules (Figure 1A). Dermoscopy findings of the latter (Figure 2) may be confused with lichen nitidus lesions.6-8In both cases, white circles with central brown, structureless areas would be observed.7,8 Histopathologically, lichen nitidus exhibits clustered lymphocytes and histiocytes in the papillary dermis, demarcated laterally by down-growing rete. Miliaria crystallina is due to an intraepidermal eccrine sweat duct obstruction. Histopathologically, mpox infection shows mixed inflammatory infiltrates with eosinophilic, ballooning degeneration of keratinocytes; multinucleated keratinocytes may also be observed.9

caption: A, Red-brown plaques without secondary change were scattered on the chest and abdomen. White patches with focally retained follicular pigment were also noted on the trunk. B, A square biopsy reveals thickened collagen bundles, increased spindle cells, loss of follicular units, and superficial displacement of eccrine glands with absent perieccrine adiposity.
scenario: A man in his 60s with anti-RNA polymerase 3–positive diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) diagnosed 1 year prior, presented with a 6-month history of lesions on the abdomen. Physical examination demonstrated red-brown, ovoid, smooth hypertrophic plaques on the upper and lower abdomen (Figure 1A), in addition to confluent sclerosis involving the bilateral fingers and hands with proximal extension to involve the upper extremities. The abdominal lesions were asymptomatic, and he had not applied any topical treatments to the affected skin. He denied any preceding trauma or acne. Despite ongoing treatment with oral mycophenolate sodium, 720 mg, twice daily, and subcutaneous tocilizumab, 162 mg, weekly, his cutaneous sclerosis had continued to progress. A punch biopsy of an abdominal plaque was obtained to guide the diagnosis and management of the new lesions (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathology demonstrated a square-shaped biopsy specimen with an unremarkable epidermis. An increased population of interstitial spindle cells in the superficial dermis was noted, which decreased in density as the collagen bundles became more noticeably thickened in a descending pattern (Figure 2). There was also superficial displacement of eccrine glands with loss of perieccrine fat. A significant inflammatory infiltrate was absent, but rare perieccrine plasma cells were identified. Verhoeff–Van Gieson stain showed a normal density of elastic fibers. CD34 demonstrated complete loss of dermal dendritic cells within the spindled infiltrate. SMA showed focal and patchy expression. Based on the clinical presentation and histological findings, nodular (keloidal) morphea in the setting of dcSSC was diagnosed. The patient was continued on his systemic immunomodulatory treatment with mycophenolate and tocilizumab. He was recommended to initiate UVA-1 phototherapy, but due to issues with insurance coverage, he was unable to do so. The patient started a topical regimen alternating calcipotriene, 0.005%, cream and clobetasol, 0.05%, to the hands, which stabilized sclerosis progression at this site. Treatment was deferred for the abdominal plaques given the asymptomatic nature. Nodular morphea is a rare variant of localized scleroderma, first described by Thomas Addison in the 1800s as an “untrue keloid.”1It presents as firm, indurated plaques or nodules, often mimicking granulomatous, inflammatory, and neoplastic cutaneous conditions, such as sarcoidosis, hypertrophic scars and keloids, and smooth muscle tumors.2Although the origin of nodular morphea remains unknown, the pathogenesis is related to excessive fibroblast activation and collagen deposition.3The classification of nodular morphea as a distinct entity remains debated. While some consider it a variant of localized scleroderma, many case reports involve patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc), often with concurrent visceral involvement.4Similar to this patient, the lesions associated with nodular morphea typically appear within the first 6 months following a diagnosis of SSc, during the active disease phase.5,6However, in some instances, nodular morphea may precede other signs and symptoms of SSc, and may potentially serve as a harbinger of systemic disease.6 Given the nonspecific presentation of nodular morphea, thorough clinical history and histopathology are critical for accurate diagnosis. Nodular morphea often resembles hypertrophic scar both clinically and histologically, making accurate diagnosis challenging. Clinically, a history of trauma should be present in hypertrophic scar and absent in morphea. However, nodular morphea may closely mimic a hypertrophic scar due to nodular fibrosis and increased cellularity that is not typically observed in other variants of morphea.3On immunohistochemistry, while hypertrophic scars may also demonstrate loss of CD34 and focal SMA expression, they also demonstrate elastolysis, which was not present in this patient’s results. In this patient, the biopsy revealed diminished adnexal structures, superficial displacement of eccrine glands with perieccrine fat pad loss, and hypercellularity more prominent in the upper dermis. While there was not a significant lymphocytic infiltrate, the overall findings and history support the diagnosis of nodular morphea as opposed to hypertrophic scar.7 Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma presents with multiple cutaneous leiomyomas (CLMs), which typically appear as smooth pink papules and plaques that may resemble nodular morphea. However, CLMs are characteristically painful and may occur concurrently with uterine leiomyomas and renal cell carcinoma.8Histopathologic examination of CLMs additionally revealed disorganized clusters of smooth muscle cells with positive immunohistochemical staining for smooth muscle markers. While dermatomyofibroma and nodular morphea may have overlapping clinical and histological features, dermatomyofibroma usually spares the adnexal structures. In this patient, the spindle cells and thickened collagen have replaced normal follicular units.9,10 Treatment is not standardized owing to the rarity of nodular morphea. Topical corticosteroids and immunomodulators are often used, and UVA-1 phototherapy may be beneficial in some patients.2In this patient, additional treatments were deferred as he was asymptomatic, already on systemic therapy for dcSSc, and UVA-1 phototherapy was not feasible. Further research is needed to clarify the pathogenesis and optimal management strategy of nodular morphea, both in patients with and without underlying SSc. Distinguishing this entity from its clinical mimickers is essential to reduce unnecessary interventions and initiate effective treatments.

caption: A, Hundreds of reddish-brown 2- to 5-mm flat-topped papules are scattered on the patient’s bilateral lower extremities and dorsal feet with great toenail dystrophy. B, Histopathological imaging shows basketweave hyperkeratosis overlying areas of acanthosis and epidermal thinning and sparse lymphohistiocytic perivascular dermatitis with subepidermal separation and dermal fibrosis (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
scenario: A woman in her 40s presented to our immunobullous disease clinic with a 30-year history of an intensely pruritic eruption predominantly affecting her legs, forearms, and hands. She also reported a nearly lifelong tendency for skin sloughing with minimal trauma but denied mucosal or nail involvement. Previous treatments, including topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, and oral antihistamines, had been ineffective. Her family history was unknown. Results of prior biopsies at an outside institution showed perivascular and focal lichenoid lymphohistiocytic inflammation with milia and a subepidermal separation, suggesting possible epidermolysis bullosa acquisita vs artifactual separation. Physical examination was notable for hundreds of brown to violaceous scaly, lichenoid papules on the anterior lower legs, dorsal feet (Figure, A) and dorsal forearms, some with a linear configuration, with a few scattered lesions on the upper and lower back. Her great toenails and 2 others were dystrophic, but all other nails appeared normal. No blisters were present, and the remaining examination results were otherwise unremarkable. A biopsy for direct immunofluorescence was taken; a repeat biopsy for hematoxylin-eosin staining was performed; and serum was obtained for collagen type 7 antibody assay and genetic testing to rule out epidermolysis bullosa.
explanation: Repeat hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed sparse perivascular to focally lichenoid dermatitis with subepidermal separation and dermal fibrosis without vacuolar change or eosinophilic infiltration (Figure, B). Areas of acanthosis, orthohyperkeratosis, and epidermal thinning were present. Direct immunofluorescence showed no linear deposition of immunoreactants at the basement membrane zone, and the result of the type 7 collagen enzyme-linked immunoabsorbent assay was negative. Genetic testing identified heterozygosity in theCOL7A1gene for a sequence variant,c.7247G>T, confirming the diagnosis of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB). In the setting of lichenified papules on the patient’s extremities, severe refractory pruritus, skin fragility, and subepidermal split on hematoxylin-eosin staining, a diagnosis of DEB, pruriginosa subtype (DEB-P), was supported. Gabapentin provided partial relief, and addition of dupilumab resulted in significant symptomatic improvement. DEB results from various genetic variants encoding type 7 collagen, a major component of anchoring fibrils essential for adhesion along the dermo-epidermal junction. DEB-P is a rare subtype described in 1994, with a variety of genetic variants ofCOL7A1, including the specific variant present in this patient.1,2DEB-P is often autosomal dominant, but autosomal recessive and sporadic cases have been reported.2Patients often lack blistering and instead show markedly pruritic papules commonly on lower legs. Pathology typically shows orthohyperkeratosis and acanthosis with perivascular mononuclear infiltration, in addition to a subepidermal separation as noted in this patient.1However, more brisk infiltrates, including eosinophils, have been observed.3Milia and fibrosis may also be present. Diagnosis is made with a combination of consistent clinical features, pathology, family history, genetic testing, and/or immunofluorescence mapping. In this patient, we initially considered lichen planus, lichen amyloidosis, and prurigo nodularis as differential diagnoses. Absence of dense lichenoid inflammation, vacuolar change, sawtooth rete ridges, and lack of colloid bodies opposed a diagnosis of lichen planus, as did the decades-long duration of her disease.4There was no significant amyloid deposition to support lichen amyloidosis.5The repeat biopsy showed a convincing subepidermal separation, which did not support simple prurigo nodularis. This separation is seen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita along with the sparse inflammatory infiltrate, but the direct immunofluorescence, serum examination, and lack of blistering clinically did not support this diagnosis.6The pauci-inflammatory infiltrate and subepidermal separation were consistent with epidermolysis bullosa, and genetic testing confirmed a diagnosis of DEB. In conjunction with the clinical findings, this patient's presentation is consistent with DEB-P. Although pruritus is a common symptom in all forms of epidermolysis bullosa, those with DEB-P have particularly severe itching.2This is associated with the distinctive clinical presentation: extensive scaling, papulonodules coalescing into plaques primarily found on lower legs, often with a linear configuration, resembling lichen amyloidosis or lichen planus, thus leading to diagnostic confusion.7The skin is mostly spared elsewhere. Intact blisters are rarely seen, but scarring, milia, and nail dystrophy can be present.3Onset may be at birth but can be delayed by several decades, adding to the potential for misdiagnosis.3,7 The basis for the intense pruritus is unclear, but dysregulation of cytokine pathways, particularly those related to Th1, Th2, and Th17, an impaired skin barrier, inflammation associated with wound healing, and abnormal epidermal sensory nerve activation have been implicated in the pathogenesis.2Treatment for the pruritus associated with DEB-P typically includes antihistamines, neuropathic agents, topical steroids, and adequate wound care, but these may not be sufficient. Cyclosporine and thalidomide have been used successfully.8There are several recent reports of dupilumab being highly effective, as with this patient, supporting a Th2-mediated process.9,10This case report highlights a rare form of DEB, which has a largely nonblistering, papulonodular presentation, making the diagnosis challenging, and reminds us that sometimes genetic diseases may not be diagnosed until adulthood.

caption: Diffuse, blanchable, reticulated telangiectatic macules located on the left inner thigh.
scenario: A man in his 60s with a medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and coronary artery disease presented with multiple asymptomatic purpuric macules that had been persistent for more than 2 decades. The lesions began on the bilateral lower legs and extended to the inner thighs, with recent extension to the forearms. The lesions worsened with prolonged standing and were occasionally accompanied by mild itching. On examination, there were symmetrical diffuse, blanchable, reticulated telangiectatic macules covering the legs (Figure 1) and forearms. The patient had no involvement of mucosal surfaces or nails, no positive family history of telangiectasias, and no clinical signs of systemic disease or bleeding diathesis. Dermoscopy revealed prominent fine telangiectasias, which was blanchable on pressure (Video).
explanation: Skin biopsy over the left lower leg revealed dilated small vessels in the upper dermis, along with amorphous concentric pink hyaline material deposited within the vessel walls, which had positive findings on periodic acid–Schiff staining but negative findings on Congo red staining (Figure 2). No signs of vasculitis or fibrin thrombi were seen. In the absence of systemic symptoms or involvement, observation was recommended, and the lesions remained stable at 3-month follow-up. Cutaneous collagenous vasculopathy (CCV) is a rare primary cutaneous microangiopathy that affects the superficial dermal blood vessels. It typically presents as asymptomatic telangiectasias or petechiae, primarily on the lower limbs, with a tendency to spread cephalically.1CCV occurs in middle-aged to older individuals with a nearly equal distribution between men and women, although it can also affect pediatric, middle-aged, and older patients.2Histologic features help distinguish CCV from similar clinical conditions. Typical CCV pathology shows dilated capillaries in the papillary and reticular dermis, along with perivascular deposits of hyaline material, which can be observed with periodic acid–Schiff staining. Pathogenesis suggests a pauci-inflammatory injury to endothelial cells caused by unknown angiogenic factors, leading to local intravascular fibrin thrombi.3Fibrin subsequently leaks and incorporates into the vessel walls, ultimately resulting in reparative perivascular fibrosis.3 Primary telangiectasias refer to idiopathic capillary dilation, which shares some clinical features with CCV. Both CCV and generalized essential telangiectasia present with the appearance of multiple symmetrical telangiectasias on the lower limbs, which gradually extend to the rest of the body. These conditions do not involve the mucosa or nail beds, and there are no preexisting lesions or associated systemic diseases, making clinical differentiation challenging.4However, histopathological examination of generalized essential telangiectasia typically demonstrate mild ectasia of thin-walled capillaries in the papillary dermis, without eosinophilic hyaline material within the vascular wall.5Schamberg disease predominantly affects men of any age, presenting as asymptomatic brownish macules and nonblanchable purpura or petechiae primarily located on the lower extremities with a characteristic cayenne pepper–speckling appearance.6Dermoscopy typically reveals red dots and red globules within a coppery brown background.7Histopathological findings of Schamberg disease include perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, reactive endothelial changes, extravasated red blood cells, and prominent hemosiderin-laden macrophages, which can be identified with an iron stain.8Venous insufficiency and chronic alcohol consumption appear to be related to the development of Schamberg disease.8Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is an autosomal-dominant disease characterized by the presence of multiple arteriovenous malformations, commonly found on the hands, face, ears, lips, tongue, and inside the mouth. These lesions are often absent during childhood and typically increase with age, with the most common clinical manifestation being spontaneous and recurrent epistaxis.9Unlike CCV, individuals with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia exhibit mucosal and visceral involvement, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract and lungs, along with a family history of similar telangiectatic processes or abnormal bleeding.9Histology reveals dilated small vascular channels in the affected organs.9Since extracutaneous involvement is extremely rare, the management of CCV currently focuses on local treatment due to cosmetic concerns, with pulsed dye laser therapy being the most effective approach.10 In conclusion, CCV has characteristic clinical and histopathological findings. Blanchable telangiectasias have perivascular hyaline deposits. The typical microscopic appearance can help distinguish CCV from clinical mimics.

caption: A, Clinical image showing vesicular and papular lesions on the vulva and thighs. B, Multiple dilated lymphatic channels containing proteinaceous fluid in the superficial dermis, lined by a flat endothelium.
scenario: A woman in her 60s presented with a 2-year history of painful pink vesicular and papular lesions on the vulva and thighs. The patient had undergone hysterectomy, adnexectomy, and concurrent chemoradiotherapy for cervical cancer 8 years prior to the visit. She had a 7-year history of hypertension but no sexually transmitted infections or other systemic diseases. Physical examination revealed scattered or clustered pink translucent vesicles and papules in the bilateral labia majora and inner thigh (Figure 1A). The lesions were soft to moderately firm in texture and contained clear fluid. No enlargement of the inguinal lymph nodes was detected on palpation. Results of pelvic magnetic resonance imaging and abdominal computed tomography revealed no abnormalities. A histopathological biopsy was performed (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathological examination revealed multiple dilated lymphatic channels containing proteinaceous fluid in the superficial dermis, lined by a flat endothelium (Figure 1B). Immunohistochemical staining was positive for D2-40 in endothelial cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of acquired vulvar lymphangioma (AVL) was made. AVL, also known as acquired lymphangiectasia of the vulva, is a rare, benign condition associated with architectural disruption, obstruction, and further dilation of previously normal lymphatic channels. It can occur secondary to cancers, trauma, radiotherapy, surgery, infections, and inflammatory diseases.1,2Cervical carcinoma, especially cervical squamous cell carcinoma, is the most common AVL-associated cancer.3Clinically, AVL presents as skin-colored papules or translucent, reddish vesicles, which may be scattered or clustered in a frog-spawn pattern on the vulvar region. Lesions may be asymptomatic or associated with pruritus, burning sensations, serous fluid leakage, or secondary infections. Histopathologically, AVL is characterized by dilated lymphatic channels lined with flat endothelial cells. Additional features include varying degrees of papillomatous changes in the epidermis, hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and erosion. Immunohistochemistry staining with lymphatic markers such as D2-40 can help to confirm the nature of the vessels as being of lymphatic origin.4Treatment is challenging because of the high recurrence rate, with an overall recurrence rate of approximately 43% after initial treatment.1Surgical excision is the most common treatment, with postsurgical recurrence rates of 23.1% to 25%; complete excision of skin, including lymphatic cisterns in subcutaneous tissue, may prevent recurrence.5,6Other treatments include sclerotherapy, laser therapy, cryotherapy, electrocautery, radiotherapy, or photodynamic therapy.2The present patient was referred to the gynecology department for surgical resection of the vulvar lesions; however, the procedure was postponed due to the sudden onset of acute lower extremity lymphangitis. Although the condition improved after anti-inflammatory therapy, the patient refused further treatment and was lost to follow-up. Differential diagnoses in the present case include syringoma, molluscum contagiosum, and condyloma acuminatum. Molluscum contagiosum, caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus, is clinically characterized by asymptomatic, small, shiny, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication. Large cells with granular, eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic molluscum bodies are a typical histopathological feature.7Vulvar syringomas are benign adnexal tumors typically characterized by multiple small, firm, skin-colored to light brown papules scattered on the labia majora. These lesions are usually asymptomatic or present with pruritus or pain. Histopathological examination reveals nests of eccrine ducts and tadpolelike structures embedded in fibrous stroma.8Condylomata acuminata, or genital warts, is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by the human papillomavirus. Lesions may manifest in various forms, including smooth, flat, keratotic papules or exophytic cauliflowerlike masses. Koilocytic change is a helpful histopathological feature of condylomata acuminata and serves as a critical clue for differential diagnosis.9 This patient’s presentation illustrates findings typical of AVL, an uncommon complication from patients with a history of cervical cancer, radiation therapy, or surgical intervention. AVL should be considered in the differential diagnosis when papular or vesicular lesions develop in the vulvar region.

caption: A, Clinical image of yellow-brown plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet, with prominent scale and a healing biopsy site on the right great toe. Plaques are centered on the interphalangeal joint, potentially an area of high friction.
