B, Histopathologic examination showed large cells with small, round, dark blue central nuclei and abundant light pink cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis.
scenario: A man in his 30s presented with an approximately 6-month history of asymptomatic plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet. He had no relevant medical history or any known inciting factors. Physical examination demonstrated thick yellow to brown plaques overlying the interphalangeal joints of both first digits of the feet (Figure, A). A combination of urea cream, 20%, and clobetasol ointment, 0.05%, applied twice daily to the affected area for approximately 4 weeks yielded no improvement. At a follow-up visit, a tangential shave biopsy specimen was taken from the right dorsal first digit toe (Figure, B).
explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.

caption: A, Erythematous, indurated plaques and erosions on right anterior thigh. B, Interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, mild papillary dermal edema, and a lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate around adnexal structures and vessels in both the superficial and deep dermis. Overt panniculitis was absent.
scenario: A woman in her 40s with a medical history of complex regional pain syndrome presented to the dermatology department for evaluation of a pruritic recurrent rash on her right anterior thigh that started 1 month prior. She had used ice packs to relieve her symptoms. Examination was notable for numerous indurated red nodules and plaques, with erosions over the right anterior thigh (Figure 1A). She reported no similar lesions elsewhere on her body and denied any constitutional symptoms. A skin biopsy was performed from her right thigh (Figure 1B).
explanation: Hematoxylin-eosin staining demonstrated interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, predominantly located at the basal layer of epidermis. Mild papillary dermal edema and brisk periadnexal and perivascular lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate in the superficial and deep dermis were noted. Rare vessels in the subcutis showed perivascular inflammation, but no overt panniculitis was seen. Increased dermal mucin was observed with Alcian blue stain (Figure 2). CD123 results highlighted occasional small clusters of plasmacytoid dendritic cells in the superficial and deep dermis. The patient admitted to daily application of hot/cold patches across her body, as well as the daily use of ice packs specifically on the affected area. This with the histopathological findings confirmed the diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. Ice-pack dermatosis is an uncommon condition cataloged under cold-induced dermatoses. Most cases reported in the literature involve patients with chronic pain who use ice packs for therapeutic purposes, potentially leading to vasoconstriction and reduced perfusion in areas where lesions develop. The typical presentation includes painful erythematous purpuric papules and plaques with ulceration on the lower back or buttocks.1,2Histopathological examination is challenging, as it shares similarities with cold panniculitis, perniosis, and cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE).3Treatment consists of avoidance of ice-pack use. The clinical picture of the present patient could be similar to that of lupus erythematosus panniculitis in that it manifests as tender erythematous subcutaneous indurated nodules or plaques. However, it can affect the face, arms, buttocks, and thighs, and this patient only had lesions on her right thigh.4,5Common histopathological findings between CLE and ice-pack dermatosis include perivascular and perieccrine infiltrates, increased dermal mucin, and vacuolar interface changes with necrotic keratinocytes. CLE typically exhibits larger clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells. In contrast, the present patient also had small clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells, consistent with findings of the ice-pack dermatosis case series reported by West et al.3 Cold panniculitis and perniosis are the most prevalent cold-induced dermatologic disorders. Cold panniculitis manifests as indurated and erythematous nodules and plaques at sites exposed to cold and wet conditions. While it is more frequent in infants, adult cases affecting the thighs of equestrians and cold-therapy device users have been documented.6Cold panniculitis is characterized by lobular panniculitis, predominantly composed of lymphocytes. Neutrophilic infiltrates or granulomas may be present. Typically, the dermis shows a deep perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, and inflammation is most intense at the dermal-subcutaneous junction. Fat necrosis with foamy macrophages is evident.3,7Even though the present patient had a lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate in the deep dermis, there was no overt panniculitis. Moreover, an important difference between ice-pack dermatosis and cold panniculitis is that the latter lacks vacuolar change as well as papillary dermal edema.7 Acquired cold urticaria (ACU) is one of the most frequent forms of physical urticaria, predominantly affecting young adults. It can be idiopathic or secondary to various conditions such as infections, cryoglobulinemias, or cancers. Clinical manifestations of ACU vary from localized skin reactions triggered by cold stimuli to systemic reactions that may progress to anaphylaxis. Patients typically present with pruritic erythematous wheals in areas exposed to cold air, liquids, or objects; lesions appear 5 to 30 minutes after exposure and can last around 30 minutes.8This differs from the current case and cases of ice-pack dermatosis reported in the literature, which describe a more gradual onset and a duration of weeks to months.1-3,9 Histologically, ACU is characterized by mast cell degranulation and perivascular infiltrates, including neutrophils, eosinophils, erythrocytes, monocytes, and fibrin deposition.8ACU could be distinguished from ice-pack dermatosis through a screening cold stimulation test, which involves applying a localized cold object, usually an ice cube, to an unaffected area of the skin for 5 minutes, eliciting a wheal and flare response within 10 minutes that would favor ACU and rule out ice-pack dermatosis.8,10 This case highlights the importance of obtaining a thorough medical history and clinicopathologic correlation in making a diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. The histologic features of this condition can overlap with those of cold panniculitis, perniosis, and lupus erythematosus.

caption: A, Clinical image of a slightly sunken red plaque on the chest. B, Histopathology reveals significant proliferation of spindle cells in the superficial to mid-dermis, arranged in a bandlike distribution (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×100).
scenario: A 6-year-old girl presented to an outpatient clinic with a history of a red plaque on her chest for over 4 years. Her parents first noticed the asymptomatic, round red lesion, approximately 3 mm in diameter, when she was 2 years old. The lesion had well-defined borders, a smooth surface, and visible dilated blood vessels. She was evaluated at a local hospital at the time, diagnosed with a birthmark, and no treatment was administered. However, the lesion gradually enlarged and became slightly sunken. The girl was conceived through in vitro fertilization and was vaginally delivered at term. She had no other significant medical or family history. Upon physical examination, a slightly sunken red plaque was observed on the chest, approximately 1.5 cm in diameter, with a smooth surface, associated vascular dilation, well-defined borders, and no scaling or ulceration (Figure 1A). A skin biopsy was performed from the edge of the plaque.
explanation: D. Plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma The pathological results indicated that the epidermis was generally normal, with significant proliferation of spindle cells in the superficial to mid-dermis, arranged in a bandlike distribution, without significant mitotic figures or cellular atypia. Additionally, there was considerable vascular proliferation in the stroma (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed strong positivity for CD34, scattered positivity for S100, and Ki67 positivity of less than 2%, while P63, desmin, and SMA were negative. Further fluorescence in situ hybridization testing was performed, yielding negative results for theCOL1A1/PDGFBfusion gene. Thus, the patient was ultimately diagnosed with plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma (PDF) (Figure 2). Given that this condition is a benign skin tumor, we proceeded a standard excision for the patient, as opposed to wide local excision. PDF, also referred to as medallion-like dermal dendrocyte hamartoma, is a rare benign skin tumor. It was first reported by Rodríguez-Jurado et al1in 2004, describing this congenital, mildly atrophic reddish-brown lesion in 3 girls. The pathogenesis of PDF remains unclear and may be related to postzygotic mutation leading to cutaneous mosaicism.2Clinically, the typical presentation is a reddish or brown, round or oval plaque, approximately the size of a coin or larger, with slight atrophy or sclerosis; although rare presentations include skin-colored papules3or subcutaneous nodules.4 Histopathologically, PDF is characterized by bandlike infiltration of spindle fibroblasts in the superficial and mid-dermis, surrounded by dense collagen fibers, with fragmented or reduced elastic fibers. The lesion is rich in blood vessels and may occasionally extend into the subcutaneous fat. Immunohistochemical staining reveals strong CD34 positivity, with some tumor cells also co-expressing factor XIIIa. The differential diagnosis includes spindle cell tumors, particularly lipofibromatosis-like neural tumor (LPF-NT), fibroblastic connective tissue nevus, and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP). LPF-NT is a rare soft tissue tumor that primarily occurs in children and young adults. Histologically, it is typically characterized by infiltrative proliferation of spindle cells within subcutis.5Recently, a dermal subtype has been reported, which mainly involves the entire dermis with minimal involvement of the subcutaneous tissue.6The proliferative cells in LPF-NT are positive for CD34, S100, and NTRK1, which aids in distinguishing it from PDF. Fibroblastic connective tissue nevus is a benign skin mesenchymal tumor belonging to the connective tissue nevus spectrum, characterized by solitary, ill-defined, slowly growing and painless plaques or nodules and primarily seen in young female individuals younger than 10 years. The distinction lies mainly in the histopathology showing spindle cell proliferation in the deep dermis, arranged in intersecting fascicular patterns. Immunostaining typically shows weak positivity for CD34 and SMA, while desmin and S100 protein are negative.7DFSP is a rare, low-grade malignant soft tissue dermal tumor, which clinically presents as slowly growing skin-colored plaques without significant symptoms, and gradually develops into purple or reddish-brown nodules. It is often overlooked due to its gradual, localized infiltrative growth. There are various clinical and histological subtypes, among which the atrophic type is a rare variant, characterized by slightly atrophic, painless, indurated dark red plaques.8The atrophic variants of DFSP and PDF are very similar in their clinical manifestations, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry. However, DFSP requires wide excision or Mohs micrographic surgery because it is a locally aggressive, low-grade sarcoma with a risk of metastasis (although rare), and complete excision with clear margins is essential to reduce the chance of recurrence. Due to the presence of the chromosomal translocation t (17;22) (q22; q13) in more than 90% of DFSP,9further fluorescence in situ hybridization  analysis is required to detect the presence of the fusion geneCOL1A1/PDGFBto differentiate DFSP from PDF.10 It is important to differentiate PDF from some CD34-positive spindle cell tumors since PDF is a benign tumor that typically does not recur after surgical excision; in this case, the patient has shown no signs of recurrence during follow-up.

caption: Erythematous papule on the medial surface of the right labium minus.
scenario: A woman in her 40s presented with a 20-year history of intermittent tender papules and nodules that were localized to the medial surface of her labia majora and labia minora. Purulent drainage was often reported from the lesions. The lesions were episodic and did not recur in the same locations. Flares occurred with inconsistent frequency, sometimes coinciding with the mid menstrual cycle. She denied lesions occurring on the hair-bearing labia majora or buttocks. Physical examination revealed an erythematous papule on the right medial labium minus (Figure 1) and an erythematous nodule on the left lateral labium minus. Surface swabs of the lesions were obtained for aerobic culture and herpes simplex virus (HSV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR). A 4-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained from the left lateral labium minus for histopathological examination.
explanation: Histology revealed spongiosis with neutrophils in the epidermis, while the dermis showed diffuse neutrophilic infiltration. There was inflammation surrounding sebaceous glands and neutrophils focally noted within the sebaceous gland epithelium. Special stains for infection also yielded negative results. Results of the HSV PCR and aerobic culture were also negative. Given these findings, the patient received a diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis. The patient had undergone numerous treatments before presentation and after a diagnosis was rendered for prophylaxis of flares and short-term management of flares. This included clindamycin, 1%, gel, mupirocin ointment, topical compounded spironolactone, clascoterone cream, and the following oral agents: doxycycline, minocycline, sarecycline, cephalexin, amoxicillin/clavulanate, and spironolactone. She found the minocycline and the amoxicillin/clavulanate to be the most effective oral medications. Mupirocin ointment provided mild relief during flares. Unfortunately, she did not experience improvement while taking spironolactone, 25 mg, daily and was unable to tolerate a higher dose due to hypotension. Due to her history of migraines, her neurologist had advised her not to take combined oral contraceptives. She declined treatment with isotretinoin and drospirenone-only oral contraceptives. Characterized by inflammation of the sebaceous glands of the vulva (Figure 2), vulvar sebaceous adenitis was first reported in 2014.1Other names for this disease entity include genital neutrophilic sebaceous adenitis and vulvar Fordyce adenitis.2,3Occurring in premenopausal adult women, clinical manifestations include recurrent tender papules, pustules, or nodules affecting the labia minora and, less commonly, the medial aspect of the labia majora.1-4Suppuration of lesions and pitted scars have also been described. Vulvar sebaceous adenitis has often been reported to flare during the late luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.1-4Given the timing of exacerbations in many patients, in addition to it affecting women between puberty and menopause, the condition points toward having a hormonal effect. Known treatment options that can be associated with improvement or complete remission of symptoms include antiandrogens and the tetracycline class of antibiotics.1-4The latter is used for its anti-inflammatory properties rather than its antimicrobial effects.1,2In what is to our knowledge the largest cohort published to date,3zinc and isotretinoin additionally showed complete remission for several patients. However, the authors acknowledged that the improvement with oral zinc cannot definitively be attributed to the medication alone.3Although these treatments may be associated with complete remission and improvement for many patients, they also have been reported to have no effect for others.1,3 Histologically, sebaceous adenitis is characterized by dense neutrophilic inflammation that is centered around the sebaceous unit. Infectious studies are negative, and no viral cytopathic change is present. The diagnosis requires clinical correlation. The differential diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis includes hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), HSV, vulvar syringomas, and hidradenoma papilliferum. Histopathological examination and HSV PCR are helpful at narrowing the differential diagnosis. HS clinically presents as recurrent inflamed nodules, abscesses, and fistulae that occur on hair-bearing skin of the axillary, inguinal, inframammary, vulvar, and gluteal regions. HS is diagnosed clinically, and histologic confirmation is typically unnecessary. However, if performed, histology of HS is characterized by follicular hyperkeratosis and subsequent inflammation of apocrine glands.5A key distinguishing clinical feature between HS and vulvar sebaceous adenitis is the anatomical location affected: HS occurs on the hair-bearing aspect of the labia majora, while vulvar sebaceous adenitis occurs on the mucosal surfaces of the labia majora and labia minora. Genital HSV is an infection that typically presents with painful vesicles or erosions on the anogenital area. The virus can remain dormant and shed asymptomatically or recur as outbreaks during the individual’s lifetime. There are numerous ways to test for HSV, with PCR being the standard molecular diagnosis technique. Histology results show vesicle formation with viral cytopathic change, multinucleated giant cells, molding of cells together, and chromatin margination.6 Syringomas are benign adnexal tumors that present as flesh-colored papules. The papules most commonly occur periorbitally, but also rarely occur on the vulva. The lesions may be pruritic or asymptomatic and are thus found incidentally. Vulvar syringomas are diagnosed via skin biopsy specimens, with microscopy revealing sweat ductlike glandular structures.7Symptomatic presentation of tenderness and cyclical patterns are key clinical characteristics that distinguish vulvar sebaceous adenitis from vulvar syringomas.

caption: A, Clinical image of periorbital xanthomas. B, Diffuse lipid-laden foamy histiocytes (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
scenario: A man in his 60s presented to the hospital with fever, joint pain, and second-degree atrioventricular block. His medical history included several years of diffuse xanthomas of the skin, peripheral hypereosinophilia, mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy with pulmonary nodules, bilateral anterior uveitis, avascular necrosis of the wrist, and IgG κ light chain monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. No diagnosis had been identified, and treatments had included corticosteroids and methotrexate. Physical examination revealed diffuse xanthomata most prominent in the periorbital region (Figure 1A) and multiple swollen and tender small joints in the hands and wrists. A 2 × 2-mm biopsy from the right periorbital lesion was obtained. Histopathologic features are shown inFigure 1B. There was no evidence of necrobiosis. Results ofBRAFimmunostaining were negative. κ and λ Stains by in situ hybridization showed rare scattered positively staining plasma cells. Laboratory studies demonstrated an absolute eosinophil count of 3180 cells/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001; reference range, 0-400 cells/μL) and normal lipid panel results; testing results for antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative, and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level was normal. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) showed lucencies in the right parietal bone and fluorodeoxyglucose avidity of the right iliac bone, bone marrow, spleen, cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules, and multiple axillary, thoracic, and pelvic lymph nodes. Biopsies of the bone marrow and a subcarinal lymph node demonstrated aKRASG12D gene alteration.
explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed diffuse infiltration of the dermis by CD68 immunostaining–positive foamy histiocytes (Figure 2). Results of additional immunostaining were positive for CD163 and factor 13a and negative for CD1a and S100 in the lesional cells. The patient had recently started treatment with low-dose cobimetinib, a reverse inhibitor of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) kinase 1 (MEK1) and MEK2 proteins in the MAPK pathway. Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) is a rare, systemic non-Langerhans histiocytic disorder commonly manifesting with multifocal sclerotic long bone lesions with sheets of foamy histiocytes seen on biopsy of osseous and extra-osseous tissues. Since its first description in 1930, approximately 1500 cases have been reported in the literature.1ECD most often affects adults in the fifth decade of life and demonstrates a 3:1 male predominance. Xanthelasma, typically involving the eyelids or periorbital spaces, is among the most frequent cutaneous manifestations of ECD; papulonodular lesions affecting the legs, back, or trunk may also be observed. Cardiac involvement has been reported in 40% to 75% of patients2and may include right atrioventricular sulcus infiltration, pseudotumor, or pericardial disease. Other systemic involvement may include the lungs, kidneys, and central nervous system, though nearly any organ system can be involved. Characteristic histopathological features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei and surrounding fibrosis, multinucleated giant cells, and Touton giant cells, though a variety of features within the xanthogranuloma family can be seen.3ECD histiocytes are positive for CD68, CD163, and factor XIIIa and negative for CD1a, corresponding to non-Langerhans cell type histiocytosis.1Most cutaneous involvement in ECD is nodular and diffuse with foamy histiocytes and, in some cases, shows subtle interstitial-perivascular histiocytic infiltration with variable cytologic features.4Ki-67 levels are typically low in most tissue histiocytes, consistent with a slowly progressive proliferative mechanism. Although sarcoidosis can cause cutaneous lesions that may resemble xanthomas, histopathology typically demonstrates epithelioid rather than foamy histiocytes. Plane xanthomas can be diffuse or limited to specific anatomic locations, such as the eyelids, but more than half of cases are associated with an underlying lipid abnormality, which was absent in this patient; this diagnosis would also not explain the patient’s other clinical findings. Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is a cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis that commonly affects periorbital structures and is typically associated with a paraproteinemia. This patient had a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) but no frank hematologic or other malignant neoplasms, and skin lesions did not show histologic evidence of necrobiosis. ECD has been shown to be caused by activating somatic variants in the MAPK pathway, with most affecting theBRAFgene (specifically,BRAFV600E), while other patients demonstrate variants in theKRAS,NRAS,MAP2K1,ARAF, andMAP3K1genes. Certain phenotypic patterns have been described in association with specific activating variants, such as the skin-orbital–dominantKRAS-mutant non-Langerhans disease phenotype observed in this patient.5﻿KRASvariants can be associated with hematologic malignant neoplasms6; this patient exhibited MGUS and peripheral eosinophilia but did not meet criteria for myeloma or leukemia, and the bony lucencies on PET/CT were attributed to ECD infiltration. The appreciation of somatic variants as the drivers of ECD pathogenesis has greatly enhanced therapeutic options for patients with this rare condition. In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration approved single-agent vemurafenib forBRAFV600E–mutant ECD based on a phase 2 trial that included 22 patients with ECD and demonstrated a 100% overall response rate by fluorodeoxyglucose-PET criteria.7Patients with ECD are now routinely treated with agents that target their specific activating variant, such as BRAF inhibitors and MEK inhibitors. Conventional nontargeted therapies also include anakinra, cladribine, and interferons, and investigations are ongoing into blockade of other cytokines and cellular pathways.8

caption: A, Clinical photograph of a hyperpigmented, indurated plaque on the right forearm, with a postbiopsy round white scar. B, Low-magnification hematoxylin-eosin staining showing a dense infiltrate of spindled tumor cells, some as fascicles extending into the subcutaneous fat (original magnification ×40). A group of pigmented cells is present in one of the fascicles.
scenario: A 12-year-old boy was referred to the dermatology clinic with a nonprogressive hyperpigmented plaque on his right forearm for 5 years. He did not have any other medical conditions. Physical examination revealed a hyperpigmented and indurated plaque on his right forearm (Figure 1A). A punch biopsy was taken for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
explanation: B. Pigmented dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (Bednar tumor) The histopathologic study showed a dense proliferation of monomorphic spindle cells throughout the dermis. The spindle cells extended into the subcutaneous fat in storiform and honeycomb patterns. A group of pigmented cells was present in one of the fascicles extending into the subcutaneous fat (Figure 2). CD34 stained all of the spindle cells. Melan-A, human melanoma black 45 (HMB45), and S100 stained only the pigmented cells. A reverse transcriptase–polymerase chain reaction, which was carried out on complementary DNA extracted from the biopsy’s paraffin block, showed the presence of a t(17;22)(q22;q13) translocation, resulting in a fusion gene between the genesCOL1A1andPDGFB. The diagnosis of pigmented dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP), also known as Bednar tumor, was validated based on the histological, immunohistochemical, and molecular features. Bednar tumor is a distinctive pigmented variant of DFSP.1It constitutes 1% to 5% of all DFSP cases.1The tumor occurs predominantly in early adulthood, although it may also appear in childhood.2The extremities are the most common site. Most tumors present as slow-growing bulging lesions.3Metastasis is rare and late, and dissemination may occur via hematogenous routes, mainly to the lungs.4Histologically, it consists of monomorphic spindle-shaped cells intermingled with melanin-containing cells.5The origin of the tumor cells and the histogenesis have not been fully determined. They are suggested to be derived from neuroectodermal cells, based on ultrastructural and immunohistochemical findings and the presence of melanosome-containing cells.5The lesions appear clinically as colored brown to black due to the pigmented cells. The neoplastic spindle cells display positivity for CD34, while the pigmented cells show positivity for melanocytic markers, such as Melan-A, HMB45, and S100 protein.5On the molecular level, Bednar tumors are also characterized by t(17;22)(q22;q13) translocation, leading to fusion between the genesCOL1A1coding for collagen type I alpha 1 chain andPDGFBcoding for platelet-derived growth factor, B chain (PDGFB), which characterizes DFSP. The fused gene results in overexpression of PDGFB, leading to cellular proliferation and the formation of the tumor.6 The clinical diagnosis of Bednar tumor may be challenging due to its similarity to other pigmented lesions, such as fibrous histiocytoma (dermatofibroma), desmoplastic melanoma, and morphea. Dermatofibroma of the hemosiderotic variant may appear as a hardened pigmented plaque, simulating pigmented DFSP. Pathologically, it is composed of cellular proliferation of spindle and fusiform fibro-histiocytic cells with scattered hemosiderin-laden multinucleated giant cells, rather than melanin-containing cells. The cells stain positively for factor XIII, A chain, but negatively for CD34.7Desmoplastic melanoma is a rare variant of malignant melanoma, appearing as a slowly enlarging area of thickened skin, sometimes described as a scarlike neoplasm, which may be pigmented. Pauci-cellular atypical spindle cells separated by fibro-collagenous stroma within the dermis or subcutaneous fat are typical histopathological features. Often, there is an overlying melanoma in situ of the lentigo maligna type.8Results of S100 and Sox10 stains are usually positive, whereas results of HMB45 and Melan-A stains are mostly negative. Findings of CD34 staining are also negative. Burnt out morphea may appear as pigmented plaque. However, it is not characterized by CD34+spindle cell proliferation and may show lymphocytic infiltrates among sclerotic collagen bundles.9 Complete surgical resection using the Mohs micrographic surgery technique, while ensuring negative margins, is considered the criterion standard for the treatment of DFSP.10Inadequate resections may result in high rates of local recurrence. These rates are shown to decrease using Mohs micrographic surgery compared with wide local excision.10The patient underwent complete surgical excision followed by Mohs micrographic surgery. He maintained complete remission after 3 years of follow-up.

caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
scenario: A man in his 40s presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging yellow-red plaque on his chest that was accompanied by mild pain. The lesion was circular and measured approximately 3 cm in diameter, with multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia (Figure 1A). Further examination revealed no similar lesions on the face, including the periorbital area, or on the limbs, and there was no ocular involvement. The patient had uncontrolled diabetes. He denied any similar family history and was not currently taking any medications. A biopsy specimen was obtained from the periphery of the circular lesion (Figure 1B).
explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.

caption: A, Erythematous, well-circumscribed, lobulated firm nodule extending from the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint to the nail plate on the right index finger. Local invasion from the tumor has caused resultant lifting of the overlying nail plate, which appears thinned, split and shortened, failing to cover the distal nail bed. B, Punch biopsy showing acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion.
scenario: A right-handed man in his 50s with a history of hepatitis C presented to clinic with a 1-year history of an enlarging painless nodule on his right index finger, which was now causing destruction of his nail. No preceding trauma was reported. On examination, an erythematous 15 × 10-mm well-circumscribed lobulated firm nodule was seen extending from the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint to the nail plate of the right index finger, causing destruction of the adjacent nail plate (Figure 1A). The lesion did not transilluminate. No other findings were noted on full skin examination. A radiograph of the right hand revealed erosion of the distal phalanx, and 4-mm punch biopsies were taken from the proximal and distal pole of the nodule, highlighting similar histological features (Figure 1B).
explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10

caption: A, Clinical image of the anterior trunk showing scattered erythematous papules, many umbilicated, with a pseudovesicular/varicelliform appearance. B, Histopathological image (original magnification ×40) showing minimal changes within the epidermis and dermis.
scenario: A 41-year-old immunocompromised man with aplastic anemia was admitted to the medical intensive care unit (MICU) for pancytopenia and neutropenic fevers. His thrombocytopenia and anemia required daily platelet transfusions and intermittent blood transfusions. For further treatment of his aplastic anemia, a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) line was inserted into his right upper extremity. His hospitalization was complicated by right lower extremity cellulitis and suspected fungal pneumonia, for which he was treated with vancomycin, cefepime, and isavuconazole, in addition to prophylactic atovaquone and acyclovir. After a week in the MICU, he developed oral ulcers and tender, diffuse, erythematous pseudovesicular papules, many umbilicated, on an erythematous base on the face, trunk, and all extremities (Figure 1). An infectious workup, including skin biopsies, was initiated.
explanation: Serial sectioning of the biopsy specimen revealed focal clusters of smudged bacteria extravasating from some vessels in the midreticular dermis with minimal inflammatory response, likely related to the patient’s leukopenia (Figure 2). Gram stain results were negative. Skin, blood, and sputum cultures grewStenotrophomonas maltophilia. Transthoracic echocardiogram did not show endocarditis. Viral polymerase chain reaction swab results were negative. The patient’s PICC line was removed and replaced with a peripheral intravenous line. Based on the patient’sS maltophiliasusceptibilities, treatment was initiated with cefiderocol, 2 g every 6 hours, and minocycline, 200 mg every 12 hours, in addition to linezolid for concurrent vancomycin-resistantEnterococcus faeciumbacteremia. Blood cultures were cleared ofS maltophilia1 day into treatment. Skin lesions resolved with postinflammatory hyperpigmentation by day 35. After 38 days ofS maltophilia–directed therapy, cefiderocol was stopped and minocycline was continued as prophylaxis. In the setting of persistent neutropenia, the patient’sS maltophiliaand vancomycin-resistantE faeciumbacteremia recurred approximately 1 week later. After extensive discussions with the MICU, infectious diseases, hematology/oncology, palliative care, and ethics teams, the patient elected to stop medical treatment and pursue home hospice care. S maltophiliais a multidrug-resistant opportunistic gram-negative bacterium with high morbidity and mortality in immunocompromised patients; it is currently the top pathogen in carbapenem-resistant gram-negative bacteremia and the sixth leading cause of ICU pneumonia.1,2Risk factors include ICU stays, prolonged hospitalization, mechanical ventilation, PICC lines, and broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure.3﻿S maltophilia’s biofilm formation facilitates adherence to living tissues and nonliving surfaces, evasion of immune defenses, and antibiotic resistance to β-lactams, including traditional cephalosporins and carbapenems, which often delays appropriate treatment and results in higher mortality.2,4,5 Cutaneous involvement ofS maltophiliainfection is rare with intact skin but can manifest as cellulitis, soft tissue necrosis, ecthyma gangrenosumlike lesions, mucocutaneous ulcers, or metastatic cellulitis due to hematogenous spread and puncture through mucocutaneous surfaces.6,7This case report demonstrating disseminated pseudovesicular papules, many umbilicated, on an erythematous base with a varicelliform appearance expands the literature on the morphologic descriptions of cutaneousS maltophilia. IfS maltophiliainfection is suspected, high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, 15 mg/kg/d, should be empirically started before susceptibilities return. In patients with sulphonamide allergy, minocycline or levofloxacin can be started and continued if tissue culture demonstrates sensitivities to these antibiotics.7If nonsusceptibility to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, minocycline, and levofloxacin is demonstrated, appropriate second-line agents should be started.7Combination therapy may also be considered.7AlthoughS maltophiliais typically resistant to β-lactams, such as traditional cephalosporins, cefiderocol is a novel cephalosporin that has demonstrated in vitro activity against multidrug-resistantS maltophiliadue to its siderophore-based transport into bacteria and stability against β-lactamases.4The duration of antibiotics is typically 7 to 14 days, determined by the patient’s clinical response.7Management also involves the removal of infected devices.7 The differential diagnosis for disseminated pseudovesicular papules in an immunocompromised patient includes bacterial, viral, and fungal infections. Unlike this patient’s monomorphic eruption, disseminated varicella (chickenpox) presents with lesions in various stages of development, including macules, papules, vesicles (often with central umbilication), pustules, and crusts. Histopathologically, varicella is characterized by intraepidermal and subepidermal vesicles, keratinocytes with viropathic effects, and multinucleated giant cells. Disseminated talaromycosis (formerly penicilliosis), which is endemic in Southeast Asia and southern China, presents cutaneously in 40% to 70% of immunocompromised individuals, with manifestations ranging from papules with central necrosis, to pustules, nodules, cysts, ulcers, abscesses, and Sweet syndrome–like eruptions.8,9Histopathologically, talaromycosis exhibits granulomas with filamentous hyphae or sausage-shaped yeast cells. Disseminated cryptococcosis can manifest with ulcers, palpable purpura, umbilicated papules mimicking molluscum contagiosum, and nodules.10Histopathologically, cryptococcosis features organisms with prominent mucinous capsules and variable granulomatous inflammation, depending on the patient’s immune status. Both talaromycosis and cryptococcosis may present with scattered varicelliform erythematous papules.10 This case report highlights the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion forS maltophiliain immunocompromised patients. Early dermatologic consultation can facilitate prompt diagnosis and initiation of appropriate antibiotics.

caption: A, Smooth, firm, skin-colored papules on the nasal dorsum and bilateral alae. B, Superficial telangiectatic vessels, thick collagen bundles, and prominent sebaceous glands (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
scenario: A healthy 19-year-old man with Fitzpatrick skin type V presented with a 2-year history of bumps of the nose (Figure 1A). Physical examination was notable for several smooth, firm, skin-colored papules on the nasal dorsum and bilateral alae. The patient had previously been treated for moderate acne vulgaris of the face (temples, cheeks, nose, and chin), chest, and back that had since been well-controlled using tretinoin cream, 0.1%. The nasal papules persisted, despite resolution of the remainder of his acne without residual scarring. The patient was otherwise healthy without history of developmental delay, seizures, hypopigmented skin macules, or other notable cutaneous, cardiac, or neurologic lesions. A punch biopsy was obtained to guide further diagnosis and treatment.
explanation: A. Acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules Histopathologic findings were notable for stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels (Figure 1B). Prominent sebaceous glands and deep dermal fibrosis were also observed (Figure 2). The combined clinical and histopathologic findings supported a diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules. The patient was subsequently given twice-daily sirolimus petrolatum, 1%, and evaluated for treatment with carbon dioxide laser. Given his Fitzpatrick skin type and the increased associated risk of hyperpigmentation, a test spot was pursued prior to laser treatment of the entire nasal dorsum (Active FX; 125 mJ; 3% density). Pretreatment with twice-daily hydroquinone cream, 4%, and posttreatment with hydrocortisone ointment, 2.5%, was recommended to aid in reducing hyperpigmentation and facilitating the further flattening of these lesions. Treatment thus far has been limited to the bilateral nasal alae, with the patient noting flattening of the nasal papules without associated hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation. Existing literature has postulated acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules as representative of an underappreciated scarring variant of acne vulgaris that is primarily seen in the adolescent population.1,2These papules exhibit an anatomic predilection for the nose and chin and are clinically characterized by their smooth, dome-shaped appearance. The lesions are persistent and do not resolve despite successful treatment of acne with conventional modalities, such as topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, oral antibiotics, and isotretinoin. An existing case series of patients with acne-associated nasal papules from within a single institution contained a high proportion of Hispanic male patients, suggesting a possible predilection of this pathology for male patients with skin of color, especially those of Hispanic descent.3These findings were consistent with this case, given the African American background of the patient described herein. Of note, this patient did not have a history of developmental delay, seizures, Shagreen patches, or cardiac or brain tumors to raise suspicion for tuberous sclerosis. Additionally, granulomas were not appreciated on histopathology, making a diagnosis of cutaneous sarcoid unlikely. Histopathology results lacked thickened collagen bundles in the papillary dermis, which also makes white fibrous papulosis unlikely. A confirmatory diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules is made following observation of essential histopathologic features, including stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma extending into the deep dermis and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels. There are a handful of syndromic conditions that manifest with numerous facial angiofibromas and can appear histologically similar to this entity, including tuberous sclerosis complex, multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 1, and Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. It should be noted that this entity is clinically and histopathologically indistinguishable from classic angiofibromas. As such, clinicopathological correlation is vital, as a thorough background of the patient’s history and clinical presentation will aid in contextualizing the key elements observed on histopathology. Diagnosis in the case presented was delayed as the initial shave biopsy was interpreted as verruca plana, highlighting the diagnostic subtlety and necessity for biopsy inclusive of mid and deep dermis associated with these nasal papules. For this reason, it is important to keep this entity on the differential diagnosis when evaluating patients with a history of acne or acne scarring, particularly in patients with skin of color.

caption: A, Clinical image of an irregular-shaped violaceous plaque with central necrosis on the lower leg. B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain.
scenario: A man in his 70s presented with a painful violaceous eruption on his left lower leg accompanied by low-grade fever and fatigue for 1 week. The patient denied a recent history of trauma. The patient had a 12-month history of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), which was very high risk according to the Revised International Prognostic Scoring System. The patient had been treated with azacytidine and a prophylactic regimen of itraconazole for recalcitrant neutropenia. On the previous day, the patient was admitted to the hematology division due to progression to acute myeloid leukemia with an increasing blast cell count. Physical examination revealed an irregularly shaped, violaceous, 2.5-cm × 2.0-cm plaque with a central ecchymotic necrosis on the left lower leg (Figure 1A). Laboratory tests revealed severe neutropenia (20/μL; reference range, 1600 to 7200/μL; to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001) and a negative 1.3 β-D-glucan (BDG) test (8.1 pg/mL; reference range, <11 pg/mL). The patient started taking intravenous antibiotics but continued to develop necrotic plaques on the extremities over the next 4 days. A biopsy was obtained from the margin of the necrotic lesion (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed angioinvasive septate hyphae branching at an acute angle and extensive thrombosis in the dermis (Figure 1B). Findings on Grocott methenamine silver and periodic acid-Schiff stains confirmed the presence of fungi. Lactophenol cotton blue staining of the skin and blood cultures revealed characteristic findings ofFusariumspecies, including banana-like macroconidia (Figure 2).Fusariumspecies were also detected with polymerase chain reaction. Although the initial BDG test had negative results, the second test performed 6 days later had positive results (17.7 pg/mL). The patient was diagnosed with disseminated fusariosis (DF). Itraconazole treatment was replaced with voriconazole. However, the decision was made to focus on providing palliative care due to the lack of effective treatment and poor prognosis for neutropenia and leukemia. Thus, we refrained from additional therapies. Shortly after the diagnosis, the patient died of multiple organ failure on hospital day 16. Fusariumspecies are ubiquitous filamentous fungi commonly found in soil, plants, and water.Fusariumspecies have emerged as major opportunistic pathogens in profoundly immunocompromised patients.1Antifungal treatment to prevent invasive fungal infections in patients with high-risk hematologic disorders has led to breakthrough infections withFusariumspecies.2Breakthrough invasive fungal infections are defined as any invasive fungal infection that occurs during exposure to antifungals such as fluconazole and itraconazole, as well as broad-spectrum azoles like posaconazole and voriconazole.3 Approximately 75% of patients with DF develop skin lesions, which typically manifest as widespread targetoid erythematous, subcutaneous nodular, or painful ecthyma gangrenosum-like scattered lesions.4The skin lesions are the first clue for the diagnosis of DF when patients with neutropenia present with refractory fever. Thus, dermatologists can play a pivotal role in the early recognition of DF. Histopathologic analysis and culture are crucial for diagnosing DF. The skin lesions reveal hyaline, septate hyphae with dichotomous acute angle branching.5Dermal necrosis may be accompanied by mycelia assaulting blood vessels with subsequent thrombosis due to the angioinvasive nature ofFusarium.6These histologic findings can also occur in aspergillosis; however,Fusariumspecies exhibit characteristic hyaline banana-shaped macroconidia in culture.5Blood cultures show positive results in up to 50% of patients with DF but these findings are rare in patients with aspergillosis.1 The serum BDG test may be useful for early recognition of invasive fungal infections when repeated testing is used (once or twice per week).7Hence, a single negative test result does not exclude the presence of DF. Patients with DF have a poor prognosis, with mortality rates of approximately 50%, even with improved antifungal therapies. The mortality rate is close to 100% in patients with recalcitrant neutropenia.1Therefore, in addition to the primary treatment with voriconazole or a lipid formulation of amphotericin B, the patient should be treated with adjunctive therapies, including granulocyte or granulocyte–monocyte colony-stimulating factors, interferon-γ, and granulocyte transfusions, to recover immune status.5 Ecthyma gangrenosum is a form of necrotizing vasculitis usually caused byPseudomonas aeruginosa. Clinically, ecthyma gangrenosum presents as necrotic ulcers with a central eschar and primarily occurs in immunocompromised patients. Histologic examination shows necrosis of the epidermis and upper dermis with a necrotizing hemorrhagic vasculitis, similar to the findings of DF. However, bacteria can be seen in the medial and adventitial walls of deeper vessels.4,8Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare debilitating inflammatory skin disease characterized by painful, rapidly evolving cutaneous ulcers with undermined irregular, erythematous-violaceous edges. Half of patients with PG have an underlying medical condition such as a hematologic disorders. Histologically, PG lesions exhibit sterile suppurative inflammation.9Leukemia cutis is an extramedullary manifestation of leukemia, including myelodysplastic syndrome. Clinical appearances are highly variable and may include nodular lesions, plaques, erythematous macules, blisters, and ulcers. The histologic findings of skin biopsies from patients with leukemia cutis shows infiltration of uniform leukemic cells.4 Immunocompromised patients with painful necrotic skin lesions should undergo an evaluation for mycological infection, irrespective of the use of prophylactic antifungal agents or a negative results on BDG testing.

caption: A, Clinical image of firm, dome-shaped, flesh-colored nodules on the proximal interphalangeal joints of the right hand. B, Histopathological examination of nodule biopsy. Low power of the dermis with fibrosis and no substantial inflammation or granulomas (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×20).
scenario: A man in his early 50s presented to autoimmune dermatology clinic for 3 years of periarticular nodules on his fingers and symmetric polyarthralgia. He had been referred by rheumatology for nodules on the bilateral proximal interphalangeal joints, which were painful with manipulation or minor trauma (Figure 1A). He had also developed bilateral arthralgia in his hands with mild morning stiffness lasting up to 20 minutes and bilateral knee crepitus. He denied joint swelling but noted occasional erythema over his knuckles. Evaluation by rheumatology did not find evidence of true arthritis. He had a family history of rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis in his parents. Results of his previous workup, including C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, rheumatoid factor, anticitrullinated peptide antibody titer, and antinuclear antibody titer, were all normal. Findings from bilateral hand radiography 1 year prior were normal, with well-preserved joint spaces. Physical examination revealed bilateral firm, dome-shaped papules that felt bound to the deep tissue overlying the proximal interphalangeal joints on the dorsal surface of the hand, with one on the right palmar surface of the hand. Anatomy was preserved without contractures. A subsequent ultrasound revealed no evidence of cystic or fluid-filled structures as well as no connection to underlying structures. A punch biopsy was taken of the nodule overlying the proximal interphalangeal joint on the palmar surface of the right fifth digit (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathology disclosed unremarkable epidermis with fibroblastic proliferation arranged in long fascicles with background collagenous stroma situated in the midreticular and deep dermis without palisading granulomas or collections of histiocytes (Figure 2). CD163 staining showed no significant increase in dermal histiocytes and isolated macrophages in the dermis. Results of periodic acid–Schiff staining with diastase were negative for fibrin. Iron staining revealed hemosiderin pigment within areas of fibrosis. After histopathologic examination, the patient was diagnosed with fibroblastic rheumatism (FR). Due to clinically mild disease, methotrexate, 15 mg, weekly was initiated. At 4-month follow-up, his arthropathy was moderately improved. At 6-month follow-up, he had further improvement in his arthropathy and noticed a new nodule on the right thumb and growth of prior nodules. Given this moderate response, his medication was increased to methotrexate, 20 mg, weekly. FR is a rare dermatoarthropathy first described in 1980.1It has been reported in approximately 45 cases worldwide since its description.2,3There is a 2:1 male-female predominance, and the mean age at onset is 44 years.2The clinical course is variable and involves rapid to insidious onset of symmetric polyarthralgia and cutaneous lesions involving the hands.2,4Skin lesions often precede or erupt concurrently with joint symptoms. Firm, flesh-colored to violaceous, variably tender nodules are always present, typically on the extensor metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, which may regress over months to years. Other manifestations include sclerodactyly, palmar erythema, palmar thickening, and Raynaud phenomenon.4The disease may progress rapidly and cause permanent articular damage2; therefore, early diagnosis and treatment is crucial. To our knowledge, there is no established laboratory test for FR,4and findings of laboratory and rheumatic profiles are generally normal, with only a minority of patients presenting with elevated C-reactive protein levels.2Results of radiological studies are typically normal,5but patients may present with an array of nonspecific findings, including erosions.2Biopsy is characteristic for thickened papillary dermis with proliferation of densely packed, uniform, spindle-shaped fibrocytic-fibroblastic cells surrounded by bundles of thickened collagen fibers and vascular granulation tissue, with a pathological absence of elastic fibers.4,5Unlike mimics, FR has only minimal inflammatory cells, histiocytes, giant cells, granulomas, or foreign bodies, although findings of immunohistochemistry may be variable.2,5 The treatment of choice is prednisone and methotrexate, with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for symptomatic pain control.2Other agents have occasionally been used. Most patients show partial response to treatment, with 1 in 5 patients worsening despite treatment. Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis presents first with symmetric polyarthralgia affecting the interphalangeal joints, followed by flesh-colored cutaneous nodules on the hands, face, and neck. Nodules may resemble FR, although the clinical course differs in that they follow—rather than precede—joint manifestations. Coral-bead papules at the nail fold are common. Histologically, abundant histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells are characteristic, unlike in FR.4 Rheumatoid nodules are a common extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis, which presents with insidious onset of symmetric polyarthritis affecting the hands, wrists, and feet.6Laboratory evaluation routinely shows elevated anticitrullinated peptides and/or rheumatoid factor, although seronegative types exist as well.7Nodules most commonly present on extensor surfaces, typically on the hands. Histological examination shows palisading macrophages enclosed by granulation tissue containing histiocytes and lymphocytes.8 Granuloma annulare presents with annular skin-colored to erythematous papules and plaques that may arise on the lower extremities or proximal extremities. Symmetry is less common, as is presence on palmar surfaces. Histologically, granuloma annulare shows palisading histocytes, multinucleated giant cells, eosinophils, lymphocytes, and neutrophils infiltrating into the dermis, with degradation of collagen and hallmark deposition of mucin.9 In conclusion, fibroblastic rheumatism is a rare disorder responsible for periarticular cutaneous nodules, polyarthritis, and skin thickening. Diagnosis is one of exclusion and is made clinically with histopathological correlation, as findings of laboratory and radiological studies are generally normal or nonspecific.

caption: A, Erythematous, scaly plaque on anterior aspect of scrotum with erosion and honey-colored crusting. B, Irregular, slender, epidermal acanthosis, vacuolar alteration, and granular layer-level acantholytic splitting, with impetiginized, neutrophilic crusting, and pigment incontinence (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×20).
scenario: A man in his 40s with a medical history of asthma presented with a dermatitis of the scrotum. The patient recalled self-treatment with several over-the-counter topical products, including an eczema cream and antibiotic ointment. He had been prescribed topical hydrocortisone, 2.5%, cream, after which he described experiencing burning, pruritus, and blistering. Physical examination revealed a dry erythematous, annular plaque with focal erosion and collarette of desquamative, honey-colored crusting (Figure 1). A shave biopsy was performed.
explanation: The biopsy revealed an erosion with markedly impetiginized, neutrophilic crusting and focal acantholytic cleavage at the epidermal granular layer. Additionally, there was irregular, narrow epidermal hyperplasia with sparse lichenoid inflammation, vacuolar alteration, and rare dyskeratotic keratinocytes with pigment incontinence. An admixture of eosinophils and neutrophils were noted in the dermis, while plasma cells were not present in a substantial number (Figure 2). Given the presence of slender rete and the sparse, lichenoid, vacuolar pattern of inflammation, aTreponema pallidumimmunohistochemical stain was performed, revealing many spirochete organisms across the epidermis, confirming the diagnosis of secondary syphilis with secondary impetiginization. The patient was subsequently referred to a government health department, where he received a single intramuscular dose of penicillin (2.4 M units). During this visit, the patient disclosed a history of unprotected oral sex approximately 1 month before the onset of the scrotal dermatitis. He also reportedly developed a more diffuse, transient lichenoid eruption with palmar involvement that did not come to clinical attention and resolved following the dose of penicillin. He declined additional confirmatory laboratory testing for syphilis, as well as screening tests for other sexually transmitted infections, including HIV. The wide range of mucocutaneous manifestations of secondary syphilis has earned it the moniker ofthe great imitator. Recognition of its less common manifestations is of great clinical importance to help limit the ongoing resurgence. Other atypical manifestations of syphilis include Follmann balanitis, phagedenic chancre, reactive arthritis-like mucosal patches (previously known as Reiter syndrome), and syphilitic pemphigus.1,2There have been reports of secondary syphilis presenting as a psoriasiform balanitis.3,4An eczematous scrotal dermatitis is a much less common manifestation that may be associated with HIV infection.1,5-7Further complicating the clinicopathologic evaluation of this sexually transmitted infection is the propensity of patients to self-medicate and secondary processes, such as impetiginization, which, as in this case, may affect its overall appearance. Although the superficial changes in the biopsy could be compatible with bullous impetigo or pemphigus foliaceus, the vacuolar change is a major clue to the diagnosis of secondary syphilis. Impetigo presents clinically with circinate to annular macules with thin-walled vesicobullae that erode with honey-colored crusting and a collarette of desquamated scale.8Histopathologically, there is typically neutrophilic, spongiotic epidermal pustule formation with neutrophil-rich and lymphocytic inflammation with acantholytic cleavage at the granular layer. Gram-positive cocci are also typically evident, representing either or bothStaphylococcus aureusandStreptococcus pyogenes.Irritant contact dermatitis, a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction, can present with erythema, edema, vesiculation, and a burning sensation. Histopathology of irritant contact dermatitis typically demonstrates ballooning degeneration, superficial epidermal necrosis, and intraepidermal bullae secondary to direct toxic effects to keratinocytes. Although the presence of eosinophils in the biopsy specimen and history in this case may lead one to consider contact dermatitis, case series of eosinophil-rich syphilis have been described; therefore, they should not distract away from the possibility of this infection.9Pemphigus foliaceus presents with well-demarcated, scaly, and crusted erosions in a seborrheic distribution involving the face, scalp, chest, and back with burning and pain. Biopsies characteristically show acantholysis in the upper epidermis at or near the granular layer, but these changes can often be focal and subtle, and in early lesions, only eosinophilic spongiosis may be seen.10Correlation with direct immunofluorescence and antidesmoglein 1 serologies is important when considering this diagnosis. Given the increasing prevalence of syphilis and its wide range of manifestations and propensity to mimic other conditions, this infectious imitator should remain on the differential diagnosis for a scrotal dermatitis with bullous impetigo-like features. A detailed history, complete skin examination, and biopsy with immunohistochemical and confirmatory serologic testing are strongly encouraged to help secure this critical diagnosis.

caption: A, A well-circumscribed, round-shaped, 10 × 8-mm diameter, nonexudative ulcer surrounded by a discrete penile swelling and an indurated yellowish plaque in the ventral aspect of the penile shaft. B, Diffuse dermal hyaline fibrosis with cystic spaces of variable size that extended to the subcutis, some of them surrounded by inflammatory infiltrate (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×4).
scenario: A man in his 30s presented with a painful ulcer on the ventral aspect of the penile shaft that had appeared 3 months before. His medical history included recent unprotected sexual intercourse 2 months prior to consultation and recurrent self-healing ulcers on both the ventral and dorsal sides of the penis over the past 3 months. Physical examination disclosed discrete penile swelling with an indurated yellowish plaque diffusely involving the ventral surface. A well-circumscribed, round-shaped, 10 × 8-mm diameter, nonexudative ulcer on the more proximal area of the plaque was also noted (Figure 1A). In addition, 3 round-shaped scars, corresponding to previously resolved ulcerations, were observed on the penile dorsum. No regional lymphadenopathy or other mucocutaneous lesions were detected. Results of a complete standard laboratory workup was normal. Results of polymerase chain reaction for herpesvirus types 1 and 2,Treponema pallidum, andChlamydia, along with bacterial cultures of the ulcer, were all negative. Results of serology for syphilis, HIV, and hepatitis C and hepatitis B virus were also negative. A cutaneous biopsy obtained from the ulcer’s periphery was performed for histopathological examination and cultures (Figure 1B).

options.C: Morphea as a sign of autoimmune syndrome induced by adjuvants

distractors: Morphea as a sign of autoimmune syndrome induced by adjuvants
explanation: A. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis Histopathological analysis revealed a diffuse dermal hyaline fibrosis with cystic spaces of variable size, some of them surrounded by histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells adopting a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern that extended to the subcutaneous tissue (Figure 1B andFigure 2). Scattered patchy neutrophilic infiltrates with focal areas of dermal necrosis and occasional plasma cells were observed. In other areas, discrete focal foreign-body granulomatous reaction with histiocytes containing intracytoplasmic lipid vacuoles, lymphocytes, and plasma cells were noted (Figure 2). Findings of periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott, and modified Ziehl–Neelsen staining, along with bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures, were all negative. On detailed anamnesis, the patient reported that 2 years before he had received several injections of kanamycin ointment, containing paraffin, for penis augmentation. He refused further treatment and was lost to follow-up. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis (SLP) is a foreign-body granulomatous reaction to lipidic substances injected into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue to enlarge genitalia.1-4The most commonly injected materials include paraffin and silicone (resulting in conditions known as paraffinoma and siliconoma, respectively), followed by olive oil, motor oil, cod liver oil, or vaseline.1-4There is an increased incidence in patients from Thailand, Korea, and Eastern Europe, where these procedures remain prevalent, especially among incarcerated individuals.1Cases of SLP due to self-injection of kanamycin ointment are almost exclusively reported in Romania,5the origin country of this patient. Penile injections are typically administered in a nonstandardized manner by nonprofessional individuals or by patients themselves.1 SLP usually affects sexually active men in their third decade of life.1Symptoms tend to appear 1 to 2 years after the injection, with genital erythema, edema, and swelling. They progress to persistent, painless preputial masses or nodules. Injected material may migrate locoregionally, causing suprapubic and scrotal involvement, acquired phimosis, or lymphangitis. Chronic inflammation finally leads to the development of foreign-body granulomas, presenting as indurated, occasionally ulcerated, yellowish fibrotic penile plaques, also known aswoody penis, as seen in this case. These patients often experience painful erections, severely impacting their quality of life.1-4 Diagnosis is usually established on the basis of a detailed anamnesis and characteristic clinicopathological features. Significant diagnostic delays occur because patients frequently postpone seeking medical attention and typically deny such practices when questioned.1-4Histologically, SLP shows marked sclerosis in the reticular dermis and subcutis with numerous vacuoles of various sizes surrounded by lymphohistiocytic infiltrates and foreign-body multinucleated giant cells, creating a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern.1-4 SLP must be differentiated from autoimmune syndrome induced by adjuvants, triggered by the injection of foreign substances, such as silicone or aluminum, leading to immune-mediated conditions that can manifest as morphealike plaques at the injection sites.
