Histologically, lesions are characterized by deep dermal sclerosis lacking vacuoles surrounded by multinucleated giant cells.6,7Atypical mycobacterial cutaneous infections, often resulting from contaminated injection materials, typically present with dermal suppurative granulomas, which differ from the foreign-body granulomatous reaction seen in SLP.8Additionally, necrobiosis lipoidica involving the genitalia, though rare, exhibits a characteristic interstitial and palisading necrobiotic granulomatous tissue reaction, sharply contrasting with the Swiss-cheese pattern of SLP.9Along with the histopathological features, the absence of systemic symptoms and isolation of infectious microorganisms permitted to exclude these diagnoses. Treatment of SLP is challenging. Surgical removal of the inoculated material is the treatment of choice; nonetheless, it is often unfeasible or results in unacceptable sequelae. Moreover, these operations are complex, time-consuming plastic and reconstructive procedures, sometimes requiring multiple stages. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging of the penis and scrotum is crucial for surgical planning to ensure complete removal of injected materials and granulomatous tissue. Alternatively, isolated cases treated with intralesional corticosteroids have shown acceptable outcomes. Systemic corticosteroids may provide temporary relief but have a high recurrence rate when used alone. In cases of necrosis, urgent debridement is required to prevent further complications.1,3

caption: A, A painful, erosive lesion around the stoma on the anterior abdominal wall of a patient with Crohn disease. B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain showing a suprabasal epidermal splitting with acantholysis (original magnification ×100).
scenario: A man in his 50s with a 10-year history of Crohn disease had intermittent bowel obstructions leading to total proctocolectomy and ileostomy. Five weeks after his surgery, he developed a painful, erosive lesion around his stoma on the anterior abdominal wall (Figure 1A). Repeated microbiological cultures were negative. The patient was initially treated with topical potent steroids followed by topical tacrolimus without any result while the erosion expanded. No additional cutaneous or mucosal lesions were present. A skin biopsy specimen was collected for histopathology, and treatment with oral prednisone (30 mg/d) tapering for 1 month was initiated without benefit (Figure 1B).
explanation: B. Peristomal localized pemphigus vulgaris Histopathology revealed epidermal erosion with suprabasal epidermal splitting with acantholysis. Direct immunofluorescence test of the perilesional skin showed an intercellular deposition of IgG and C3 throughout the epidermis, while enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay showed a high level of IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 1 (40 IU/mL) and desmoglein 3 (90 IU/mL) (normal value, 20  U/mL). After obtaining written informed consent, intralesional rituximab at a dose of 5 mg/cm2was injected on the 1st and 15th day, as in a previous study by Vinay et al.1A complete clinical response to treatment was seen at 8 weeks (Figure 2). The patient was followed up for 6 months after injections without any relapse or adverse effects. Approximately 700 000 European and 800 000 North American individuals have undergone abdominal ostomy procedures, and it is estimated that about 70% of these patients will face stomal or peristomal complications.2Skin problems are particularly noteworthy within this demographic. The most common ostomy-related complication involves a disruption in the skin barrier around the stoma, leading to compromised skin integrity and maceration. This often progresses to the formation of painful erosive or ulcerative lesions around the stoma site. Diagnosing peristomal erosive dermatitis, however, is particularly challenging because it encompasses several potential differential diagnoses with different management, including irritant or allergic contact dermatitis, pyoderma gangrenosum, and autoimmune bullous dermatoses such as pemphigus or pemphigoid.2In the present case, we observed a rare occurrence of peristomal localized pemphigus vulgaris, which has been documented only twice before, both in the context of diverticulitis complicated by bowel obstruction with perforation3and adenocarcinoma of the rectum.4Despite its infrequency, peristomal pemphigus vulgaris warrants consideration, particularly in cases where conventional treatments show no response. Histopathological examination, direct immunofluorescence, and laboratory tests are pivotal in distinguishing pemphigus from other forms of peristomal erosive dermatitis. The former typically exhibits characteristic IgG and C3 intercellular deposition in the epidermis along with the presence of antidesmoglein antibodies. Bacterial infection was ruled out by negative culture and the presence of antidesmoglein 3 and 1 autoantibodies. It is plausible that mucosal disruption resulting from gastrointestinal inflammatory diseases, neoplasms, or surgical procedures could trigger the production of autoantibodies targeting mucosal tissues. Peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum, though relatively uncommon, constitutes about 15% of all pyoderma gangrenosum cases. It presents as painful ulcers with undermined borders and a necrotic base, often accompanied by systemic symptoms, and is predominantly observed in patients with inflammatory bowel disease. While histopathological findings may be inconclusive showing a diffuse dermal neutrophilic infiltrate, they help rule out other potential causes.5 Peristomal moisture-associated skin damage (MASD) affects a considerable proportion of patients undergoing ostomy, leading to inflammation and denudation of peristomal skin due to exposure to fecal or urinary effluents. Clinically, MASD is an irritant contact dermatitis manifesting as erythema, maceration, erosions, and hypergranulation tissue. If left untreated, MASD can result in complications such as scarring, stoma stenosis, and adherence issues. Differential diagnosis should account for irritant or allergic contact dermatitis caused by ostomy device materials.6 Peristomal intestinal metaplasia, characterized by the presence of intestinal mucosa and goblet cells near the stoma, is a rare phenomenon. While its exact cause remains unclear, factors such as chronic inflammation and surgical dissemination of intestinal tissue are believed to contribute. Although the risk of cancer is low, cases with adenomatous or dysplastic changes underscore the importance of vigilant monitoring.7 Treatment strategies for peristomal dermatitis encompass both local and systemic modalities, tailored to the severity and underlying cause. While conventional interventions focus on optimizing baseplate fit and minimizing skin irritation, emerging therapies like intralesional rituximab in cases of localized or refractory pemphigus vulgaris show promise. Intralesional rituximab administration offers advantages such as localized delivery, reduced systemic exposure, and potential cost-effectiveness compared to intravenous administration.1For inflammatory dermatoses, intralesional rituximab has also been administered for lesions of mucocutaneous pemphigus, granuloma faciale, and cutaneous lymphoid hyperplasia at a dose of 10 mg/mL, either weekly, biweekly, or monthly.8Clinicians should maintain a broad differential diagnosis for peristomal erosive dermatitis, considering rare conditions such as localized pemphigus in refractory cases.

caption: Clinical image of the vulva showing swelling, erythema, and induration of the labia majora (A). Histopathology reveals intact epidermis with a nodular dermatitis composed of non-necrotizing granulomas in the superficial and deep dermis (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×20) (B).
scenario: A female patient aged 12 years was referred for asymptomatic vulvar edema of 1 month’s duration that was previously treated with topical antifungals and corticosteroids with no improvement. She did not report recent travel or sexual relationships. On examination, swelling, erythema, and palpable induration on the labia minora and majora of the vulva were noted. No lymphadenopathy was palpated in the inguinal region (Figure 1A). A 4-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathological examination from the right-sided labia majora (Figure 1B).
explanation: The medical history of the patient included growth delay, several months of constipation treated with laxatives, and hemorrhoids. Histopathological examination revealed aggregated nodules of epithelioid histiocytes in the superficial and deep dermis without necrosis. Some granulomas were poorly compact and had ill-defined borders, which is associated with a lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrate, at the periphery of the granuloma and within it (Figure 2). Results of routine blood tests detected a slight increase in erythrocyte sedimentation rate and normal values of angiotensin-converting enzyme, and interferon γ release assay results were negative. The fecal calprotectin was 297 μg/g (normal laboratory values <50 μg/g). Stool culture and parasite study results were negative. The imaging studies, including chest radiography and intestinal and pelvic magnetic resonance imaging, showed results within normal ranges. The endoscopic study revealed ulcers in the duodenal bulb, rectum, sigmoid colon, terminal ileum, and cecum, along with segments of erythematous and edematous mucosa with some aphthous ulcers in the sigmoid and rectal region. Granulomas were detected in the lamina propria through gastric and intestinal endoscopic biopsy specimens, and they were not linked to active crypt injury. Thus, a final diagnosis of metastatic Crohn disease (MCD) was made. Crohn disease (CD) is an inflammatory bowel disease with many related cutaneous manifestations, including the rare presentation of MCD, defined by granulomatous lesions in a site discontinuous from the gastrointestinal tract.1-3In 20% to 30% of the cases, the skin findings in MCD can precede the gastrointestinal symptoms, which occurs more frequently in adults.1-3Otherwise, children are more likely to receive a diagnosis of CD at the time of MCD presentation.2,3Genital swelling is the most common presentation of MCD,1-3but erythema, knife-cut fissures, ulceration of the vulva/penis/scrotum, lymphedema, skin tags, and condyloma-like growths have been described.1-3Extragenital MCD has varying morphologies (abscess like, lichenoid, erythematous, pustular) and affects the legs, intertriginous zones, trunk, breast, nipple, umbilicus, or ears.1-3The primary histopathologic finding includes noncaseating granulomas surrounded by eosinophils and lymphocytes in a perivascular location.1,2 Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown cause.4Up to a third of patients with systemic sarcoidosis develop cutaneous lesions, which may constitute the first or the only clinical manifestation of this disease.4,5These manifestations include lupus pernio, infiltrated plaques, maculopapular lesions, subcutaneous nodules, and infiltration of old scars, but genital presentation is uncommon.4,5Additionally, the distinctive histopathological feature of sarcoidosis is the presence of epithelioid cell noncaseating granulomas in the superficial and deep dermis without surrounding prominent inflammatory infiltrates.4,5In this case, given the absence of systemic symptoms, negative complementary test results, and incompatible histological features, we were led to dismiss this diagnosis. Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic granulomatous infection caused byMycobacterium tuberculosisthat can possibly affect any organ.6Cutaneous TB (CTB) has many clinical presentations that are characterized by either true cutaneous infection or tuberculids, but genital involvement is rare6and associated with contiguous/autoinoculation of the infection. The principal histopathologic features of CTB are the epithelioid cell granuloma, caseous necrosis, neutrophilic abscesses, multinucleate giant cells, and dermal fibrosis.7Moreover, acid-fast organisms should be found, or evidence of mycobacterial infection may be determined by polymerase chain reaction techniques.7In the patient, a TB screening test (interferon γ release assay) returned negative results. The histological features of the granulomas did not correspond to the classical profile of TB. Additionally, the special stains for detecting mycobacteria, Ziehl-Neelsen and Auramine-Rhodamine, were negative. Granulomatous vulvitis is a rare pathology of unknown cause associated with the localized form of Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome or Miescher granulomatous cheilitis.8-10It clinically manifests as vulvar edema, unilateral or bilateral, initially developing in bursts and then becoming permanent. Histology shows granulomatous inflammation in the dermis, often in a perivascular distribution. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, and there is an obligation to rule out MCD.8-10 MCD is an uncommon condition, especially in children. Suspecting it in patients with vulvar edema, as with this patient, may help prevent diagnostic and therapeutic delays. Histological diagnosis is crucial to differentiate genital manifestations of MCD from other conditions that may present with genital swelling and a granulomatous pattern on biopsy. Adequate screening for systemic involvement is essential to early initiation of appropriate therapy.

caption: A, Skin-colored to reddish-brown micropapules involving the neck are present. The eroded area on the right side of the neck represents a recent biopsy site. B, Dermal tumor composed of multiple small ducts lined by a twin layer of cuboidal epithelium, with occasional commalike tails, and fibrotic stroma is displayed (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×100).
scenario: A male in his 20s presented with a widespread papular eruption. The lesions initially developed on the right side of his neck when he was 2 years old and subsequently progressed rapidly over a 3-year period, extending to the periorbital and intertriginous areas when he was aged 15 years. The lesions were mostly asymptomatic, with only occasional mild pruritus. There was no family history of similar dermatological conditions. Physical examination revealed monomorphic, skin-colored to reddish-brown micropapules involving the bilateral periorbital, neck, axillary, and inguinal regions (Figure 1A). Punch biopsies were obtained from the right side of the neck and left axilla for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed dermal tumors composed of multiple small ducts lined by a twin layer of cuboidal epithelium with occasional characteristic commalike tails, with background fibrotic stroma. A diagnosis of eruptive syringoma was confirmed. At present, this patient has declined further treatment and is managing his pruritus with topical corticosteroids as required (Figure 2). Syringomas are common benign adnexal tumors that affect approximately 1% of the global population with an increased incidence in Asian and Black individuals.1,2This condition typically presents as skin-colored papules affecting the periorbital areas.1 Eruptive syringoma is a rare variant of syringoma that predominantly affects females.2In contrast to classic syringoma, the onset of eruptive syringoma typically occurs before or during puberty.3The neck is the most common site of onset for this condition, followed by the chest and abdomen.1 Differential diagnoses of eruptive syringoma include other papular dermatoses, such as lichen nitidus, Fox-Fordyce disease, Brooke-Spiegler Syndrome (BSS), and generalized basaloid follicular hamartoma syndrome (GBFHS).2Histopathologic examination is crucial in confirming the diagnosis.4The distinct histopathological features of eruptive syringoma include the presence of cystic ductal structures lined by 2 layers of epithelial cells, with characteristic comma-shaped tails. There is usually a dense fibrous stroma.2,4 Fox-Fordyce disease typically presents with persistent skin-colored papules affecting the intertriginous areas and only rarely the head and neck region.5Fox-Fordyce disease is more often seen in postpubertal young women, rather than the 2-year-old male in this case.5Histologically, Fox-Fordyce disease is characterized by perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate and spongiosis, associated with infundibular hyperkeratosis, dilatation, and plugging.5 BSS is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by the development of trichoepitheliomas, cylindromas, and spiradenomas.6Classically, BSS presents as multiple small colored papules preferentially involving the nasolabial fold during puberty.6These papules typically represent trichoepithelioma.6Patients with BSS also can present with cylindromas on the scalp that typically present as tender skin-colored nodules.6Histologically, trichoepithelioma is characterized by nests of basaloid cells with keratin horn cysts and abortive follicular bulbar differentiation (papillary mesenchymal bodies), within a fibrotic stroma. Cylindroma consists of nests of basaloid cells with densely eosinophilic basement membranelike material.6 GBFHS is a rare subtype of basal follicular hamartomas (BFH), most commonly presenting as skin-colored papules across the face, scalp, neck, trunk, and pubic area.7GBFHS most commonly presents at birth or early childhood and may occasionally regress in adolescence.7Other associated physical findings may include alopecia, hypohidrosis, hypotrichosis, and palmoplantar pitting.7Histologically, BFH presents with discrete basaloid proliferations characteristically arranged in anastomosing columns and cords with scant or absent stroma.7 Treatment of eruptive syringomas is mainly for cosmesis. A wide variety of treatment options have been reported with limited degrees of success. These include ablative lasers (carbon dioxide or erbium), electrocautery, cryotherapy, chemical peels, topical and systemic retinoids, and oral antihistamines.1,2

caption: A, Desquamative erythrodermic rash with annular, polycyclic, and arcuate plaques on the trunk, arms, legs, head, and covered with numerous sterile micropustules. B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain showing psoriasiform pattern with elongated rete ridges, Munro microabcesses, spongiform pustules of Kogoj, and moderate neutrophilic dermal infiltrates.
scenario: A healthy infant boy, born from nonconsanguineous parents, presented to the emergency department with generalized rash, fever, and severe skin pain. One month prior, the patient developed a diaper rash, and was prescribed tacrolimus ointment, 0.03%, without clinical improvement. In the past week, the infant became erythrodermic with outbreaks of pustules and fever bouts up to 40 °C. Physical examination was notable for erythroderma associated with annular and arcuate pustules all over the integument (Figure 1). Intertriginous erythema and psoriasiform scales on the scalp were noted. Mucous membranes, teeth, and nails were not affected. Laboratory test results showed high white blood cell count, platelet count, and C-reactive protein levels. Kidney and liver functions were normal. Septic workup and antinuclear antibody testing results were negative.
explanation: C. Deficiency of interleukin 36 receptor antagonist The patient received intravenous (IV) fluids, empirical IV cefazolin, IV morphine as needed, and topical steroids wet wraps. A 4-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained from the left thigh and was compatible with a diagnosis of generalized pustular psoriasis (GPP). Acitretin oral solution at 0.5 mg/kg/d was elected. Follow-up at day 21 showed complete skin clearance. Genetic ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid blood testing was positive for heterozygous IL-36RA deficiency (DITRA). Now, age 4 years, the patient’s DITRA is controlled with acitretin 0.8 mg/kg/d and betamethasone valerate, 0.05%, ointment as needed without adverse effects on growth and laboratory monitoring. GPP is characterized by recurrent episodes of generalized neutrophil-rich pustule formation, which can be accompanied by fever and systemic inflammation (Figure 2).1GPP represents 1% of all clinical cases of psoriasis and has an estimated prevalence of 2 per 1 million persons.1,2GPP can be polygenic or monogenic especially if first episodes begin early in life. Gene variants inIL36RN(IL-36RAgene), IL1RN, CARD14, AP1S3, MPO, SERPINA1, SERPINA3, BTN3A3,andTGFBR3are associated with GPP.3﻿IL-36RAregulates proinflammatory cytokines release and without it, there is an increased proinflammatory signal, which triggers GPP presentation in DITRA.2DITRA can also present with nail dystrophy, benign migratory glossitis, scrotal tongue, fever, and malaise.2 Differential diagnosis includes Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, AGEP, and Netherton syndrome. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is caused by toxinicStaphylococcus aureusinfection in infants. It presents as widespread tender erythroderma with epidermolysis starting in the skin folds and a scalded appearance without mucosal involvement. Histopathologic features show intraepidermal bullae with cleavage in the granular cell layer.4Septic workup results in this patient were negative. AGEP is an adverse drug reaction that manifests as an erythematous micropustular eruption starting in the skin folds with or without fever.5Usually pustules in AGEP are smaller in size than in GPP. In children, AGEP can be associated with upper respiratory tract infections.5This patient did not have an infectious process and was not taking any oral medications. Histopathologic features of AGEP show subcorneal pustules associated with dermal edema, eosinophilic infiltrates, and focal keratinocyte necrosis.5 Netherton syndrome is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by the variant in theSPINK5gene coding for LEKTI, a protein important in skin barrier integrity. The clinical triad of trichorrhexis invaginata, ichthyosis lineariz circumflexa, and erythroderma defines Netherton syndrome. Atopy, elevated IgE levels, hypernatremic dehydratation, diarrhea, malnutrition, and failure to thrive are frequent. The absence of detection of LEKTI antibodies in the epidermis of affected patients is diagnostic for Netherton syndrome.6 GPP and DITRA can be treated with usual psoriasis topical therapies and/or narrowband UV-B phototherapy. However, it usually require systemic and biologic therapies due to severity and frequent flare-ups.7In children, acitretin, 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg/d, is an effective and safe first-line therapy without immunosuppressive adverse effects. Methotrexate and cyclosporine are available options, but newer anti-IL23 and anti-IL17 biologics are more efficient, especially in patients with DITRA.8In adults, a recently approved IL-36–targeting biologic, spesolimab, shows promise. It is not yet approved in children.9This case highlights that early onset GPP in a child should alert clinicians to look for underlying auto inflammatory genetic disorders. A 2022 international Delphi consensus10recommend that when available, genetic IL-36RN testing in GPP patients should be offered at any age.

caption: A, Two distinct, well-defined, umbilicated skin-colored lesions measuring 2 × 2 cm each located over the glabella and right cheek with central ulceration and hemorrhagic crusting. B, Histopathological examination showing extensive dermal collection of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and macrophages (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×40). Intracellular yeasts with surrounding halos were identified.
scenario: A man in his 70s presented with a chief complaint of 2 progressively enlarging, painless nodular lesions on the forehead and right cheek, initially observed as erythematous nodules 3 months prior. The patient had noted a gradual increase in size with subsequent central ulceration and the development of blackish crusting over time. The absence of fever, pain, or discharge from the lesions and immunocompromised status due to kidney transplant in 2004 were notable. On physical examination, 2 distinct lesions were identified, measuring 2 × 2 cm each. The lesions were located over the glabella and right cheek and were firm with central ulceration with hemorrhagic crusting (Figure 1A). A thorough examination of the surrounding skin, as well as a general systemic evaluation, revealed no additional lesions or abnormalities. Dermoscopy features included arborizing telangiectasias, central ulceration with crusting, and peripheral pigment. Biopsy was obtained from the lesion for histopathological examination (Figure 1B), and tissue was sent for polymerase chain reaction analysis.
explanation: A skin biopsy was performed to confirm the diagnosis, revealing an extensive dermal collection of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and macrophages. Intracellular yeasts with surrounding halos were identified, establishing the diagnosis of histoplasmosis (Figure 1B). Polymerase chain reaction findings  for histoplasma were also positive from the biopsy specimen. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen was done, and there was no involvement of internal organs. The patient was initiated on intravenous liposomal amphotericin B, 200 mg, once daily for a duration of 2 weeks. Following the initial treatment phase, oral itraconazole, 100 mg, twice daily was prescribed for maintenance therapy. After 2 months, a complete clearance of the nodular lesions was observed, with residual hyperpigmentation. Histoplasmosis, an opportunistic fungal infection caused by the dimorphic fungusHistoplasma capsulatum, predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals. The clinical spectrum includes pulmonary, progressive disseminated, and chronic cavitary forms, with cutaneous involvement seen in up to 17% of disseminated cases. These cutaneous manifestations encompass papules, pustules, ulcers, and, rarely, molluscoid or umbilicated lesions, presenting a clinical challenge as they can mimic cutaneous blastomycosis, rhinosporodiosis, and cutaneous cryptococcosis.1Histopathologically, a dense dermal infiltrate containing numerous plasma cells, histiocytes, and lymphocytes (Figure 2), with intracellular budding yeast forms predominantly within histiocytes. A characteristic halo may be evident due to the retraction of the basophilic fungal cell cytoplasm. Special stains, such as Grocott–Gömöri methenamine silver, confirm the presence of numerous 2-μm to 4-μm fungal spores consistent withH capsulatum.2Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia is a frequent finding in histoplasmosis reported in up to 60% of cases of histoplasmosis.3 A close differential diagnosis for cutaneous histoplasmosis is cutaneous cryptococcosis, which can present as papules, maculopapular lesions, or nodular lesions with central ulceration. Cryptococcosis is characterized by variably sized yeasts with narrow-based budding, widely separated by thick mucoid capsules. The Periodic acid–Schiff stain highlights the yeasts, which are single structures with double cell walls measuring around 5 to 12 µm, and mucicarmine stain accents the highly characteristic gelatinous capsule in a bright pink color. The treatment of cutaneous cryptococcosis includes fluconazole, itraconazole, and amphotericin B.4 Rhinosporodiosis presents as diverse range of manifestations on the skin, presenting as pedunculated or sessile growths friable verruca vulgaris–like lesions, subcutaneous swellings, furuncular lesions, and even cutaneous horn. Additionally, it can manifest as nodules with overlying ulceration and crusting, as in this case. However, histopathological examination reveals a hyperplastic epithelium with chronic inflammatory cell infiltrates composed of plasma cells and lymphocytes, with characteristic sporangia with various stages of maturation seen as globular cysts of variable sizes containing endospores. The treatment of choice for rhinosporodiosis is wide local excision.5 Cutaneous blastomycosis clinically manifests as papules that later evolve into vegetative and crusted plaques with central ulceration. There may be associated lymphadenopathy and/or lymphangitis. Histopathology of cutaneous blastomycosis usually show pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with neutrophilic abscesses. The yeasts are 8 to 15 µm in diameter with thick, double-contoured walls and display broad-based budding. The size of the yeasts can be bigger in immunocompromised patients. The first-line treatment of cutaneous blastomycosis is oral itraconazole.6 This case highlights the complex clinical and histopathological landscape of cutaneous histoplasmosis, notably in immunocompromised patients, such as those who have undergone kidney transplant. The diverse presentation and similar dermatological features shared with other infections underscore the importance of a meticulous approach to diagnosis and tailored antifungal therapy to manage this potentially debilitating condition effectively.

caption: A, Exanthematous eruption of pink papules on the patient’s face. Similar presentation seen distributed generally across the trunk and extremities. B, Hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×400. Folliculosebaceous epithelium depicting scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and rare syncytial-type multinucleated epithelial cells (arrowhead).
scenario: A man in his 40s with a history of a matched, sibling allogeneic stem cell transplant for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma 7 years prior presented with a generalized eruption 1 week after receiving a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. The diffuse rash started as pink patches on the face (Figure 1A) and spread to the trunk and extremities within 4 days. Within a day of the MMR vaccination, he reported fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, loose stools, and dyspnea 7 days before the rash began. Pertinent negatives included no itch or pain associated with the rash and lack of any sclerotic skin changes.1He had received a COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna) 2 months prior, and along with MMR, an adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) 1 week prior. Following the patient’s stem cell transplant, he had relapsed disease 1 year later and was treated with donor lymphocyte infusion. Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) complication of the mouth, eyes, liver, and lungs was treated with systemic steroids and tapered off. The most recent GVHD flare occurred 1 year prior to presentation, and the patient had not been undergoing immunosuppression for 6 months. The patient had also been treated intermittently in the past with oral minocycline for rosacea. Physical examination revealed an erythematous exanthematous eruption with generalized distribution across the trunk, extremities, and face with erythematous erosions noted in the buccal mucosa of the oral cavity. Skin biopsies were performed from the upper right side of the back and right temple (Figure 1B). Further diagnostic testing involved chest radiograph and laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, and an infectious workup.
explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

caption: A, Well-circumscribed, round ulcer 15 mm in diameter with central black eschar localized on the right side of the scrotum. B, Epidermal necrosis and a dense diffuse and interstitial neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the upper and middle dermis with focal abscess formation (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A healthy young male patient was referred to the department of dermatology for evaluation of a solitary painful scrotal ulceration that developed rapidly 48 hours before consultation. One week before he had been diagnosed with acute tonsillitis and fever (temperature up to 38 °C), which were treated with oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid. No history of a traumatic event, insect bites, genital or oral ulcers, sexual risk contacts, application of topical products, or other drug treatments was recorded. Physical examination revealed a well-circumscribed, round ulceration 15 mm in diameter with central black eschar localized on the right side of the scrotum (Figure 1A). Leukocytosis with neutrophilia was detected in an initial workup. The rest of the physical examination revealed bilateral tonsillitis and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. No inguinal lymphadenopathies were palpated. A 4-mm punch biopsy from the edge of the lesion was obtained. Representative histopathological features are shown inFigure 1B. Staining for periodic acid–Schiff, periodic acid–Schiff with diastase, and Gram failed to detect microorganisms. Immunohistochemical techniques forTreponema pallidum, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) were negative. A complete hematological and biochemical survey disclosed a moderate increase of erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein blood levels. Immunological studies, including antinuclear antibodies and both C3 and C4 proteins, were normal. Microbiological studies, including bacteriological cultures of scrotal ulcer exudates and polymerase chain reaction amplification for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, EBV, and CMV, yielded negative results. Serologic tests for syphilis, HIV, CMV, EBV, and human parvovirus B19 were negative.

options.C: Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum

answer: Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum
explanation: C. Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum Histopathological examination revealed epidermal necrosis and a dense diffuse and interstitial neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the upper and middle dermis with focal abscess formation. Clear-cut signs of vasculitis were not observed in hematoxylin-eosin stains (Figure 2). A prompt clinical resolution was observed after empirical antibiotic treatment with clindamycin and ciprofloxacin. Complete healing was achieved after 3 weeks of follow-up. Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum (JGVS) is an uncommon, distinct entity manifested by an acute onset of necrotic and painful scrotal ulceration(s) occurring exclusively in otherwise healthy young individuals often preceded and/or accompanied by a febrile episode of upper respiratory tract infection. The lesions are often solitary or few in number and correspond to sharply demarcated round to polycyclic necrotic ulcers with a central eschar. Scrotal edema has occasionally been reported,1but palpable regional lymph nodes, urinary symptoms, mucous membrane involvement, or other cutaneous lesions are not present. Acute phase reactants (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein) are usually increased, whereas the other laboratory investigations are within normal ranges. JGVS is an acute, self-limiting disorder, and no association with an underlying systemic disorder has been described.2 Histopathological features are usually nonspecific. Epidermal necrosis and a dense perivascular lymphocyte or diffuse dermal neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate are observed.3In fewer than 50% of cases, fibrinoid necrosis of small blood vessel walls with extravasated erythrocytes is detected.2,4Microbiological studies usually have failed to detect a specific infectious cause.Juvenile vasculitis of the scrotumis a misleading term, and the rubric ofacute noninfectious ulcer of the scrotumprobably defines more accurately the particular and unique features of this disorder. The pathogenesis of JGVS is largely unknown. Since scrotal ulcerations appear constantly after an infectious prodrome and no further recurrences develop, a possible primary infectious disease from an unidentified microorganism could be speculated. The possibility that JGVS represents the male counterpart of the Lipschutz ulcer has been proposed.3,5,6Both disorders share many epidemiological, clinical, histopathological, and evolutive features, as well as potential associations. Some authors have also postulated that JGVS could represent a particular variant of pyoderma gangrenosum, since both disorders share similar histopathological features and neutrophilic-rich infiltrates.1,7However, the lack of recurrences and association with systemic disorders make this possibility unlikely. The diagnosis is usually established based on the characteristic clinicopathological features, age of onset, and previous upper respiratory tract infection. Skin biopsy is only performed in selected cases to rule out other possible diagnoses. The most noteworthy differential diagnosis is early lesions of Fournier gangrene, a rapidly spreading, aggressive, and necrotic cellulitis observed in male individuals older than 50 years with considerable comorbidities in which surgical debridement is the treatment of choice.8 There is no available standard treatment approach. The lesion(s) tend to resolve spontaneously or after treatment in 2 or 3 weeks with scar formation. A dramatic response after a short course of low-dose systemic steroids with or without combination with systemic antibiotics has been reported.1Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, dapsone, and surgical excision have also been described as effective therapeutic options.2However, since the disease shows a self-limited course with spontaneous healing, the exact efficacy of these treatments remains controversial. The diagnosis of JGVS should be kept in mind whenever healthy young patients present with abrupt scrotal ulcerations.

caption: A, Clinical image showing nodules of different diameters on the vulvar site. B, Vascular hyperplasia and inflammatory cell infiltration in the dermis, combined with lymphangiectasia (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A woman in her 30s presented with mildly itchy skin nodules in the vulvar region for 1 year, which occurred during pregnancy and increased gradually in size and number without any treatments. The patient denied any history of trauma, insect bites, or other disorders in the corresponding area and had no family history or other systemic diseases. Physical examination revealed multiple red, smooth, well-circumscribed papules and nodules in the left labia majora and minora (Figure 1A). The lesions were smooth surfaced, and tenderness was absent. A biopsy was performed (Figure 1B).
explanation: C. Angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia Histopathological findings included dilated vessels with perivascular eosinophils and lymphocytes (Figure 2). A diagnosis of angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia (ALHE) was made. However, this patient declined further treatment and was lost to follow-up. ALHE, also known as epithelioid hemangioma, is an uncommon, benign vascular proliferative disorder that is usually characterized by singular or multiple smooth-surfaced, pink to purple nodules. It mostly occurs on the head and neck, with pruritus, pain, pulsation, or bleeding. However, approximately 15% of cases are asymptomatic, as estimated in a systematic review.1ALHE occurs mainly in Asian patients (27.4%) or White patients (24.7%), without a meaningful difference in gender, and the mean age at diagnosis is 37.6 years. The cause remains unclear, and ALHE might be a vascular neoplasm or a lymphoproliferative disorder. Its pathogenesis is unknown, and its treatment is challenging. Surgical excision is the most common treatment with the lowest failure rate (40.8%); however, it is impractical when lesions are numerous, as in the present patient. Various laser options have an average recurrence rate of 55.5%, whereas cryotherapy has a failure rate of 80.5%. Other options such as topical or systemic corticosteroids, topical imiquimod, tacrolimus, and isotretinoin have varying risks of recurrence. The differential diagnoses in the presented case include Kimura disease, angiomyxoma, and vulvar lymphangioma circumscriptum. Histopathologic analysis is critical to clarify the diagnosis. Vulvar lymphangioma circumscriptum is a rare, benign condition associated with a previous pelvic cancer or acquired lymphatic obstruction. It shows multiple circumscribed papulovesicular lesions of different sizes that clinically contain clear fluid and histologically exhibit markedly dilated lymphatic vessels.2,3Kimura disease is a chronic inflammatory disorder that mainly occurs in Asian men in their 30s. It is characterized by deep subcutaneous nodules most commonly in the head or neck, often accompanied by regional lymph node involvement, hypereosinophilia in peripheral blood, and elevated total immunoglobulin E. Histologically, Kimura disease mainly shows hyperplastic lymphoid follicles with prominent germinal centers surrounded by abundant eosinophils.4,5Angiomyxomas are rare, benign mesenchymal neoplasms with 2 phenotypes: superficial (or cutaneous) and aggressive (or deep) angiomyxomas, both of which can involve the vulva and present as a slow-growing mass.6The most important pathological features are stellate and spindle-shaped tumor cells set in a loose myxoid stroma accompanied by numerous blood vessels, ranging from tiny capillarylike vessels to larger thick-walled vessels with a distinct smooth muscle layer.7The histologic findings for the present patient mainly showed blood vessels surrounded by lymphocytes and eosinophils with foci of lymphangiectasia, which excluded the other diagnoses. To our knowledge, only 4 cases of ALHE have been reported in the vulval region.8,9ALHE may present as vulvar nodular lesions, and histopathologic examination is helpful for a definitive diagnosis.

caption: A, Clinical presentation of a destructive mass on the nose, with multiple areas of erosion, ulcers, and exudate covering the mass. B, Histological examination showed polymorphous lymphocytic infiltration in the full-thickness dermis (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×100).
scenario: A 43-year-old man with a progressive midfacial mass for 6 months presented at our department. Just prior to presentation, he developed epistaxis, high fever, and weight loss of 10 kg. He did not have any medical disease and denied cocaine abuse. On physical examination, an egg-sized soft mass with erythema at the edge could be observed on his nose, and the mass was covered with multiple erosions, ulcers, and exudate (Figure 1A). Laboratory examination revealed moderate anemia and elevated C-reactive protein levels. Fungal microscopic examination and culture revealed negative results, while metagenomic next-generation sequencing of the lesion showed significant positivity forPseudomonas aeruginosaand Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Findings of computed tomography of the paranasal sinus were basically normal except for mucosal thickening. Skin biopsies were taken for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).

options.B: Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type

answer: Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type
explanation: B. Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type Histopathological analysis revealed that there was polymorphous infiltrate within the full thickness of the dermis, consisting of a mixture of typical small lymphocytes and atypical lymphoid cells of varying sizes (Figure 1B). Moreover, angiodestruction and fibrinoid changes in the blood vessel wall could also be seen. Immunohistochemistry staining demonstrated increased expression of CD2, CD56, and cytoplasmic CD3 in atypical cells (Figure 2). In addition, in situ hybridization revealed positivity for EBV-encoded small nuclear RNA in the dermis. The diagnosis of extranodal natural killer (NK)/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type (ENKL-NT) was validated based on histological features, laboratory findings, and clinical characteristics. Following radiotherapy, the patient died with severe cachexia. ENKL-NT is a malignant EBV-associated lymphoma characterized by rapid progression and a poor prognosis, and it occurs more commonly in Asia and Latin America than in other regions.1Clinically, it presents as a necrotizing mass involving the nose, sinuses, or palate accompanied by localized symptoms, such as nasal obstruction and epistaxis. Common systemic symptoms are fever and weight loss.2From a histological perspective, ENKL-NT is commonly distinguished by the presence of local angioinvasion and angiodestruction, leading to the gradual development of necrotic ulceration. The neoplastic cells are intermediate to large in size and display positivity for the surface markers CD2 and CD56 as well as for the cytoplasmic expression of CD3ε. However, these cells lack surface expression of CD3.2 The diagnosis of ENKL-NT may be challenging clinically due to its similarity to other midline destructive lesions, which mainly include rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and lymphomatoid granulomatosis (LYG). Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis and often occurs in immunocompromised patients and those with diabetes. Ulceration covered by black eschar on the midfacial region, periorbital swelling, and sinusitis are its 3 hallmarks.3Pathologically, the presence of characteristic hyphae provides a presumptive diagnosis that should prompt further evaluation. Widespread infiltration of normal lymphocytes and other inflammatory cells can also be observed.4Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that can involve the respiratory tract and kidneys, causing coughing, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and kidney insufficiency in addition to midline destructive lesions.5Noncaseating granulomas and leukocytoclastic vasculitis are the typical histological findings.6Similar in histology to ENKL-NT, LYG is another EBV-positive tumor that may appear at extranodal sites. However, in LYG, EBV-positive tumor cells originate from B cells and therefore express pan–B-cell markers, such as CD20, instead of markers typical of NK or T cells.7 Unfortunately, to our knowledge, no standard treatment for ENKL-NT has been determined. Radiation therapy is a fundamental part of first-line treatment for patients with localized ENKL-NT, and concurrent or sequential chemotherapy combinations may be more effective than single-agent regimens.8Chemotherapy containing L-asparaginase is an essential component of recommended treatments for advanced ENKL-NT.8A poor prognosis was significantly associated with non–nasal-type disease, involvement of distant lymph nodes, advanced disease, and age older than 60 years.9Early diagnosis and treatment of ENKL-NT can improve overall survival, prevent disfiguration, and improve patient quality of life.

caption: A, Multiple yellowish papules and nodules on the scalp and face. B, Panoramic view of the histopathologic image demonstrating sheets of histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and scattered Touton giant cells in the papillary dermis without epidermotropism or emperipolesis (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A 6-month-old girl presented with yellowish papules and nodules on the face and trunk (Figure 1A). The skin lesions appeared 2 months prior, initially on the scalp, then gradually spread to the trunk. Physical examination revealed yellowish papules and nodules on the scalp, face, abdomen, back, and perineum. No fever, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable, and she demonstrated age-appropriate developmental milestones. Results of laboratory tests, including blood cell count and liver and kidney functions, were within normal limits. After obtaining informed consent from the parents, a punch biopsy of an abdominal lesion was performed for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
explanation: D. Anaplastic lymphoma kinase–positive histiocytosis Histopathologic examination revealed sheets of histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and scattered Touton giant cells in the papillary dermis. No epidermotropism or emperipolesis was observed. Immunohistochemical staining results were negative for S100, CD1a, CD207, andBRAFV600E alteration, while positive for CD68, CD163, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) (Figure 2). Chest radiology revealed no specific abnormalities. Abdominal sonography showed no hepatosplenomegaly and normal hepatobiliary system. Neonatal neurosonography revealed no obvious brain tumor. Positron emission tomography showed no noteworthy resorption except for a nodule on the left forehead. Genetic analysis yielded positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. The clinical, histopathological, and molecular findings were consistent with a diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement. ALK-positive histiocytosis is a novel histiocytic proliferative disorder characterized by a unique gene translocation involving the fusion of theALKgene with various partners.1Infants with systemic manifestations such as pallor, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly were initially reported in a case series in 2008.2The disease has since expanded to include patients older than 40 years with local or systemic involvement.3Subsequent studies have validated the distinct clinicopathological and molecular features of ALK-positive histiocytosis, including the characteristicKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, neurological manifestations, and favorable responses to ALK inhibitors.4Currently, ALK-positive histiocytosis is recognized as a distinct histiocytic neoplasm according to the World Health Organization classification system.5 ALK-positive histiocytosis has a female predominance, in contrast with the male predominance observed in Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG).4A comprehensive understanding of ALK-positive histiocytosis requires systemic surveys, leading to further subcategorization into group 1A (multisystem involvement, including the liver, spleen, and hematopoietic systems), group 1B (multisystem involvement, encompassing the nervous systems, lungs, bone, skin, and lymph nodes), and group 2 (single-system involvement).4Of note, group 2 usually involves the skin or nervous systems and often requires surgical removal. ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG have potential similarities in clinical manifestations and histopathological findings.6,7Both ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG exhibit positive staining for CD68 and CD163, and lesional tumor cells in ALK-positive histiocytosis are positive for ALK staining.7,8Molecular testing for ALK rearrangements should be performed to confirm the diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis, particularly in patients presenting with multiple lesions with atypical histiocytic proliferation.4,8In addition to the commonly observedKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, documented cases include other gene fusions, includingDCTN1::ALK,CLTC::ALK, andTPM3::ALK.4,8It is noteworthy that patients with ALK-positive staining but no ALK rearrangements may not benefit from ALK inhibition.4In unresectable cases, disease control may require the use of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and ALK inhibitors, such as crizotinib, alectinib, or lorlatinib.4,8 Cutaneous histiocytoses encompass a diverse group of diseases characterized by the accumulation of cells in the skin exhibiting cytological and phenotypic features of macrophages or dendritic cells.7In LCH, cutaneous lesions typically present as erythematous vesicles, pustules, or papulonodules. Histopathological examination reveals monomorphous, medium-sized histiocytes containing a pink and kidney-shaped nucleus, often accompanied by epidermal exocytosis. Definite diagnosis of LCH relies on positive immunostaining for S100, CD1a, and CD207,7all of which were negative in the present patient. Rosai-Dorfman disease typically manifests as widespread, erythematous to brownish papulonodules in children. Systemic symptoms may occur and include fever, lymphadenopathy, and anemia. Histopathological examination reveals signs of emperipolesis, a feature not observed in the present patient. Immunostaining results for Rosai-Dorfman disease may be positive for S100, CD68, and CD163 and negative for CD1a and CD207.7Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) typically affects adults, with characteristic cutaneous manifestations of yellow-brown papules or plaques on the face or trunk.1,8,9Classic histopathologic features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei, Touton giant cells, and extensive fibrosis, and it is characterized by positive immunostaining for CD68 and CD163 and negative staining for CD1a and CD207.9﻿BRAFV600E alteration may also be present in ECD.8,9 This case outlines a patient presenting with typical clinical and histopathological features of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement, as confirmed by positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. Treatment options such as vinblastine/prednisolone-based chemotherapy or crizotinib were suggested, but the patient’s family expressed hesitation. Therefore, the patient was treated with prednisolone, 4 mg, twice daily and topical hydrocortisone ointment, with periodic follow-up for outcome evaluation. Although diagnosis of this unique entity is rare, it is critical for physicians to perform a thorough systemic examination and implement appropriate treatment.

caption: A, Dusky retiform purpura with associated erosions and bullae on the right medial leg. B, Acute epidermal necrosis with a subepidermal pauci-inflammatory bulla. There are telangiectatic vessels without evidence of intraluminal thrombi or vasculitis (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×90).
scenario: A man with a history of polysubstance use was admitted for a presumed drug overdose after being found unconscious. The dermatology department was consulted to evaluate new bullae on his bilateral lower extremities. On his medial right leg and lateral left leg, there were retiform, dusky plaques, several of which had overlying tense bullae and erosions (Figure 1A). An extensive diagnostic workup was performed. A complete blood cell count revealed mild leukocytosis, and the results of a basic metabolic panel demonstrated an elevated creatinine level of 1.55 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4). His creatine kinase and C-reactive protein levels were elevated at 879 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167) and 52.9 mg/dL (to convert to mg/L, multiply by 10), respectively. Laboratory workup results for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis C were negative. Coagulation studies were not performed. Urinalysis results demonstrated myoglobinuria, ketonuria, and proteinuria. A urine drug screen was not collected, but the patient reported using heroin and cocaine that day. A computed tomography scan of the head without contrast demonstrated no acute intracranial abnormality. Ultrasonography of the right and left lower extremities revealed normal, compressible veins without evidence of deep vein thrombosis. A punch biopsy was performed at the edge of a retiform plaque on the right medial thigh for histopathologic evaluation.
explanation: B. Pressure-induced necrosis (coma blister) A 4-mm punch biopsy revealed a noninflammatory bulla with full-thickness epidermal and eccrine gland necrosis without infectious organisms, vasculitis, or vasculopathy (Figure 1B andFigure 2). Tissue culture results for aerobic and anaerobic bacteria, fungus, and acid-fast bacilli were negative. Based on the distribution of retiform ulceration, elevated creatine kinase levels, and histology, a diagnosis of pressure-induced necrosis (coma blister) was rendered. The patient was treated with petroleum jelly and nonadherent dressing without new lesion formation and subsequent healing with postinflammatory pigmentary alteration. The morphology of retiform purpura is distinct and presents as reticulated, nonblanchable patches or plaques with associated necrosis from underlying ischemia that is secondary to vessel lumen occlusion or wall damage.1It can be challenging to clinically differentiate true retiform purpura from an angulated plaque mimicking a vascular process. Thus, biopsy can be helpful in evaluating lesions with retiform morphology. Pressure-induced necrosis is thought to develop from pressure-induced local ischemia that causes tissue hypoxia and subsequent tissue injury. It typically presents as noninflammatory tense bullae, although it can be seen on a base of erythema.2Retiform morphology is not usually observed. Histologically, full-thickness epidermal and eccrine gland necrosis with subepidermal or intraepidermal bullae and an absence of inflammatory infiltrate is seen.2The most common settings for these lesions to develop include neurological disease, immobilization, metabolic conditions, and drug overdose.2,3 Levamisole is currently used as a veterinary antiparasitic, formerly used as an immunomodulatory agent in humans, and popularly added to cocaine due to its psychotropic-enhancing effects.4Levamisole-associated cutaneous vasculitis is believed to occur from a combination of immune cascade activation and vasoconstriction.4,5It presents with painful purpuric retiform plaques with central necrosis, most commonly on the distal extremities, ear helices, and nose. Systemic findings include leukopenia, agranulocytosis, glomerulonephritis, and elevated antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies.5,6Leukocytoclastic vasculitis and thrombotic vasculopathy may be seen histologically. Vasculopathy suggests thromboembolism and warrants a broad hypercoagulability workup, while vessel wall destruction may be secondary to depositional disorders, infection, or vasculitides.1In a patient with a history of polysubstance use, levamisole-induced vasculitis should be considered. Neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis (NEH), a type of neutrophilic dermatosis, is believed to occur secondary to cytotoxic damage to the eccrine glands and subsequent neutrophilic migration.7,8NEH often occurs in patients with acute myeloid leukemia who are undergoing chemotherapy, although other cancers, immune conditions, and medications have been implicated.8Infection can also trigger NEH, frequently secondary to gram negative organisms. NEH clinically presents with erythematous, edematous papules and plaques on the trunk; however, variation in pain, color, number, location, and the morphology of lesions have been reported.8The characteristic histological feature of NEH is eccrine gland necrosis with vacuolar degeneration, and while dense neutrophilic infiltrate defines neutrophilic dermatosis, it is not required for diagnosis of NEH, particularly in those who have neutropenia.7 Calciphylaxis most commonly presents as painful, necrotic retiform plaques favoring adipose-rich areas, although it can present with diverse clinical manifestations.9The pathogenesis of calciphylaxis is complex and may be secondary to underlying calcium-phosphate metabolism disorders that result in medial vessel calcium deposition, intimal fibrosis, and resultant thrombotic occlusion.10Patients with calciphylaxis typically have medical comorbidities, and risk factors include female sex, being older than 60 years, diabetes, a body mass index greater than 30, use of vitamin K antagonists, and end-stage kidney disease. Patients may also have hypoalbuminemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypercalcemia. Histologic features include epidermal ulceration, focal dermal necrosis, and perieccrine, vascular, and/or interstitial calcification.9 It can be challenging to identify the underlying etiology of retiform lesions based on clinical features alone, and cognitive bias should be avoided. Clinical interpretation of morphologic clues, like a retiform appearance, may result in premature closure on a differential diagnosis that is not relevant to the patient. Pressure-induced necrosis may present as angulated plaques mimicking retiform purpura; noninflammatory bullae and eccrine gland necrosis are key clinicopathologic features in making this diagnosis.

caption: Clinical image of right elbow shows numerous pink-yellow firm papules and nodules (A), and hematoxylin-eosin staining (original magnification, ×200) of shave biopsy specimen shows sheets of foamy lipid-filled histiocytes (B).
scenario: A 38-year-old man presented for evaluation of lesions on his elbows for 10 years, hands for 1 year, and knees for a few months. The lesions were progressively increasing in number and size and were occasionally mildly tender with firm pressure. He was unaware of similar lesions or known lipid abnormalities in family members. Physical examination revealed numerous pink-yellow firm papules and nodules on the bilateral elbows (Figure 1A) and knees, and linear thin yellow papules on the palmar finger creases. A shave biopsy specimen was taken from a papule on the elbow and sent for histopathologic analysis (Figure 1B). A fasting serum lipid panel was also obtained. Based on the clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings, the patient was diagnosed with an underlying genetic disorder.
explanation: A. Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III hyperlipoproteinemia) Histopathologic findings showed aggregates of lipid-filled histiocytes, consistent with xanthoma. The patient’s distribution of lesions was consistent with xanthoma striatum palmare, tuberous xanthomas, and tuberoeruptive xanthomas, suggestive of an underlying diagnosis of familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (FD). Lipid profiling revealed elevated cholesterol (519 mg/dL; normal range, <200 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0259), elevated triglycerides (935 mg/dL; normal range, <150 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113), and reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (22 mg/dL; normal range, 40-60 mg/dL). Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol could not be calculated due to the high triglyceride levels. Altogether, the patient’s clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings confirmed the diagnosis of FD. He declined genetic testing. Statin therapy was initiated, and after 1 year of treatment, most of the lesions had completely disappeared. Despite being benign, xanthomas often herald underlying lipid metabolism disorders. Xanthomas are classified based on clinical morphologic findings, anatomic distribution, and mode of development, and include tendon, planar, tuberous, tuberoeruptive, and eruptive xanthomas.1Histologically, all xanthoma types are characterized by a dense collection of foam cells (histiocytes filled with lipid) within the dermis. Eruptive xanthomas often contain extracellular lipid and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate, whereas tuberous and tendon xanthomas frequently contain cholesterol clefts and fibrosis.2Certain xanthomas have been associated with specific underlying lipoprotein disorders, giving them diagnostic utility.1 FD is a rare disorder characterized by elevated plasma triglyceride and cholesterol levels.1,3Most cases are associated withAPOE-ε2homozygosity, transmitted in an autosomal recessive mode with variable penetrance.4Adult-onset tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are characteristic of FD.3Planar xanthomas in the palmar creases, known as xanthoma striatum palmare (Figure 2), are seen in 20% of FD cases and are pathognomonic.3,5In the present case, the coexistence of these xanthoma types allowed the diagnosis of FD to be essentially ensured before obtaining confirmatory lipid profiling. By appreciating xanthomas as diagnostic clues, dermatologists can help recognize underlying FD. This is critical given that FD is associated with a substantial increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease if untreated.3Treatment includes lipid- and cholesterol-lowering agents that mitigate cardiovascular risk and often induces full xanthoma regression.3 Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), an autosomal dominant disorder associated with defects in genes affecting the low-density lipoprotein−receptor pathway, is also characterized by elevated plasma cholesterol and xanthoma formation.3,4However, FH has normal triglyceride levels and distinct characteristic xanthomas. Tendon xanthomas, often involving the Achilles tendon and extensor tendons of the digits, and corneal arcus before age 45 years, are highly specific findings for FH, whereas tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are much less common.1,3,6Intertriginous planar xanthomas, typically in the interdigital webspaces, are pathognomonic for homozygous FH.1,3,7If xanthomas develop, they usually appear after the third decade of life in heterozygotes and as early as the first decade in homozygotes.6,7 Another genetic disorder to consider is familial hyperchylomicronemia syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder associated with variations in lipoprotein lipase; however, unlike FD, it is associated with transient eruptive xanthomas and very elevated plasma triglycerides.8Lastly, sitosterolemia (ie, phytosterolemia or xenosterolemia) is an autosomal recessive disorder (caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous variants inABCG5/ABCG8genes) in which the body accumulates excess plant sterols.9This disorder shares several clinical features with other inherited lipid disorders, including xanthoma formation and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease,3,9and could be considered but it would be dismissed through laboratory and clinical assessments. Similar to FH and in contrast to FD, patients often present early in life with tendon xanthomas.9What distinguishes sitosterolemia from FH, FD, and other lipoprotein disorders is the presence of markedly elevated plasma levels of plant sterols3,9; these patients may have elevated total cholesterol levels, but a standard lipid panel does not provide specific diagnostic information.9

caption: Dermoscopic findings of an 8-mm red nodule on the scalp show irregular red lacunae without septa and irregular linear vessels (A), and hematoxylin-eosin staining shows a vascular proliferation in dermis and subcutis composed of ectatic thin-walled vessels containing multiple branching structures (B).
scenario: An otherwise healthy man in his 40s was referred to our dermatology clinic for a slowly growing tumor on the scalp. Skin examination revealed an 8-mm red, firm, mobile nodule on the left temporal scalp. On dermoscopic evaluation, irregular red lacunae with irregular vessels and absence of septa were observed (Figure 1A and B). The lesion was excised for histopathologic analysis.
explanation: Hematoxylin-eosin staining of the lesion demonstrated a well-circumscribed dermal vascular tumor extending to the superficial subcutaneous tissue and composed of ectatic thin-walled vessels with multiple intravascular branching papillary structures (Figure 1B). These structures were covered by swollen endothelial cells with numerous intracytoplasmic eosinophilic hyaline globules, positive on periodic acid−Schiff (PAS) (Figure 2). The papillae core contained collagenous stroma, pericytes, and normal-appearing capillary vessels. Tumor vessels were positive for CD-31, and negative for D2-40 (podoplanin) and HHV-8; α-smooth muscle actin highlighted the pericytes in the papillae. The basal membrane and stroma inside the papillae were positive for collagen IV. Papillary hemangioma (PH) is a benign tumor that was first described in 2007 by Suurmeijer et al.1To our knowledge, only 16 cases have been described in the English-language literature.1-4Most of the reported cases have occurred in male adults on the head and neck.2Histopathologic mimickers of PH include tufted angioma (TA), Masson tumor (MT), intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia, and glomeruloid hemangioma (GH), among others. Most of these neoplasms exhibit intravascular capillary proliferations similar to PH. TA differs from PH in that it presents as a slow-growing plaque, most frequently in children and young adults. In some cases, this lesion has been associated with hyperhidrosis or hypertricosis. On dermoscopic examination, skin colored to light pink structureless areas have been described. TA may develop Kasabach-Merritt phenomena, which does not occur in PH. Histopathologically, TA presents multiple lobules of packed capillaries scattered throughout the dermis and the subcutis separated by normal stroma (cannonball pattern). Unlike PH, papillary structures or hyaline globules are not seen. MT is a reactive proliferation of endothelial cells secondary to an unusual thrombus within a vein, a proliferation inside a preexisting vascular lesion, or rarely, associated with a hematoma. MT affects young adults and presents as a bluish or red nodule or papule on the extremities.5Histologically, the papillary structures of MT are characterized by an acellular fibrous core coated by endothelial cells. These papillae lack capillaries, and it is sometimes possible to observe thrombosis in different stages of organization within the dilated vessel. GH is the most important PH histopathological differential diagnosis because both conditions show a proliferation of capillary vessels within a dilated vascular structure and hyaline globules; however, its clinical presentation and associated diseases differ. Clinically, GH presents as multiple, small, red papules on the trunk and limbs, with a rapid onset of days or few weeks.6,7In contrast, PH presents in adults as a solitary tumor on the head and neck. Additionally, GH is considered to be a hallmark finding of POEMS (polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal plasma cell disorder, skin changes)6and TAFRO (thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever, reticulin fibrosis, and organomegaly) syndromes. PH has no associated underlying diseases. Cases reported as solitary GH without associated disease are likely PH.2,8 On dermoscopic examination, GH displays red lacunae and/or red-white backgrounds, linear irregular vessels, and red rounded structures.6,7In the present case, PH dermoscopic findings showed red lacunae without septa, white structureless areas, and irregular vessels. These findings have not been previously described. Histopathologically, there are important architectural differences among these. GH is a superficial dermal proliferation composed of a big sinusoidal central vessel with multiple capillaries inside forming loops, which resemble a kidney glomerulus. GH lacks a prominent stroma and substantial pericytes.8PH is a deep dermal to subcutaneous tumor composed of interconnected intravascular papillae with abundant stroma, pericytes, and scant capillaries. In both GH and PH, swollen endothelial cells with hyaline globules may be observed. These globules correspond to thanatosomes, secondary lysosomes that would represent cellular damage.9 In some cases, differentiating GH from PH can be challenging. Suurmeijer et al8reported that the best immunohistochemical marker to differentiate GH from PH in complex cases is collagen IV, which is abundant in the stroma and shows a thick basement membrane in PH and a thin basement membrane in GH. Recently, somatic variations inGNA11andGNAQwere described in pediatric cases of PH.GNA11andGNAQvariants could be an aid in PH differential diagnosis.10In conclusion, we report a case of PH with its clinical and histologic characteristics and describe the dermoscopic features of PH. It is important for clinicians to be familiar with this entity because confusion with GH may lead to unnecessary laboratory testing.

caption: Clinical images of hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules on the dorsal hand (A), and Wood lamp examination demarcating the hypopigmented lesions (B).
scenario: A woman in her 60s presented for evaluation and treatment of oral lichen planus. During regular follow-up in our clinic, on physical examination, we noticed hypopigmented and depigmented patches next to multiple light brown hyperpigmented macules, 2 to 4 mm in diameter, on the dorsal aspects of her hands and cheeks (Figure 1A). These findings were asymptomatic. Mucosal findings included a lattice-like network of white lines, typical of oral lichen planus. The nails were normal. Wood lamp examination revealed demarcated borders of hypopigmented lesions (Figure 1B). During repeated questioning, the patient stated that she had noted these pigmentation changes since childhood. In addition, her parent and sibling have similar findings.
explanation: A 4-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained from a hypopigmented macule on the dorsal hand. The epidermis showed dense hyperkeratosis and hypergranulosis. The papillary dermis showed sparse perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates. Immunohistochemical analysis with Fontana-Masson (Figure 2) and MART-1 stains showed absence of melanin in the basal layer. Whole-exome sequencing analysis of DNA extracted from the patient’s blood revealed a heterozygous variation in the adenosine deaminase acting on RNA1 (ADAR1) gene c.2559_2560delinsGCC (p.Asn853LysfsTer5). This frameshift variation is expected to produce a premature stop codon. Thus, a diagnosis of dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (DSH) was made. DSH is a rare pigmentary genodermatosis that is acquired by autosomal dominant inheritance. DSH is mostly reported from countries in East Asia, mainly Japan.1Hyper- and hypopigmented macules appear during early childhood and increase in size and number until puberty; they darken with sun exposure. DSH involves the distal extremities, predominantly the dorsal aspects of the hands and feet while the palms and soles are spared. The face may be affected, whereas the mucosa is usually spared.2 DSH is caused by variations inADAR1, located on chromosome 1q21.3. It encodes a double-stranded (ds) RNA-editing enzyme that converts adenosine to inosine (A-to-I) posttranscription. This modification decreases the amount of endogenous dsRNA, thus reducing its recognition by the immune system. The exact mechanism associatingADAR1function to depigmentation remains unclear. ReducedADAR1function may lead to decreased A-to-I RNA editing in keratinocytes, elevated dsRNA levels, and subsequent activation of interferon pathways as well as increased cytokine production.3,4Therefore, Shallev et al4suggested that reducedADAR1editing activity may contribute to autoimmunity, such as in psoriasis. Accordingly, a few cases of psoriasis coexisting with DSH have been reported.3 The differential diagnoses in this case included reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura (RAK), familial progressive hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation (FPHH), and xeroderma pigmentosum (XP). RAK is a rare autosomal dominant genodermatosis, characterized by atrophic, hyperpigmented, and reticulated macules, with no accompanying hypopigmentation. These macules develop during childhood on the dorsal aspects of the hands and feet and spread during adulthood. Another feature is a break in the dermatoglyphics. Biopsy specimen findings show epidermal atrophy and elongated rete ridges, with an increased amount of melanin. Loss-of-function variations in the disintegrin and metalloproteinase 10 gene,ADAM10, underlie RAK.2 FPHH is characterized by diffuse hyperpigmented and hypopigmented patches, which present during infancy and increase in both size and number during childhood. FPHH has no associated systemic symptoms. Biopsy specimen taken from hyperpigmented patches show increased melanin in the basal layer, whereas hypopigmented patches show decreased melanin. The underlying gene isKITLG.2,5 Lastly, XP is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by increased sensitivity to UV radiation. An early clinical sign is severe sunburn after short sun exposure during infancy. During childhood, these patients develop hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules on the dorsal aspects of hands and feet, face, and other exposed areas. There is a highly increased risk for cutaneous neoplasms, sunlight-induced ocular involvement, neurological degeneration, and internal malignancies. The disease is associated with defective nucleotide excision repair, or error-free bypass (XP-variant) of UV-induced DNA damage.2,6 This is a rare case of DSH in a patient who is not Asian, and the first to our knowledge to present with coexisting lichen planus.
