The role ofADAR1in autoimmunity raises the question of whether it also plays a role in the pathogenesis of lichen planus, or whether this was just a coincidence.

caption: A, Thin, deeply erythematous plaque with studded papules and pustules interspersed in the lesion located on the right anteromedial thigh. B, Photomicrograph of a hematoxylin-eosin–stained section from the right anterior thigh.
scenario: A male patient was evaluated by the dermatology inpatient consult service. He reported a 5-week history of a skin lesion on the right anterior thigh with intermittent itching and mild tenderness to palpation. There was no preceding trauma to the area. The lesion was stable in size. He denied systemic symptoms of fever, chills, cough, shortness of breath, and dyspnea on exertion. He was unhoused and sleeping on the streets with his dog prior to hospitalization. Physical examination was remarkable for a 5-cm erythematous plaque studded with papules and pustules (Figure 1A). No pus or granules could be expressed with pressure. The patient had no similar skin lesions elsewhere on the body. A 6-mm punch biopsy was obtained from the lesion. One half was sent for routine histopathology with special stains, and the other half was submitted for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial culture (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathologic sections demonstrated foci of mixed granulomatous inflammation in the deep dermis containing thick-walled fungal yeast forms with equivocal budding (Figure 2), which were highlighted by Grocott-Gömöri methenamine stain. The fungal morphology raised the possibility ofBlastomycesinfection. Further tests and evaluation, including urineBlastomycesantigen, serumBlastomycesantibodies, HIV serology, chest computed tomography, and brain magnetic resonance imaging, were unrevealing. Given the unremarkable imaging, the patient was diagnosed with a deep dermal fungal infection, possibly representing primary cutaneous blastomycosis. While fungal culture results were pending, he began taking empirical itraconazole, 200 mg, 3 times daily for 3 days, followed by itraconazole, 200 mg, 2 times daily for an additional 1 to 2 weeks with input from the infectious disease department. Despite attempts to reach the patient, he was lost to follow-up after hospital dismissal. The fungal cultures ultimately grewTrichophyton verrucosum3 weeks later. The treatment plan outlined herein was considered adequate, if followed as directed. Dermatophyte infections occur frequently worldwide and often affect the stratum corneum, hair, and nails. Most infections in humans are caused by 3 types of dermatophytes:Trichophyton, Microsporum, andEpidermophyton.1In immunocompetent hosts, these dermatophytes may not penetrate beyond the stratum granulosum. Severe dermatophytosis is not well described but can be generally categorized as extensive or invasive. Invasive dermatophytosis is defined by dermal invasion that presents in 2 clinical forms: Majocchi granuloma or deep dermatophytosis.2 Primary cutaneous blastomycosis should be included in the differential diagnosis because it demonstrates round thick-walled yeast forms with broad-based budding.3In this patient’s scenario, urine antigen and serum antibodies forBlastomyceswere negative; additionally, cultures grewTrichophyton. Given the infrequency of deep dermatophytosis in an immunocompetent host, as well as the fact that the patient lived in an area endemic forBlastomyces, blastomycosis was originally favored as a result of availability bias. It was important to avoid premature closure, particularly given the negative serum and urine test results forBlastomyces. Three prior case reports have illustratedT rubruminfection mimickingBlastomyces, with sporelike shapes and pseudobudding on histological findings.3-5This ambiguity in fungal morphology reaffirms the importance of verifying organism classification through polymerase chain reaction or fungal culture to ensure appropriate therapy and systemic evaluation. Granulomatous pyoderma gangrenosum could be considered in the differential diagnosis because it also showcases granulomatous and suppurative inflammation on histopathology.6However, there is usually ulceration with undermined edges. Fungi would not be identified on special stains. Furthermore, pyoderma gangrenosum is a diagnosis of exclusion, and other causes of mixed dermal inflammation must be ruled out.6Cryptococcoid Sweet syndrome is a rare histopathologic variant of Sweet syndrome named for the presence of basaloid, pseudoyeast forms on tissue that do not actually represent fungus.7,8These forms are negative with fungal special stains, vacuolated in a way that mimics encapsulation, and smaller than those seen here. Primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma typically presents with a monomorphic infiltrate of atypical lymphocytes, which show a predilection for the epidermis and may form Pautrier microabscesses.6Oftentimes, lymphocytes show irregular nuclear contours and may display cerebriform or convoluted nuclei,6which were not seen in the histopathology of the present patient. Although there is no standardized treatment for deep dermatophytosis, systemic antifungals such as terbinafine, fluconazole, and itraconazole have been reported to be efficacious.4,9Clinicians should remain suspicious of fungi as a potential cause of deep-tissue infection in both immunocompromised and immunocompetent patients. Fungal culture or polymerase chain reaction should be performed to confirm pathogen speciation.

caption: A, Erythematous annular thin plaques without surface change on the patient’s right cheek and an erythematous, edematous plaque on the patient’s nose. B, Erythematous, edematous, annular papules and plaques on the patient’s left upper arm.
scenario: An 11-year-old girl presented to the dermatology clinic in autumn with an asymptomatic rash on her arms, face, and legs of a 3-week duration. She was otherwise healthy with a history of having seasonal allergies and taking cetirizine. She had negative results from the review of systems and denied any recent illnesses, vaccinations, or new medications. Physical examination was notable for erythematous annular thin plaques without surface change on her right cheek (Figure 1A), an erythematous, edematous plaque on her nose (Figure 1A), and erythematous, edematous, annular papules and plaques on her arms, hands, and thighs (Figure 1B). A biopsy specimen was obtained from the right arm for histopathologic analysis.
explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed a subtle thickened basement membrane zone and lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate (Figure 2). The patient was prescribed topical corticosteroids. Two months later, the patient presented to the dermatology clinic for worsening rash and new sun sensitivity. Laboratory examination revealed positive findings for speckled antinuclear antibodies (titers ≥1:160), antidouble-stranded DNA antibodies, anti-Smith antibodies, antiribonucleoprotein antibodies, and anti-Ro/Sjögren syndrome A antibodies. Complete blood count test results showed leukopenia (white blood cell count of 0.003/μL). Aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase levels were elevated at 59 U/L and 69 U/L, respectively. The patient’s mother at this time reported that the patient had been fatigued more recently with nonspecific abdominal and shoulder pain. The patient demonstrated overlapping features of acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE) and subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE), pointing to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). She had antinuclear antibody levels of more than 1:80 (entry-level criterion) and had 21 weighted points across 4 different domains according to the American College of Rheumatology/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology classification criteria for the diagnosis of SLE (the minimum requirement is 10 points). Therefore, her disease was classified as SLE.1 The patient’s rash improved dramatically with sun protection. Referred to the rheumatology division, she started a 200-mg hydroxychloroquine regimen 5 days per week (<5 mg/kg/d). The results of a liver evaluation pointed to lupus hepatitis. Test results for viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, celiac disease, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, and elevated α1-fetoprotein were negative. This case report details a unique presentation of ACLE and SCLE overlapping as initial signs of SLE in a pediatric patient. Cutaneous lupus erythematosus can be subdivided into the acute, subacute, and chronic forms. In pediatric patients, the chronic form is most common, while the acute and subacute forms are rare. Because the subacute form (SCLE) is exceedingly rare in the pediatric population, this presentation is even more distinctive. The localized form of ACLE may present as photosensitivity and the characteristic butterfly malar rash, sparing the nasolabial folds, while generalized ACLE can present as a morbilliform rash on sun-exposed skin. SCLE classically presents in patients as annular psoriasiform erythematous plaques without scarring.2,3This patient exhibited photosensitivity consistent with ACLE and annular plaques on her arms that were consistent with SCLE. The plaques on her arms lacked scales; although common in SCLE, scales are not necessary for diagnosis. This overlapping presentation of ACLE and SCLE in a pediatric patient has not yet been described in the literature, to our knowledge, and thus may be underrecognized. Differential diagnosis of an erythematous annular eruption with no surface change in a pediatric patient includes urticaria, polymorphous light eruption (PMLE), and interstitial granulomatous drug reaction (IGD). Urticaria is defined as the sudden development of pruritic transient wheals and angioedema or both. The histopathologic characteristics include upper dermal edema with a mild mixed perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils, basophils, and neutrophils. The interface dermatitis that was noted in this case is not a typical feature of urticaria. Additionally, the rash found in this patient was completely asymptomatic and was not transient.4 PMLE, a common photodermatosis, causes pruritic lesions on sun-exposed skin, sparing the face. The photosensitive cutaneous manifestations of lupus erythematosus can be difficult to distinguish from PMLE. The presence of antinuclear antibodies was an early differentiating criterion, but recent studies have established that patients with PMLE can also have elevated antinuclear antibody titers. The histologic characteristics of PMLE are nonspecific and may not distinguish PMLE from lupus erythematosus. In this case, the onset of symptoms in autumn, in addition to joint pain, leukopenia, and facial rash, makes PMLE less likely.5 IGD can have a wide clinical presentation. The skin lesions are usually asymptomatic and have a predilection for the trunk and extremities. The histologic characteristics of IGD are characterized by histiocytes scattered throughout the dermis typically arranged around foci of degenerated collagen and may form small granulomas. The histopathologic characteristics in this case did not include histiocytes but instead, an interface dermatitis that would not be seen in IGD.6 Diagnosing annular erythematous eruptions in pediatric patients can be challenging. This case report highlights diverse lupus erythematosus presentations, emphasizing the need for a thorough workup for prompt diagnosis and treatment.

caption: On examination, there were scattered, well-defined, annular gray hyperkeratotic plaques with an atrophic center with a slightly elevated edge on the scrotum, buttock, groin, and intergluteal cleft (A). Biopsy findings included hyperkeratosis, irregular papillomatosis, parakeratotic column (cornoid lamella), and several dyskeratotic keratinocytes in the epidermal invagination with hypogranulosis and perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes in the dermis (B; hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A man in his 40s presented with a 10-year history of pruritic lesions on the scrotum and buttock. He was diagnosed with eczema and treated at the local clinic with little improvement. He had no relevant medical history and no family history of similar skin problems. Physical examination revealed scattered, well-defined, annular gray hyperkeratotic plaques with an atrophic center and a slightly elevated edge on the scrotum, buttock, groin, and intergluteal cleft (Figure 1A). There was no inguinal adenopathy, and results of routine blood work, including blood biochemistry, syphilis serologies, and HIV testing, were normal or negative. We took 2 specimens from the scrotum and buttock, respectively, for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathological examination of both specimens revealed hyperkeratosis, irregular papillomatosis, parakeratotic columns (cornoid lamella) overlying dyskeratotic keratinocytes, and hypogranulosis with a perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes in the dermis (Figure 2). Based on the skin lesion location and clinical and histological findings, a diagnosis of genital porokeratosis (GP) was confirmed. The patient was treated with topical imiquimod cream with good response, and the plaques became thinner with focal disappearance. He is receiving regular medication and follow-up. Porokeratosis is a group of epidermal keratotic disorders characterized by well-demarcated annular lesions with cornoid lamella histologically. Porokeratosis can affect the whole body surface but rarely involves the genitogluteal area. GP, a rare variant of porokeratosis, presents as pruritic or asymptomatic centrally atrophic annular plaques with raised keratotic margins involving the penis, scrotum, or vulva. Biopsy findings include 1 or a few cornoid lamella on histopathology.1 GP mostly affects middle-aged to elderly men and has no family history.1The cause remains unclear. Repeated frictional and scratching trauma due to the humid climate, tight-fitting underclothes, or a contact reaction to some agents may contribute to the pathogenesis of GP.2Some factors, such as genetic variation, environmental change, immunosuppression, drug intake, virus infection, and UV exposure, also may play an important role. Once diagnosis is clarified, porokeratosis should be actively treated because of its potential malignant transformation. In general, the risk of cancer is greater in long-standing, larger lesions; among elderly and immunocompromised patients; and in the clinical types of linear porokeratosis and porokeratosis of Mibelli. GP is relatively difficult to diagnose due to its rarity. The diagnosis of GP is based on the clinical and histopathological manifestations. Dermoscopic findings can assist in the diagnosis with demarcated annular lesions and central pigmentation with dotted vessels surrounded by a keratotic peripheral rim.3,4 Clinically, GP may mimic verruca vulgaris,5but the latter is typically not annular and presents as papillomatous papules and plaques, and pathological findings include hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and identifiable koilocytes, associated with fingerlike vascular-pattern features surrounded by whitish halos in dermoscopy. Bowenoid papulosis presents as isolated or multiple red-brown papules and plaques in the anogenital area with a skin biopsy demonstrating acanthosis with full-thickness epidermal atypia, and dermoscopic findings include brown linear dots or globules as well as glomerular vascular structures.6Porokeratosis ptychotropica appears as verrucous plaques in a butterfly pattern, mostly involving the natal cleft and the buttocks but sometimes also on the genital area. Often, biopsy findings include multiple cornoid lamellae.7 Therapeutically, surgical treatment includes excision, cryosurgery, dermabrasion, electrodesiccation, and carbon dioxide laser vaporization.8,9For more widespread lesions, long-term medication management, including topical 5-fluorouracil, 5%; topical calcipotriol; imiquimod cream; and oral aromatic retinoids, may treat the disease.2However, it has been difficult to develop therapeutic protocols for GP due to underreporting. Most patients have only symptomatic relief with poor response to various treatments.

caption: Erythematous, nondesquamative, annular plaques, some with overlying vesicles in a cluster of jewels pattern on the flexor aspect of the wrists (A) and the lower limbs (B).
scenario: A woman in her 80s presented with mildly pruritic skin lesions on her upper and lower extremities that had progressively appeared during the previous month. The patient had no systemic symptoms or unexplained weight loss. Physical examination revealed erythematous, nondesquamative, annular plaques, some of which had overlying vesicles in a cluster of jewels arrangement on the flexor aspect of both wrists and lower limbs (Figure 1). There was no mucosal involvement, and the Nikolsky sign test result was negative. Chest radiography results were normal and laboratory studies—complete blood cell count, kidney, and hepatic function; urinalysis; and indirect immunofluorescence—were unremarkable except for positive circulating IgG against desmoglein-1 antigen. A skin biopsy specimen was collected from a lesion on the anterior aspect of the left wrist for histopathologic and immunofluorescent analyses, and treatment with oral prednisone (30 mg/d) tapering for 1 month was initiated.
explanation: Histopathologic examination of the biopsy specimen from a lesion on the anterior surface of the left wrist revealed perivascular superficial dermatitis with abundant eosinophils, epidermal spongiosis, and intraepidermal vesicles filled with eosinophils (Figure 2). Direct immunofluorescence analysis demonstrated epidermal positive intercellular C3 and IgG deposition. By the 1-month follow-up, the skin lesions had resolved rapidly with the treatment administered. No recurrence was observed at the 6-month follow-up. First described by Jablonska et al in 1975,1pemphigus herpetiformis (PH) is an intriguing bullous disease considered to be a rare subtype, accounting for approximately 7% of pemphigus vulgaris (PV) cases.2The age range of onset is 2 to 92 years, with only 6 pediatric patients reported.3,4Clinical features include erythematous, vesicular, bullous, or papular pruritic lesions that appear in a clustered pattern and tend to be annular, probably due to centrifugal spread of the inflammatory process.3For this reason, skin lesions may acquire a rosette or cluster of jewels pattern similar to that of typical linear IgA bullous dermatosis lesions—ie, the present case. In PH, regardless of the area of skin involved, there is no involvement of the mucous membranes.1,5 Suggested criteria for the diagnosis of PH3are the presence of intercellular epidermal IgG and/or C3 on direct immunofluorescence microscopy and a grouped distribution of pruritic, erythematous, vesicular/bullous/papular lesions, often in an annular pattern. For this reason, PH has been described as a combination of the clinical features of dermatitis herpetiformis or linear IgA bullous dermatosis with the immunologic features of PV.5Other variable diagnostic features include the presence of eosinophilic or neutrophilic spongiosis or intraepidermal microabscesses with or without acantholysis, intercellular IgG on indirect immunofluorescence microscopy, and the detection of circulating IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein-1 and/or -3 or desmocollin-1 and/or -3. Given that clinical and histologic findings are often atypical, immunopathology is most reliable for diagnosing PH.5 PH is considered to have a more favorable prognosis compared with other autoimmune bullous diseases and typically, a good response to dapsone, which is the first line of treatment with or without the addition of low-dose systemic corticosteroids.3However, dapsone was not necessary for treating this patient given the rapid resolution with an initial administration of oral corticosteroids alone. Although the association with other diseases and malignant neoplasms is rare and has only been observed in individual case reports, a comprehensive work up should be performed when any sign or symptom suggests malignancy.3 In the context of PH, the differential diagnosis of herpes simplex virus, bullous pemphigoid (BP), and linear IgA dermatosis (LAD) must be carefully considered.3In herpes simplex virus, clinical presentation may be similar to that of PH, with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base; however, histologic examination reveals shallow vesicles and ulcers with ballooning keratinocytes, necrosis, and characteristic cytopathic changes, eg, multinucleated cells and eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions.6BP differs from PH in that it presents with pruritic tender vesicles and eosinophilic infiltrates in the dermis, with IgG and C3 staining in the basal membrane zone and circulating autoantibodies against BP180 and/or BP230 antigens. Finally, LAD may present with a clinical picture very similar to PH, with vesiculobullous arciform lesions in a cluster of jewels configuration, but with a neutrophilic infiltrate on histopathologic results, and IgA and C3 deposition in the basal membrane zone, with circulating autoantibodies directed against LAD-1 and BP180. PH is speculated to exist within a spectrum alongside PV and pemphigus foliaceus, with reported transitions between these diseases, likely associated with epitope expansion mechanisms.7In contrast to classic pemphigus, PH shares similarities with other pemphigus subtypes that showcase substantial inflammation sometimes leading to acantholysis.8Notably, many patients with PH and desmoglein-3 autoantibodies (typically associated with mucosal involvement in PV) do not exhibit mucosal lesions, suggesting the involvement of alternative pathophysiologic mechanisms in shaping the distinct phenotype of PH and setting it apart from the classic form of pemphigus.9

caption: A, Clinical presentation of unilateral skin hardening on the right thigh, accompanied with mild hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation. B, Magnetic resonance imaging of the right thigh demonstrated slight thickening of subcutaneous tissue and T2 signal abnormality (arrowhead).
scenario: An 11-year-old boy presented to our department with progressive unilateral skin hardening on his right thigh and buttock for 7 years. Recently, the motion of his right limb joint was slightly limited. He was born to healthy parents and did not have any medical disease. On physical examination, there was an ill-defined, stony-hard plaque involving his right thigh above the patella extending to his right buttocks with loss of skin elasticity. The affected skin was associated with mild hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation (Figure 1A). Laboratory tests revealed normal results for routine blood tests, autoantibodies, immunoglobulins, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right thigh demonstrated slight thickening of subcutaneous tissue and T2 signal abnormality (Figure 1B). A skin biopsy was taken from the affected thigh for histopathological examination and alcian blue staining.
explanation: C. Segmental stiff skin syndrome Histopathological examination revealed normal epidermis and a mild pigmentation along the basal layer with a subtle increase in density of fibroblasts extending to the subcutis and forming adipocyte entrapment but no evidence of inflammation. Dense reticular dermis extended below well-preserved appendages (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining revealed an increased expression of CD34 in the reticular dermis. Alcian blue staining was negative. Based on the clinical morphology, histological features, and results of magnetic resonance imaging examination, the diagnosis of segmental stiff skin syndrome (SSS) was confirmed. The patient was treated with physical therapy to prevent joint contracture. SSS is a rare cutaneous connective tissue disorder characterized by stony-hard skin, mild hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation. It often occurs in areas with rich fascia, such as buttocks and thighs. Extracutaneous features are also common, including abnormal gait and posture, joint contractures, and restricted movement of chest and abdomen.1The cause and pathogenesis of SSS is obscure, although it has recently been reported to be associated with primary fibroblast disorder, primary fascial dystrophy, or heterozygous mutations in theFBN1gene.2,3 Segmental SSS is a distinct clinical variant of SSS, with the same histopathologic characteristics as generalized SSS, including thickening and compactness of collagen fibers in dermis with entrapped adipocytes, no infiltration of inflammatory cells, no atrophy of adnexa, and thickening of fascia. Segmental SSS has the characteristics of unilateral predominance, later onset, and lack of evolution into a generalized disease. SSS is associated with mutation in theFBN1gene, likely resulting in profibrotic activity.4 The diagnosis of segmental SSS may be difficult clinically due to its rare or atypical presentation. The differential diagnoses should include linear morphea, linear connective tissue nevi, and eosinophilic fasciitis. Linear morphea is a variant of localized scleroderma presenting with unilateral skin tightness and induration in a linear distribution following the Blaschko lines. It tends to have a later onset as well as more localized and asymmetric alterations of the skin.5Pathologically, linear morphea is characterized by homogenization of collagen bundles in the dermis and subcutis associated with lymphoplasmacytic infiltration and perivascular inflammation.6Eosinophilic fasciitis is considered a variant of scleroderma presenting with sudden-onset, rapidly appearing tender swelling, which is gradually replaced by symmetrical, platelike hardness of the distal limbs. Eosinophilic fasciitis may have onset following very strenuous physical exercise.6Cutaneous involvement may be accompanied by peripheral eosinophilia and systemic symptoms including fever, weight loss, fatigue, and asthenia.7Linear connective tissue nevi is a hamartomatous lesion characterized by painless, normal skin-colored or hypochromic plaques or nodules of slow growth in linear arrangements, which often involve the trunk and limbs during early childhood.8Pathologically, it typically presents as an irregular increase of collagen fibers in the dermis without fibroblastic proliferation. Early recognition of segmental SSS may help prevent joint contracture and avoid inappropriate medical treatment. Treatment of SSS is limited and unsatisfactory. Losartan and mycophenolate mofetil have antifibrotic properties and have been reported to provide mild and moderate improvement in patients.9Rehabilitation exercises at an early stage could prevent joint restriction and preserve mobility. A 2023 study showed that secukinumab may provide an additional supplementary treatment of SSS by improving skin stiffness and range of motion.10

caption: A, Clinical image of confluent erythema with scales on the abdomen. B, Histopathologic findings shows psoriasiform hyperplasia, diffuse parakeratosis and spongiosis, hypogranulosis, necrotic keratinocytes with intense eosinophilic cytoplasm in the epidermis. Dermis showed superficial perivascular dermatitis, with focal vacuolar degeneration at the interface, which suggests graft-vs-host disease–like dermatitis (original magnification ×10)
scenario: A woman in her 30s with myasthenia gravis diagnosed at age 27 years presented to the emergency department with severe erythroderma over the past 2 months. She had excision of a thymoma 10 years before, which was classified as type B2 according to the World Health Organization histologic classification system. She reported severe pruritus in the affected area. She had no history of skin diseases, allergies, or cardiovascular disease. Medications for the patient’s myasthenia gravis included prednisone tablets (20 mg daily), tacrolimus (1.5 mg twice per day), pyridostigmine bromide (30 mg daily), and losartan potassium (50 mg daily) for hypertension. On presentation, the patient’s temperature was 37.8 °C; heart rate, 120 beats/min, blood pressure, 120/65 mm Hg; and oxygen saturation levels, 97% on room air. On physical examination, the confluent erythema with scales involved more than 95% of body surface area, including the patient’s head, trunk (Figure 1A), and extremities, but results on mucosal examination were unremarkable. Laboratory testing results revealed whole white blood cell count of 12 200/μL (81.6% neutrophils; to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001); C-reactive protein levels, 5.58 mg/dL (to convert to mg/L, multiply by 10.0); aspartate aminotransferase levels, 0.7 µkat/L (to convert to IU/L, multiply by 0.0167); alanine aminotransferase levels, 45 IU/L (to convert to µkat/L, multiply by 0.0167); and lactate dehydrogenase levels, 454 IU/L (to convert to µkat/L, multiply by 0.0167). Skin biopsy from the abdomen was performed for histopathologic examination (Figure 1B).
explanation: Skin biopsy results revealed a psoriasiform hyperplasia, diffuse parakeratosis and spongiosis, hypogranulosis, and necrotic keratinocytes with intense eosinophilic cytoplasm. There was subtle, focal vacuolar degeneration at the interface (Figure 2). The fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-positron emission tomographic (PET) computed tomographic (CT) scan showed a mass in left anterior mediastinum with high FDG uptake, which indicated recurrent or residual thymoma. Thymoma-associated multiorgan autoimmunity (TAMA) was diagnosed. In this patient, the location of the recurrent thymoma posed a great surgical risk and reoperation was abandoned.1The IL-23/Th17 pathway in myasthenia gravis relating to thymoma was active2; therefore the patient was given a combination treatment of radiotherapy (total of 60 Gy in 28 fractioned doses) for the recurrent thymoma and subcutaneous injection of ixekizumab. After 2 months of presentation, the patient’s skin symptoms were greatly improved. Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD)–like dermatitis can be a presenting sign of TAMA.3TAMA is defined as an autoinflammatory disorder of the liver, intestines, or skin in patients with malignant thymoma who have not undergone hematopoietic stem cell transplant.3TAMA is a very rare disease, and its cutaneous manifestations are even less reported.4-7GVHD-like dermatitis with diffuse erythroderma with or without scaling located on the face, trunk, extremities, palms, and soles. Although the prevalence of TAMA is unknown, it appears to be higher among Asian populations.7 The underlying mechanisms of TAMA are still not clear, but it is believed to be related to altered T-cell development and selection in thymoma, which eventually develops into autoimmunity.8A serological immune cell absolute value count was investigated in this patient, and we found an increase in CD4+T-cell count, a decrease in nature killer cell count and B cell count, and CD8+T-cell count was within the normal range, supporting altered T-cell selection in this patient. The differential diagnosis of GVHD-like erythroderma includes paraneoplastic autoimmune multiorgan syndrome, erythrodermic psoriasis, and drug eruption.6,7In this patient, the liver function elevation and histopathologic findings of subtle vacuolar change with high necrotic keratinocytes in the epidermis supports TAMA over erythrodermic psoriasis; the clinical history and course did not support a drug eruption; paraneoplastic autoimmune multiorgan syndrome is characterized by typical mucosal erosions and skin involvement characterized by histopathologic findings of acantholysis or interface dermatitis; direct immunofluorescence findings include intracellular and/or linear basement membrane deposition of immunoreactants. Indirect immunofluorescence findings may be positive, and patients can have circulating antibodies to desmoplakin, envoplakin, cadherins, or other intercellular proteins.7 Until recently, no consensus on treatments of TAMA has been established. It involves treatment of thymoma such as thymectomy, radiotherapy or chemotherapy, systemic and topical steroids, oral cyclosporine, intravenous immunoglobulin, extracorporeal photopheresis, and narrow-band UV-B phototherapy.6-9Resection of the thymoma is the most important way to improve the prognosis and is recommended whenever possible.5However, more than half of reported patients died from serious infectious diseases secondary to the use of high-dose systemic steroids10or chemotherapy for unresectable thymoma,8especially after GVHD-like erythroderma onset.8TAMA also has been associated with increased risk of opportunistic infections as well as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.10In this case, no sign of infections or other complications were observed after a half year of treatment.

caption: A, Hyperkeratotic plaques with distinct borders and annular appearance. B, Histopathology of an erythematous scaly plaque revealed hyperkeratosis, spinous cell vacuolization, and vesicles in the epidermis (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A full-term girl was born with multiple areas of erythema, vesicles, and bullae on the face, trunk, and extremities. Her vital signs, including temperature, respiration, and heart rate, were within normal ranges. One month later, she returned due to skin eruptions that continued to wax and wane. Physical examination revealed multiple round or irregularly shaped erythematous macules and slightly scaly plaques of various sizes on the face, trunk, and extremities. Bullous and vesicular lesions were observed on the thighs, with scattered facial erosions. Mucous membranes were not found to be affected. She was born to healthy, nonconsanguineous parents. Growth and development were normal for her age and sex. The patient’s family medical history was unremarkable. A skin-punch biopsy and direct immunofluorescence (DIF) assays taken from 1 of the erythematous scaly plaques were performed for further analysis. At the 3-year follow-up, it was found that the vesicles and bullae began to decrease in number when she was 6 months old but intermittently returned after 1 year of age. The number of annular hyperkeratotic plaques had increased (Figure 1A). Thickened, brown, corrugated plaques developed over the neck, armpits, wrists, and ankles, along with palmoplantar hyperkeratosis.
explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, distinct vacuolization in the granular and upper spinous layers (Figure 1B andFigure 2), and bullae formation within the epidermis, with sparse inflammatory cells in the superficial dermis. The DIF results were unremarkable. Whole-exome sequencing revealed a heterozygous variation c.482T>C (p. L161P) inKRT1, which is typically detected in epidermolytic ichthyosis.1,2Accordingly, the diagnosis of annular epidermolytic ichthyosis (AEI) was confirmed. AEI, first described by Sahn et al in 1992, is a rare autosomal-dominant nonsyndromic ichthyosis. AEI is a milder phenotype of epidermolytic ichthyosis (EI) caused byKRT1andKRT10, which are expressed in suprabasal keratinocytes and maintain cytoskeletal stability and skin barrier function.3Keratin variations result in increased transepidermal water loss and inflammation on exposure to noxious environmental factors.4Typical features of AEI include superficial erosions, vesicles and bullae with or without erythema early on, and recurrent migratory annular and polycyclic erythematous plaques on the trunk and extremities.5Palmoplantar keratoderma (PPK) is associated withKRT1variations, rather than those ofKRT10.2,3During the intermittent period, all lesions, excluding PPK in patients withKRT1variations, demonstrate near-complete resolution, distinguishing AEI from the major EI forms.3AEI’s histopathology is characterized by epidermolytic hyperkeratosis.6Management of AEI includes symptomatic treatments, including emollients, topical keratolytics, calcipotriol, and systemic agents, such as retinoids. Secukinumab, an interleukin-17α inhibitor, may be an effective remedy for AEI based on the common immune profile of psoriasis.7 Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) is a rare autoimmune disease in childhood.8Typical manifestations of SCLE include annular polycyclic plaques evolving from erythematous plaques, as observed in this patient. However, the lesions are usually distributed in photosensitive areas. Serum markers, including anti-Ro/SSA, antinuclear, and anti-La/SSB antibodies, are generally positive, and C4 levels are frequently low.8Typical histopathology of SCLE includes epidermal atrophy, hydropic degeneration of basal cells, dermal edema, and mononuclear cell infiltration around dermal blood vessels. Additionally, the DIF demonstrates fine granular or dustlike immunoglobulin G depositing on epidermal keratinocytes.8 Annular erythema of infancy is benign, with self-resolving progression and unclear cause. Initially, it manifests as small erythematous papules and evolves into annular or polycyclic urticarial plaques.9The age at onset is usually within 1 year of birth but ranges from the first day of life to 4 years old.9Multiple sites, including the trunk, extremities, and face, are generally affected. Histopathological examination reveals a perivascular mixed lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with increased eosinophils. Tests such as anti-SSA/Ro and anti-La/SSB antibodies and rapid plasma reagin are recommended to exclude serious systemic and infectious diseases.9Annular erythema of infancy lesions usually resolve without atrophy or scarring. Netherton syndrome (NS) is a rare, multisystemic, autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused bySPINK5variations. It classically presents as congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma with hair shaft abnormalities and atopic diathesis.10Erythematous plaques with double-edged marginal scale are typical features of NS. It can be misdiagnosed as similar disorders, including AEI, because patients do not always exhibit the complete triad. Histopathology of NS shows hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and superficial dermis perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. Negative lymphoepithelial Kazal-type–related inhibitor immunostaining may suggest NS. AEI is rare and easily confused with other annular erythematous diseases, particularly during early stages. This case emphasizes the typical features of annular epidermolytic ichthyosis, which are vital for early diagnosis. In infants presenting an erythematous annular polycyclic rash, an inherited ichthyosis should be considered in the differential diagnosis.

caption: A, Clinical image of fast-growing subcutaneous nodule in the glabella. B, Spindle cells arranged in a storiform to loose fascicular pattern admixed with a sclerotic stroma and scattered erythrocytes (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A woman in her 20s presented with a firm, mobile, painful, and fast-growing subcutaneous nodule in the glabella (Figure 1). Ultrasonography performed in B mode with a high-frequency (6-18 MHz) linear transducer revealed a hypoechoic lesion with well-defined borders in the hypodermis. After 2 months, the nodule had increased and seemed to be adhered to deep layers. A computed tomography scan was performed, which showed a 0.8 × 1.5 × 1.5-cm ovoid subcutaneous lesion with well-defined borders located in the glabella. The lesion was not affecting the epidermis and reached the muscular layer in depth without eroding bone structures. Given these findings, the lesion was excised.
explanation: The histopathologic examination revealed sections of mesenchymal proliferation consisting of mildly pleomorphic spindle and stellate cells arranged in a storiform to loose fascicular pattern admixed in a sclerotic stroma. Scattered lymphocytes, multinucleate giant cells, extravasated erythrocytes, and pseudocystic spaces were present (Figure 2). The immunohistochemical study results showed diffuse positivity for actin and negativity for desmin, S100, CD34, and factor XIIIa. Considering the histological findings and immunohistochemical profile, as well as the fast-growing nature of the lesion, nodular fasciitis (NF) was diagnosed. NF is a benign and often self-limited myofibroblastic neoplasm that usually manifests as a fast-growing nodule on the limbs or trunk. Head and neck involvement is more common in children and accounts for 7% to 20% of cases.1,2The peak incidence is in the third and fourth decades.3Awareness of this entity is of great importance, as NF may be misdiagnosed as a sarcoma due to its rapid growth, high cellularity, and sometimes prominent mitotic activity. Traditionally, NF was considered a reactive lesion likely triggered by trauma. However, recent studies have identifiedUSP6gene rearrangements in most cases of NF, often withMYH9as a fusion partner, confirming the neoplastic nature of the lesion.3,4 Histologically, NF lesions are composed of spindle to stellate cells with bland nuclei, arranged in short fascicles in a tissuelike culture growth. The stroma may be myxoid or collagenous. Pseudocystic spaces, mitotic figures, extravasated erythrocytes, and inflammatory cells are common findings. Immunohistochemical testing is useful to confirm the diagnosis. The lesional fibroblastic/myofibroblastic cells are typically positive for smooth muscle actin and muscle-specific actin and negative for S100, CD34, desmin, and factor XIIIa. Skeletal muscle involvement is usually limited and superficial and appears to be more frequent in the head and neck region.1 Differential diagnosis is broad and should be made with other spindled cell neoplasms. Cutaneous solitary fibrous tumor usually manifests as a slow-growing subcutaneous nodule that may resemble a cyst or a lipoma. Histologically, it is composed of spindled cells with a patternless architecture in a stroma with staghorn vessels and contains alternating hypercellular and hypocellular areas. Immunohistochemistry results are positive for CD34 and STAT6.5Deep benign fibrous histiocytoma arises in subcutaneous or deep soft tissue and is characterized by bland ovoid to spindle cells arranged in a storiform pattern with admixed lymphocytes. Foam cells, multinucleate giant cells, and staghorn vessels are common findings.6CD163 is expressed in most cases of deep fibrous histiocytoma, and CD34 may show weak and patchy positivity in the periphery.7,8Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is a slow-growing tumor histologically composed of monomorphic spindle cells arranged in a storiform distribution that infiltrate the hypodermis in a honeycomb pattern. CD34 positivity is an immunohistochemical hallmark.9 Surgical removal of NF is considered the treatment of choice. However, some cases may undergo spontaneous regression. For lesions occurring in the face, intralesional corticosteroid injections or pinhole CO2laser may be recommended to reduce the potential aesthetic disfigurement. Nevertheless, a sufficiently deep skin biopsy should be performed first to rule out sarcoma.2,10

caption: A, Multiple pink papules and umbilicated nodules on the face. B, Numerous yeasts surrounded by hyaline capsules (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A man in his 20s presented to the dermatology department with a monthlong history of gradually progressing papules and nodules on the face, accompanied by fever, fatigue, and weight loss. On physical examination, multiple pink papules and umbilicated nodules were found on the face (Figure 1A). He had a 5-year history of HIV infection but self-discontinued his antiretroviral treatment due to treatment-related gastrointestinal and neurologic reactions 4 years prior. A biopsy specimen was taken for pathological examination (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathology of a biopsy specimen showed numerous yeast forms surrounded by clear spaces (Figure 1B andFigure 2). The white blood cell count was 2040/μL, and the CD4-positive lymphocyte count was 2/μL (to convert both to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). Multiple enlarged lymph nodes were found in the neck, axilla, groin, and posterior peritoneum. Capsular polysaccharide antigen ofCryptococcus neoformansin the serum and cerebrospinal fluid was positive. Fungal cultures of blood and cerebrospinal fluid were also identified asC neoformans. T-cell spot test for tuberculous was negative. A diagnosis of disseminated cryptococcosis was made. Liposomal amphotericin B and fluconazole were given to treat cryptococcosis, and antiretroviral therapy was restarted for HIV infection. The cutaneous symptoms resolved after 2 months. Fungi are major contributors to the opportunistic infections and death in patients with HIV/AIDS.1,2Cryptococcosis can affect any organ system, especially the brain, lungs, skin, bones, and vasculature, and is often generalized.3Cutaneous manifestations of cryptococcosis include acneiform papules, molluscum contagiosum–like lesions, Kaposi sarcoma–like lesions, ulcers, pustules, plaques such as eczematous plaques, nodules, abscesses, subcutaneous swellings, and cellulitis.1There are 2 histopathologic types: granulomatous and gelatinous. The former type shows fewer yeasts and scant necrosis, while the latter type is characterized by numerous organisms with little inflammation. The yeast is oval, measuring 5 to 12 μm in diameter, enclosed by a capsule that presents as an empty space around yeast in hematoxylin-eosin preparations.4These yeasts are not actually intracellular. Umbilicated rash is a typical skin feature of cryptococcosis in immunocompromised patients and needs to be distinguished from talaromycosis5and histoplasmosis.6A comprehensive evaluation is necessary to make diagnostic confirmation by laboratory testing and biopsies of affected areas. Talaromycosis is an opportunistic mycosis caused byTalaromyces marneffei(formerlyPenicillium marneffei), which is a dimorphic fungus. A biopsy specimen exhibits numerous round fungal structures, 2 to 4 μm in diameter, packed within histiocytes or scattered through the tissue. Tissue culture growsT marneffei.7Histoplasmosis, a widespread disease, is caused by 2 distinct organisms in humans:Histoplasma capsulatumvarduboisiiandHistoplasma capsulatumvarcapsulatum. Common skin lesions of histoplasmosis include hemorrhagic, maculopapular eruption, and ulceration; patients with HIV are at higher risk for infection. Histopathologic examination of histoplasmosis lesions reveals dermal granuloma with small, narrow-budding yeasts often found within macrophages. Anti-Histoplasmaantibodies can be detected.8Lobomycosis is a chronic, deep fungal infection caused byLacazia loboi.It is characterized by the appearance of slowly developing keloidlike cutaneous lesions. Histopathological assessment shows dermal granulomas with multinucleated giant cells filled with fungal cells 6 to 12 μm in diameter with doubly refractile walls.9 Diagnosis requires a high level of clinical awareness and confirmation by culture and histopathology. Criterion-standard antifungal therapy remains the combination of amphotericin B deoxycholate and flucytosine.2

caption: A, Pink papule on the right arm. B, Papule with telangiectasias and white background on dermoscopy.
scenario: A woman in her 60s with previous breast carcinoma diagnosed 11 years prior, currently in complete remission, presented with pruritic lesions on her upper body. Physical examination revealed more than 10 monomorphous, 5- to 10-mm, pink papules with telangiectasias and white background on dermoscopy, distributed on the chest, arms, and back (Figure 1). There were palmoplantar keratosis and pits. The patient underwent thyroid ultrasonography, abdominal ultrasonography, colonoscopy, and central nervous system magnetic resonance imaging. These explorations revealed 1 Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS) level 5 lesion, a kidney mass, and more than 100 colonic polyps.
explanation: Shave biopsy specimens were obtained for pathologic examination (Figure 2) and revealed well-circumscribed, nonencapsulated dermal nodules with hypocellular, thickened, and homogenized eosinophilic collagen bundles arranged in a laminated manner with intervening prominent clefts. Histopathological examination findings were consistent with sclerotic fibroma or storiform collagenoma. A second nodule on the patient showed similar findings. Multiple sclerotic fibromas can be associated with Cowden syndrome (CS) or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2). Given the presence of acral pits, the patient fulfilled a pathognomonic criterion for CS according to the International Cowden Consortium diagnostic criteria. Five biopsied polyps were hamartomatous polyps. The samePTENvariation was detected in the skin and hamartomatous polyps. Furthermore, DNA analysis in peripheral blood detected aPTENmosaicism with an allelic frequency of 5.5%. CS is an autosomal dominant genodermatosis, withPTENvariations occurring in 35% of patients. It is characterized by the presence of cutaneous lesions and systemic neoplasms, either benign or malignant, such as thyroid carcinoma, breast carcinoma, colonic hamartomatous polyposis, kidney carcinoma, and dysplastic gangliocytoma of the cerebellum (Lhermitte-Duclos disease), among others. Cutaneous lesions related to CS include trichilemmomas, acral keratosis and acral pits, mucocutaneous neuromas, oral papillomas, and sclerotic fibromas.1,2Dermoscopic features of sclerotic fibromas were first reported in 2018 by Ebadian et al.3They described the presence of a white background with peripheral arborizing vessels.3This dermoscopic pattern can also be seen in atypical dermatofibromas, late stages of sclerotic dermatofibromas, and amelanotic blue nevi.3,4 MEN2 syndrome is characterized by the presence of thyroid medullary cancer, pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism. Cutaneous features associated with MEN2 are sclerotic fibromas, macular amyloidosis (MEN2A), and mucosal neuromas (MEN2B). MEN2 is caused byRETvariations that interplay with the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B/mammalian target of rapamycin (PI3K/AKT/mTOR) pathway, wherePTENalso participates. This close association could explain the overlapping clinical findings in CS and MEN2.5 Neurofibromatosis type 1 is caused by variations in theNF1gene and also entails a higher risk for breast carcinoma. Cutaneous findings encompass cafe-au-lait macules, axillary and groin freckling, and neurofibromas.6Histologically, neurofibromas are composed of delicate cells with an oval or spindle-shaped nucleus in a light pink stroma.6-8Multiple eruptive dermatofibromas are an uncommon clinical entity characterized by the appearance of multiple dermatofibromas in a short period of time. While initially defined as the presence of 15 dermatofibromas, 5 to 8 dermatofibromas in 4 months has more recently been considered as sufficient to establish the diagnosis. It has been associated with lupus erythematosus and HIV infection, but it also has been detected in healthy individuals. Dermoscopic features of dermatofibromas are diverse, including sclerotic fibromalike features, but the most typical appearance is the presence of a central white area surrounded by a delicate pigmented network.9Clinically, dermatofibroma is typically a firm papule that dimples inward with lateral pressure. In the current patient, CS presented with subtle cutaneous lesions, which permitted the identification of the syndrome and its multidisciplinary approach.

caption: A, Clinical image demonstrating papulopustules and ovoid ulcerated plaques with elevated, pink borders on the elbows. B, Tzanck smear using Wright-Giemsa staining of specimen demonstrating ballooning of keratinocytes and peripheralization of nuclear material (original magnification ×20).
scenario: A man in his 30s with AIDS presented with acute-onset painful scattered umbilicated papulopustules and ovoid ulcerated plaques with elevated, pink borders on the face, trunk, and extremities (Figure, A). The patient also had a new-onset cough but was afebrile and denied other systemic symptoms. Due to his significant immunocompromise, the clinical presentation was highly suspicious for infection. For rapid bedside differentiation of multiple infectious etiologies, a Tzanck smear was performed by scraping the base of an ulcerated lesion and inner aspect of a pseudopustule and scraping its base with a #15 blade. These contents were placed on a glass slide, fixed, and stained with Wright-Giemsa and subsequently Papanicolaou staining to further characterize the changes seen.
explanation: The photographs demonstrate a Tzanck smear using Wright-Giemsa stain (Figure, B) with large ballooning keratinocytes with peripheral nuclear staining seen in a patient with subsequently polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-confirmed mpox. Mpox is a member of the pox virus family, which presents with nonspecific symptoms such as fever followed by characteristic skin changes including macules, papules, vesicles, and pustules progressing with cephalocaudal spread or in the genital and/or gluteal region in the most recent outbreak. On histopathologic findings, mpox features vary depending on the stage of the lesion.1,2Early lesions tend to demonstrate ballooning degeneration, whereas later lesions have few viable keratinocytes.2The viral cytopathic changes, most often seen in pseudopustular lesions, include multinucleated keratinocytes with ground glass appearance and nuclear contents pushed to the periphery, resulting in a basophilic halo.2The lack of a true pustule with collections of neutrophils in the stratum corneum have led some to describe these lesions as pseudopustular. Tzanck smear is an inexpensive, rapid, and simple technique to perform cytologic analysis from skin. Initially described in 1947 by Arnault Tzanck for diagnosing vesiculobullous disorders, it is commonly used in diagnosing herpetic infections, which have characteristic features of acantholysis, acute inflammation, and keratinocytic ballooning and specific nuclear changes of molding, multinucleation, and chromatin margination.3The findings of acantholysis and nuclear cytopathic changes are similarly seen in histopathologic examination of herpes simplex virus (HSV). Herpetic infections may present with clustered vesicles with a pink inflammatory rim, although more verrucous lesions have been described in immunosuppressed patients. In the Tzanck smear from a lesion of mpox in this patient (Figure, B), enlarged keratinocytes were seen with expanded cytoplasm and nuclear material pushed to the periphery, and the nuclear changes associated with HSV were all absent. The observed difference in cytologic features including the nuclear material rimming or pushed to the periphery of the cells is due to the location of viral replication; herpes viruses replicate in the nucleus, whereas mpox replicates in the cytoplasm.4Although not part of routine practice, Papanicolaou staining was performed in this case to confirm infected cells and provide additional nuclear detail because Tzanck smears in patients with mpox were not previously reported. The findings highlighted the peripheralization of nuclear material in cells with eosinophilic staining, confirming the keratinocyte origin to the cells. A background inflammatory infiltrate was noted and can be seen in most infections. Tzanck smear can also be used to diagnose other viral and fungal infections. Molluscum contagiosum, which presents with multiple umbilicated papules, demonstrates the characteristic large (30-40 µm) ovoid homogenous basophilic staining keratinocytes called Henderson-Patterson bodies that correspond to the identically named intracytoplasmic inclusions seen on histopathologic findings.5,6Using bedside diagnostics (including Wright Giemsa staining), blastomycosis is diagnosed with 8- to 15-µm spores with broad-based budding, similar in appearance to the organism in histologic examination.5Histoplasmosis has small (2 to 3 µm) intracellular organisms in macrophages with artifactual clearing (pseudocapsule).5Both of these fungal infections may manifest clinically as nonhealing ulcerations, verrucous plaques, or multiple papules or nodules and can histologically demonstrate pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with characteristic organisms. The use of the Tzanck smear in diagnosis of any infection depends on the timing of the lesion and is most sensitive with vesicular or pustular lesions.6Although we only tested 1 stage of lesions, we hypothesize this test will similarly be more sensitive for earlier lesions in patients with mpox. Tzanck smear is a useful technique that can be used to differentiate mpox from other infections at the bedside or in remote settings where PCR or additional culture techniques are not easily accessible. Infection prevention and control precautions are important to help prevent additional spread of this virus with sharp injuries, and caution with unroofing of the lesions is critical to avoid additional spread.7Knowledge of the cytologic differences of mpox compared with other viral infections is important in the early recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of these patients.

caption: A, Multiple well-defined brown erythematous scaly plaques with central scarring, saddle nose deformity, and necrotic lesions on the ear with loss of ear cartilage. B, Perforation of the hard palate. C, Infiltrate of foamy histiocytes and pigmented yeasts without multiaxial septation (Fontana-Masson).
scenario: A woman in her 30s presented for evaluation of asymptomatic erythematous scaly plaques over the face and proximal extremities. The lesions started as an erythematous papule on the face, which had progressed to larger plaques within 10 years. There was involvement of the upper respiratory tract, causing palatal perforation and stridor, necessitating a tracheostomy a year ago. In addition, there was history of wheezing and breathlessness. There was no history of preceding trauma, fever, malaise, joint pain, cough, epistaxis, hemoptysis, or hematuria. Examination revealed multiple well-defined brown erythematous scaly plaques with central scarring measuring 2 × 1 to 8 × 7 cm on the face, arm, and thighs. The patient also had saddle nose deformity, perforation of the hard palate, and necrotic plaques on the ear, causing destruction of ear cartilage (Figure, A and B). There was cervical lymphadenopathy: multiple, nontender, discrete nodes, ranging from 1.5 to 2 cm without any surface changes. The results of sensory examination and peripheral nerve examination were within normal limits. Respiratory examination and chest radiography results were normal. Hemogram showed anemia (hemoglobin, 10.1 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0]); the results of a kidney function test, a liver function test, a fasting blood glucose test, and routine urinalysis were within normal limits. Serologic analysis results for HIV-1/2, antinuclear antibody, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Punch skin biopsy was obtained for histopathologic analysis and culture (Figure, C).
explanation: Histopathologic results showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, parakeratosis, dense dermal infiltrate of histiocytes, foamy histiocytes, neutrophils, and multinucleate giant cells along with pigmented hyphae. Fungal skin culture showed black yeastlike colonies characteristic ofExophiala spiniferaspecies. Based on clinical presentation, histopathologic analysis, and fungal culture, the diagnosis of phaeohyphomycosis was made. The patient will be treated with intravenous amphotericin B, followed by itraconazole. Phaeohyphomycosis is a rare subcutaneous mycosis caused by dematiaceous fungi found in soil, wood, and decomposing vegetation. The disease, caused by dematiaceous fungi, is classified into 2 types based on fungal forms in the tissue: phaeohyphomycosis (presence of yeasts and hyphae) and chromoblastomycosis (muriform bodies). The literal meaning ofphaeohyphomycosisis dark fungus with hyphae. The pigment melanin in the fungus is a virulence factor that inhibits phagocytosis by scavenging free radicals produced by the host. The common etiological agents areExophiala,Aureobasidium,Cladosporium,Alternaria,Phialophora,Wangiella, andCurvularia.1Phaeohyphomycosis can affect skin, subcutaneous tissue, paranasal sinuses, and, rarely, the central nervous system. Commonly, it presents as asymptomatic cystic swelling on exposed areas, usually after traumatic inoculation involving the hands, feet, and legs. Facial involvement is uncommon and can extend to involve the upper respiratory tract, causing perforation of the palate and destruction of the nasal bridge, leading to mutilation and disfigurement.2-4Other rare presentations include verrucous plaques, erythematous papules, and noduloulcerative lesions. The diagnosis can be confirmed by demonstration of pigmented septate hyphae with occasional globose swelling on histopathologic analysis and fungal culture. Panfungal real-time polymerase chain reaction is an emerging tool in the diagnosis of phaeohyphomycosis. Treatment with azole antifungal agents (itraconazole, posaconazole, or voriconazole) is the mainstay of treatment. Other treatment options include amphotericin B, terbinafine, flucytosine, and griseofulvin along with physical modalities, such as excision, heat therapy, and cryotherapy.5 The common deep mycoses that can cause mutilation include chromoblastomycosis, hyalohyphomycosis, blastomycosis, and phaeohyphomycosis. Both chromoblastomycosis and phaeohyphomycosis are caused by dematiaceous fungi. Chromoblastomycosis (option A) is commonly caused byFonsecaea pedrosoi,Fonsecaea monophora, andCladophialophora carrioniiand usually presents with localized, verrucous, hyperkeratotic, irregular plaque on distal extremities with scarring.6Hyalohyphomycosis (option B) is a rare opportunistic fungal infection caused by various fungi, which produce nonpigmented septate hyphae. It has myriad presentations, which include erythematous macules, papules, vesicles, indurated verrucous plaques, necrotic ulcers, and discharging sinus.7Blastomycosis (option C) is a suppurative fungal infection caused byBlastomyces dermatitidis, endemic in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, the Great Lakes, and the Saint Lawrence River. It presents with papulopustular lesions, violaceous nodules, plaques, abscesses, ulcers, and verrucous or crusted lesions on exposed body parts.8All these infections can have systemic involvement. Chromoblastomycosis involves lungs, lymph nodes, and bone, and hyalohyphomycosis primarily affects paranasal sinuses and lungs. Blastomycosis involves lymph nodes, bone, prostate, and testis, and phaeohyphomycosis commonly involves lungs and heart. All the differential diagnoses show suppurative granuloma on histopathologic analysis; the establishment of the respective fungal form helps in confirming the diagnosis. Chromoblastomycosis is characterized by thick-walled, multicellular, globe-shaped, cigar-colored inclusion bodies with multiaxial septation calledsclerotic bodies(Medlar bodies).6Hyphae in cross-sections in the index case resembled Medlar bodies, and the absence of septation was a clue indicating phaeohyphomycosis.7Hyalohyphomycosis is characterized by nonpigmented septate hyphae, and culture helps in confirming the diagnosis.8Large (8-15 μm) thick-walled yeast cells, prominent broad-based budding, and centrally retracted cytoplasm help in the diagnosis of blastomycosis.9 Although many clinical differential diagnoses were considered in the case presented, histopathologic analysis and culture played decisive roles in arriving at a diagnosis of phaeohyphomycosis. This case highlights the importance of recognition of rare presentation of deep mycosis and the value of histopathologic analysis and fungal cultures in establishing the right diagnosis.

caption: A, Multiple pruritic erythematous to violaceous lichenified papules and plaques on the left shin. B, Close-up of the skin lesions showing an erosion with partially detached epidermis and multiple milia. C, Histopathologic examination revealed dermoepidermal separation (hematoxylin-eosin stain). D, Histopathologic examination revealed several milia (hematoxylin-eosin stain).
scenario: A woman in her 30s presented with progressive, multiple itchy erythematous to violaceous papules and plaques localized to the left shin for more than 10 years (Figure, A and B). On close inspection, milia and a few erosions with partially detached epidermis were identified. There were no abnormalities of the mucous membranes, nails, hair, or teeth. No extracutaneous involvement was observed.
explanation: C. Epidermolysis bullosa pruriginosa (EBP) We performed a skin biopsy under the impression of prurigo nodularis and to exclude hypertrophic lichen planus. Histopathologic examination revealed a dermoepidermal cleft (Figure, C) and several milia (Figure, D) in the superficial dermis, features that were inconsistent with either PN or HLP but suggestive of epidermolysis bullosa (EB). Whole-exome sequencing using genomic DNA extracted from the patient’s peripheral blood mononuclear cells identified a novel heterozygous missense variant, c.6832G>T, p.Gly2278Trp, inCOL7A1(NM_000094), which was graded as “likely pathogenic” based on American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics guidelines. Further inquiry of the patient led to identification of 2 other affected family members: 1 who had typical EBP (intensely itchy, symmetric, hypertrophic papules and plaques on both shins) and nail dystrophy, and another, who only had dystrophic toenails. Sanger sequencing confirmed cosegregation of this variant with variable phenotypes, supporting its pathogenicity and the patient’s diagnosis of autosomal dominant EBP. The patient had a 2-year old relative who had only very mild nail dystrophy and no skin disease who also harbored this pathogenic variant. Epidermolysis bullosa is an inherited, heterogeneous group of rare genetic dermatoses characterized by mucocutaneous fragility, blister formation, and abnormal wound healing.1It is categorized into 4 major subtypes, EB simplex, junctional EB, dystrophic EB (DEB), and Kindler EB, based on the ultrastructural level of skin cleavage and inherent molecular pathology.2Dystrophic EB is caused by pathogenic variants in theCOL7A1gene, which encodes type 7 collagen. Epidermolysis BP is a rare subtype of DEB characterized by intensely pruritic, prurigo-like nodules and plaques affecting the lower legs, thighs, and arms, often associated with nail dystrophy.3Unlike other forms of EB, except for some localized subtypes of EB simplex and some rare late-onset forms of junctional EB, it is not uncommon for patients with EBP to present beyond the neonatal/childhood period, and sometimes well into adult life. Epidermolysis BP is traditionally considered a rare subtype of DEB, but it seems to be more prevalent in some countries, including Taiwan.4So far, no clear genotype-phenotype correlation has been established in EBP.5Epidermolysis BP is also often misdiagnosed as other dermatoses because blisters are often inconspicuous. Diagnostic clues of EBP include nail dystrophy, the most common associated feature of EBP,6as well as a history of blistering during infancy and family medical history of other subtypes of DEB,1which makes it distinct from factitial dermatitis. Although the histopathologic features of factitial dermatitis are nonspecific, milia are usually absent. In this case, however, the unilateral, localized presentation of EBP and undisclosed family medical history of EB at the patient’s initial visit made the diagnosis difficult. It was the milia and dermoepidermal separation on histopathologic findings that prompted subsequent genetic investigations. Still, had we been more vigilant, we might have noticed the milia and partially detached epidermis and put DEB in our initial differential diagnoses. The present case needs to be distinguished from PPPD, HLP, and LA. Overall, PPPD is characterized by extremely pruritic, discrete, smooth, flesh-colored to erythematous papules, caused by persistent rubbing of the anterior surface of the legs. Histopathologic features include minimal compact orthokeratosis, mild acanthosis with flattening of the rete ridges, and superficial and middermal perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrates with a variable number of eosinophils.7In most cases, there is evidence of superficial dermal fibrosis, characterized by the presence of multinucleated fibroblasts and thickened collagen bundles arranged in a random pattern, without the dermoepidermal cleft and milia seen in EBP. Hypertrophic lichen planus presents as extremely pruritic, violaceous, hyperkeratotic flat-topped papules and plaques affecting the extremities.8Histopathologic findings of HLP show compact orthokeratosis, acanthosis, wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, saw-tooth appearance of the undersurface of the epidermis with necrotic keratinocytes, and a band-like infiltrate of lymphocytes at the dermoepidermal junction, which is distinct from EBP. Generally, LA is the most common form of primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis, clinically characterized by pruritic, discrete hyperkeratotic hyperpigmented papules with a predilection for the shins.9The key component of the histologic findings is the deposition of pink amorphous amyloid material in the papillary dermis, which exhibits a bright apple-green birefringence under polarized light when stained with Congo red. These findings distinguish LA from EBP, despite both conditions presenting similar epidermal changes induced by chronic scratching.10 To our knowledge, this is the first case of unilateral EBP ever reported. This case highlights the importance of considering EBP even when the prurigo-like lesions are unilateral and without nail involvement. Milia and erosions provide diagnostic clues for such atypical cases, as in other subtypes of DEB.

caption: A, Clinical picture. B and C, Hematoxylin-eosin stain.
scenario: A female patient in her early 50s presented with multiple (approximately 10) bluish, partially keratotic papules and nodules on the lower legs (Figure, A). Since the age of 24 years, the lesions had been growing very slowly in number and size and had been bleeding occasionally after a trauma. The patient used a wheelchair due to a right-sided hemiparesis and hemianopsia caused by an intracranial hemorrhage. At the age of 4 years, recurrent seizures had led to the diagnosis of cerebral venous malformations. Clinical examination also demonstrated a lipolymphedema of the lower legs that had been attributed to a functional venous insufficiency with insufficient venous pump activity. The patient had been wearing compression stockings for years. The family history was positive for cerebral venous malformations involving the patient’s father and aunt, the father having died of an intracranial hemorrhage in his early 70s. Sonography of the skin lesions demonstrated intradermal slow-flow vascular malformations with a maximum diameter of 1.2 cm. A biopsy of a lower-extremity papule was performed (Figure, B and C). Mutational analysis resulted in the detection of a heterozygous pathogenicKRIT1variant.
explanation: B. Familial cerebral cavernous malformations Skin biopsy revealed a well-circumscribed lesion with hyperkeratosis and acanthosis of the epidermis overlying a conglomerate of dilated venous-like malformations with continuous smooth muscle in the upper dermis, partly showing thrombosis. Histomorphology together with a positive personal and family history of venous malformations and the identification of a pathologicKRIT1variant led to the diagnosis of familial cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) in the current patient. Cerebral cavernous malformations or cavernomas (International Society for the Study of Vascular Anomalies [ISSVA] simple vascular malformations III) are slow-flowing venous malformations that are lined by a single layer of endothelium with no involvement of brain parenchyma.1They can occur in sporadic (80%) or familial (20%) form, affecting up to 0.5% in the general population.2Familial CCMs are frequently inherited as multiple lesions in an autosomal dominant manner. Following the Knudson hypothesis, they are caused by germline loss-of-function variants inKRIT1,CCM2, orPDCD10in association with a somatic “second hit” in the other allele.3Among patients with CCMs, 40% to 70% present with neurological symptoms, such as seizures, focal deficits, and headaches due to intracranial hemorrhages. Extraneurological manifestations may involve the skin, retina, kidney, and liver. In a study of 417 patients with familial CMMs, 38 patients (9%) had cutaneous venous malformations, which is a higher rate than in the general population (0.3%).4In this study, the lesions were associated withKRIT1variants and further classified as hyperkeratotic capillary-venous malformations, capillary malformations, and venous malformations. Prognosis and management are determined by the location, number, and size of the cerebral venous malformations. Recent advances in understanding CCM pathophysiology have revealed new strategies to control disease progression, ie, Rho kinase inhibition by atorvastatin.5 Blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome (BRBNS; ISSVA simple vascular malformations III) is another rare disorder characterized by multiple, most commonly cutaneous and gastrointestinal venous malformations.1Skin lesions present as rubbery, bluish, easily compressible nodules since birth or early childhood.6Histopathology reveals large, thin-walled vessels with discontinuous or no smooth muscle separated by variable amounts of fibrous tissue scattered through the dermis.7Gastrointestinal malformations typically cause recurrent hemorrhages resulting in chronic anemia and may occasionally lead to volvulus, intussusception, or perforation. Thirteen percent of patients have central nervous system involvement.8Familial occurrence is extremely rare, as BRBNS is due to somatic double (cis) variants inTEK, the gene encoding endothelial cell tyrosine kinase receptor TIE2.9 Glomuvenous malformations or glomangiomas (ISSVA simple vascular malformations III) are bluish, tender, noncompressible papules and nodules of the cutis that histologically represent venous-like channels surrounded by 1 or 2 layers of glomus cells, and no intracranial involvement is seen.1Glomuvenous malformations are inherited in over 60% of cases in an autosomal dominant manner and are due to loss-of-function variants in the glomulin gene.7Verrucous venous malformations (ISSVA simple vascular malformations III) are sporadic congenital hyperkeratotic nodules—mainly on the legs—that show a deep vascular component and no further associations and, in particular, no intracranial involvement.1Histopathology reveals a compact hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, and acanthosis overlying dilated vessels extending into the deep dermis and the subcutis.7A somatic missenseMAP3K3variant has been recently identified.10

caption: Multiple firm skin-colored papules and nodules coalesce to form a large plaque on the anterior aspect of the left lower leg.
scenario: A woman in her 60s with long-standing thickening and induration of the legs presented with 1 week of left leg pain. The patient had previously been diagnosed with elephantiasis nostras verrucosa, and she was advised to elevate and compress the leg but was unavailable for follow-up. Her medical history was notable for morbid obesity, hypertension, diabetes, and stroke. She reported no fever, fatigue, weight changes, gastrointestinal symptoms, difficulty concentrating, anxiety, or hyperhidrosis. Physical examination results revealed multiple firm skin-colored papules and nodules coalescing to form a large plaque on the anterior aspect of the left lower leg, whereas the right lower leg had diffuse induration and hyperpigmentation (Figure 1). There was no palpable lymphadenopathy. Laboratory analysis revealed normal complete blood cell count, thyroid function, serum protein electrophoresis, and serum immunofixation. A biopsy of a left leg nodule was performed.
explanation: Histopathologic examination showed an atrophic epidermis, angioplasia with vertically oriented vessels, horizontal fibrosis, hemosiderin deposits, and increased mucin deposition, extending from the papillary to the reticular dermis (Figure 2). Pretibial mucinosis in a patient with euthyroid due to obesity and venous stasis was diagnosed. The patient’s cutaneous mucinosis was complicated by cellulitis, which resolved with a short course of antibiotics. Weight loss was recommended, and compression and leg elevation were suggested for the management of chronic skin changes. Detailed vascular studies to explain the asymmetry were planned, but the patient was unavailable for follow-up after multiple hospital admissions for her comorbidities. Classically, accumulation of mucin on the shins is associated with pretibial myxedema (choice A), prompting thyroid function testing. However, in a small percentage of patients with pretibial mucinosis, thyroid dysfunction is not identified.1Pretibial mucinosis in patients with euthyroid has been described in states of chronic stasis, such as venous insufficiency and obesity with lymphedema, termedpretibial stasis mucinosis and obesity-associated lymphedematous mucinosis(OALM).1,2These conditions often overlap and share a similar pathogenesis. Chronic venous insufficiency and/or obesity-associated lymphedema have been suggested to induce hypoxia, leading to angiogenesis and plasma protein extravasation, ultimately resulting in increased production and deposition of mucopolysaccharides.3 Patients with stasis mucinosis and OALM present with skin-colored to yellow-red papules, plaques, and/or nodules. Symptoms can be bilateral or asymmetric, involving a single extremity. Distinct histopathologic findings, such as epidermal atrophy, angioplasia with vertically oriented capillaries, increased stellate fibroblasts, and hemosiderin deposition, aid in confirming the diagnosis and differentiating it from other forms of cutaneous mucinosis.4Treatment entails weight loss and modalities that improve lymphatic and venous blood flow, such as compression stockings. Second- and third-line therapeutics include topical corticosteroids or intralesional corticosteroids, pentoxifylline, octreotide, plasmapheresis, and intravenous immunoglobulins. Differential diagnosis of multiple long-standing papules and nodules on the lower legs includes pretibial myxedema and elephantiasis nostras verrucosa (choice B) and lobomycosis (choice C). Clinical and histologic features are essential to differentiate these conditions. Pretibial myxedema in thyroid disease often precedes skin manifestations, and it is commonly associated with coexisting orbitopathy in Graves disease.4Histologically, it is characterized by mucin deposition in the upper dermis, with a grenz zone present in the superficial dermis.5Euthyroid pretibial mucinosis lacks this feature, showing mucin deposition throughout the dermis. Elephantiasis nostras verrucosa may be distinguished clinically from pretibial mucinosis, as it develops on the dorsa of the feet and extends proximally over time. It can be differentiated histologically by the presence of pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and exhibits dilated lymph channels in the early stages and extensive dermal fibrosis in the later stages. Mucin is absent.6Pretibial mucinosis nodules can be mistaken for lobomycosis, an uncommon fungal infection acquired in tropical areas of Central and South America, that is histopathologically is characterized by granulomas containing sclerotic bodies.7

caption: A, A tumor on the patient’s right shoulder.
