In some cases, as with the current patient, the morphologic characteristics can be reminiscent of a Lipschütz ulcer, which is typically seen in young, otherwise healthy female individuals and is also driven by EBV infection but not indicative of a lymphoproliferative disorder.5 Biopsy is needed to establish the diagnosis of EBVMCU and shows large, atypical lymphocytes, immunoblasts, and/or Reed Sternberg–like cells within a polymorphous infiltrate.1,4Staining with EBER, when performed, is invariably positive and may help to establish the diagnosis.1,6Treatment depends on the size of the lesion and the clinical context; smaller lesions may resolve spontaneously within 4 to 12 weeks.1,6,7When feasible, reduction of immunosuppression aids clearance. More extensive lesions associated with pain or frequent bleeding should be treated; in such cases, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vinblastine, and prednisone, as well as radiation therapy, have been successfully used.6,7 The differential diagnosis for this patient’s ulcers includes chronic ulcerative HSV infection, Crohn disease associated with pyostomatitis vegetans, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, and ulcers secondary to fungal infection. Chronic ulcerative HSV infection does not typically spontaneously resolve, and while histopathology may show a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate, atypical lymphocytes are not a common histopathologic feature. Pyostomatitis vegetans is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, and perianal ulcers and fistulas are often a feature of Crohn disease. However, in pyostomatitis vegetans, mucosal microabscesses and pustules coalesce on an erythematous base to form a “snail track” morphologic appearance8that may erupt, creating an ulcer; these features were not seen in this patient. Furthermore, large, atypical lymphocytes as seen in this case would not be expected in pyostomatitis vegetans. Isolated mucosal ulceration is an uncommon presentation of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, though oral mycosis fungoides may present as ulcers, erythematous plaques, or tumors.9However, histopathology for mycosis fungoides (including oral mycosis fungoides) shows an infiltrate of atypical lymphocytes at the dermoepidermal interface. Lastly, invasive fungal infections, including cryptococcosis and histoplasmosis, can present with mucosal ulcerations but histopathology often shows suppurative and granulomatous inflammation in the presence of fungal organisms.

caption: A, Erythematous plaques involving the right chest and flank at the initial presentation. B and C, Large atypical cells with clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm forming papillary and glandular architectures are present in the deep dermis; lymphovascular invasion was observed in the superficial and deep dermis (hematoxylin-eosin). D, Contrast-enhanced computed tomographic scan of the abdomen and pelvis showing a large heterogeneous mass in the right rectus abdominis muscle (blue arrowhead) and cystic lesion in the left ovary (pink arrowhead).
scenario: A woman in her 40s presented with painful erythematous plaques on her trunk (Figure, A). Skin lesions developed 2 months earlier and progressively spread. She reported abdominal discomfort, weight loss, and vaginal bleeding. A solid mass on her lower abdomen that had been palpable about 10 years prior had rapidly increased in size within the past few months. Physical examination revealed erythematous plaques on the right chest and flank without warmth. Punch biopsy of a lesion from the chest was sent for histopathological examination (Figure, B and C).
explanation: Results of histopathological examination showed atypical cells with intracytoplasmic vacuoles forming a glandular architecture in the deep dermis, and lymphovascular invasion was observed (Figure, B and C). Immunohistochemical staining results were positive for CK7 and negative for CK20, estrogen receptors (ERs), GATA-binding protein 3, gross cystic disease fluid protein 15, Wilms tumor 1 (WT1), and thyroid transcription factor-1. Findings from chest and abdominopelvic computed tomography revealed a 13-cm heterogeneously enhancing mass in the right rectus abdominis muscle and a 3-cm ovarian cystic lesion (Figure, D). Positron emission tomography/computed tomography findings revealed intense abnormal18F-fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the abdominal wall, lung, liver, and lymph nodes. Laboratory examinations revealed increased concentrations of lactate dehydrogenase (558 U/L; reference, 135-214 U/L; to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167), cancer antigen 15-3 (143.8 U/mL; reference, <26.4 U/mL; to convert to kU/L, multiply by 1.0), and cancer antigen 125 (2528 U/mL; reference, <35 U/mL; to convert to kU/L, multiply by 1.0), and a normal carcinoembryonic antigen level (2.2 ng/mL; reference, <6 ng/mL; to convert to μg/L, multiply by 1.0). The patient underwent debulking surgery, and pathologic examination revealed poorly differentiated carcinoma positive for MOC31, napsin A, and PAX8, and negative for calretinin, WT1, CK5/6, ERs, gross cystic disease fluid protein 15, and p53. The patient was diagnosed with primary peritoneal clear cell carcinoma (PPCCC) with multiple distant metastases. She underwent chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin, but the disease progressed continuously. Another metastatic lesion developed in her abdomen. Despite treatment with topotecan and cisplatin, she died 6 months after the initial diagnosis. Primary peritoneal carcinoma (PPC) is a rare malignant epithelial tumor, and PPCCC is an extremely rare subtype of PPC, with only 15 cases, to our knowledge, having been reported since 1990.1Because of its rarity, the clinical characteristics of PPCCC are not well understood. In the previous reports, all patients with PPCCC were female, and the average age was 53.7 years. The initial symptoms included abdominal pain, distension, and an abdominopelvic solid mass. Imaging studies commonly revealed large heterogeneous cystic and solid masses with a mean size of 13 cm. Histologically, PPCCC closely resembles primary peritoneal serous carcinoma and malignant mesothelioma. For diagnosis, extensive immunohistochemical staining is required. Primary peritoneal serous carcinoma expresses CK7, ERs, and WT1, but PPCCC is typically negative for WT1.1Malignant mesothelioma is typically positive for CK5/6, calretinin, and WT1, and negative for MOC31, but PPCCC shows the opposite features.1 Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis usually manifests as indurated erythematous to violaceous plaques symmetrically distributed on the lateral trunk and proximal extremities.2Histologically, interstitial and perivascular histiocytic infiltrates with small foci of collagen degeneration are observed in the reticular dermis.3Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis is often associated with rheumatic diseases, hematologic disorders, and internal cancers, but pathogenesis of interstitial granulomatous dermatitis is currently not well understood.3Wolf isotopic response is a rare cutaneous reaction in which a new and unrelated dermatosis occurs at the site of a previously healed dermatosis, most commonly in areas of post–varicella-zoster virus scarring.4Histologically, granulomatous and lichenoid reactions were frequently reported.5Cutaneous endometriosis usually manifests as reddish-brown nodules on the umbilicus or a firm mass on the scar site. Histopathological examination shows the columnar epithelium surrounded by stroma, which consists of capillary vessels, fibroblasts, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages.6 To our knowledge, cutaneous metastasis of PPCCC has not yet been reported. Primary peritoneal carcinoma most commonly metastasizes within the peritoneal cavity; metastases to the skin, liver, brain, lung, and breast are rarely reported.7Because PPC behaves similarly to ovarian carcinoma,7,8PPC may also manifest with lesions similar to those associated with ovarian carcinomas, such as inflammatory metastases, cicatricial plaques, or cellulitislike or lymphangitislike lesions,9and similar features can be expected in PPCCC. Patients with PPCCC are commonly treated with debulking surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin. Primary peritoneal clear cell carcinoma is considered to have a poor prognosis because the majority of patients die of the disease within 6 months or experience recurrence within 3 years.10Because of the poor prognosis, prompt diagnosis and optimal treatment are required.

B, A biopsy specimen taken from the edge of the depressed lesion showing normal epidermis and dermis, no inflammatory cell infiltration within the dermis, and somewhat diminished subcutaneous fatty tissue (hematoxylin-eosin). scenario: A 2-year-old girl who was otherwise healthy presented with a 10-month history of asymptomatic skin depressions in her neck, nape, and submandibular regions. The lesion initially occurred as an erythema in the neck and progressed centrifugally to the nape and submandibular areas. Atrophy was observed in the center of the lesion, surrounded by an erythematous border, with underlying blood vessels being visible deep to the atrophy (Figure, A). Cervical lymph nodes were palpable bilaterally. Tactile responses within the depressed as well as surrounding areas were normal. Other physical examinations were without abnormalities. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Her parents denied drug injection or trauma history. Results of routine laboratory tests, HIV test, serological test of antibodies forBorrelia, and antinuclear antibody test were within normal limits or negative. After obtaining informed consent from her parents, a biopsy specimen was taken from the edge of the depressed lesion for histological examination.

options.D: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn

distractors: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn
explanation: C. Lipodystrophia centrifugalis abdominalis infantilis Histopathologic examination revealed normal epidermis and dermis, no inflammatory cell infiltration within the dermis, and somewhat diminished subcutaneous fatty tissue (Figure, B and C). Results of direct immunofluorescence staining were negative. The subcutaneous fat of the skin lesion was considerably thinner than that of the surrounding area (Figure, D), and cervical lymph nodes were slightly enlarged bilaterally, as indicated from results of ultrasonic examination. We diagnosed lipodystrophia centrifugalis abdominalis infantilis (LCAI) based on clinical and histopathologic features and ultrasonic examination, and prescribed oral vitamin E and topical tacrolimus therapy for 4 weeks. The enlarged lymph nodes disappeared, and the erythematous margin resolved. The depressed lesions did not progress further during a 3-month follow-up period. Lipodystrophia centrifugalis abdominalis infantilis is a localized idiopathic lipodystrophy, first described by Imamura et al1in 1971, and mainly affects young children in Asian countries. At present, more than 168 cases of LCAI have been reported.2Lipodystrophia centrifugalis abdominalis infantilis has some characteristic features that may help confirm diagnosis, including (1) depression of the skin as a result of reduced cutaneous fat, (2) centrifugal spread of the depressed area, (3) erythema and scaling at the border of the lesion, (4) onset before the age of 3 years, (5) no associated abnormalities of other organs, and (6) histopathological findings of absent or decreased cutaneous adipose tissue in the depressed skin area and lymphocytic inflammatory infiltration in the surrounding areas.1,3Depressed lesions occur during the first 4 years of life, most commonly in the groin and neighboring areas, with minor erythematous changes around them.1,2Other areas of the initial rashes involve the abdomen, axilla, lumbar area, thighs, and chest and sometimes unusual sites, such as the neck, face, and head. To our knowledge, occurrence in the neck is still rare. The 2 most common presenting signs are depressions or atrophy and skin discoloration. The lesions in atypical areas should be differentiated from various disorders that may manifest as subcutaneous atrophy, localized skin depressions, or panniculitis, including morphea, lupus panniculitis, and subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn. These can be distinguished readily with characteristic clinical and pathologic features. Morphea en plaques typically present as central sclerotic depressions and hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation, with a border showing a characteristic violaceous ring, local anhidrosis, hairlessness, and being hard and smooth to touch. Histologically, morphea is a process of dermal (and sometimes subcutaneous) sclerosis. Early morphea lesions present with perivascular infiltrates of lymphocytes in the reticular dermis, swelling of endothelial cells, and partially thickened collagen bundles. Late morphea lesions are characterized by diminished inflammatory infiltrate, reduced capillaries and other small vessels, atrophy of eccrine glands, and thickened collagen bundles, as well as “fat trapping,” caused by collagen bundles infiltrating the entire dermis and partially extending into the subcutaneous fat.4Lupus panniculitis is a rare subtype of lupus erythematosus, which clinically presents with skin atrophy, infiltrative erythema, and painful and recurrent plaques or nodules. It mainly occurs in the neck, scalp, and proximal limbs. Previous reports of LCAI have described biopsy results that may overlap considerably with this entity, including lobular lymphocytic inflammation, perieccrine lymphocytic inflammation, and mucin deposition.5Other histopathologic features used to distinguish this entity from LCAI are liquefaction of basal epidermal cells, paraseptal lymphoid nodules around fat lobules containing germinal centers, and hyaline necrosis of fat.6Otherwise, direct immunofluorescence in patients with lupus erythematosus panniculitis may show immunoreactive deposition at the dermoepidermal junction.6Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn, a panniculitis characterized by fat necrosis, is a rare benign fat disorder that usually affects full-term newborns. It presents with well-defined erythematous sclerotic nodular fat necrosis. Common sites of occurrence include the cheeks, back, buttocks, arms, and thighs.7Results of histological examination show granulomatous necrosis in the subcutis, extensive inflammatory cell infiltration in the subcutaneous fat, adipocyte necrosis, and acicular fatty crystals in abnormal giant cells.7 The etiopathogenesis of LCAI remains unknown, and several hypotheses have been proposed, including trauma, infection, metabolic or genetic abnormalities, apoptosis, and immunological dysfunctions.8The lesions almost cease to enlarge by 13 years of age, with complete or partial recovery in more than 60% of patients.2There had been a case of successful treatment with topical tacrolimus,9but no effective therapy has been currently recommended. Fat transplantation can be considered for those with unresolved lipoatrophy.10

scenario: A man in his 40s with a medical history of factor VII deficiency hemophilia presented with acute hypoxic respiratory failure secondary to COVID-19. Following admission, he was intubated with prone positioning, and treatment with tocilizumab and dexamethasone was started. He was also found to haveStaphylococcus hemolyticusbacteremia, and treatment with cefepime was initiated. Three days after admission, the patient developed erythema and edematous necrotic plaques of the bilateral ears (Figure, A and B). No devices had been used on the ears. The necrosis progressed during the following days, primarily involving the earlobe of the right ear and a large portion of the helix of the left ear. A punch biopsy specimen was performed (Figure, C and D).
explanation: Results of the biopsy specimen of the left ear revealed epidermal and dermal necrosis and ulceration; there was also necrosis of the eccrine glands (Figure, D). Although eccrine necrosis is not a specific finding, it is a consistent finding in pressure necrosis. The necrotic plaques improved and then resolved after prone positioning was discontinued and further pressure on the ears was avoided. Pressure necrosis occurs from a lack of blood flow secondary to mechanical stress on the skin. Pressure necrosis in patients who are bedridden involves the sacral region. However, patients who are persistently hypoxemic often require prone positioning, subjecting other anatomic sites to prolonged pressures that exceed local capillary pressure.1Prone positioning, often greater than 16 hours a day, is used as a therapy for moderate-to-severe cases of COVID-19 that require intubation. A retrospective cohort study highlighted the high incidence of facial pressure injuries in patients with severe COVID-19 who require prone positioning (47.6%), with a substantial association of duration of proning with ulcer development.2 The differential diagnoses included levamisole-induced vasculitis. Levamisole, a synthetic imidazothiazole anthelminthic agent, is used as a cocaine-bulking agent and can produce painful purpuric macules and papules on the face and helix of the ears that progress to skin necrosis. Neutropenia is a common finding, but the diagnosis of levamisole-induced vasculitis depends heavily on a drug history. Additionally, histopathologic findings would have demonstrated a thrombotic vasculopathy with prominent fibrin thrombi.3 The incidence of acroischemia was shown to be 23% among patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome associated with COVID-194and is secondary to complement-mediated microvascular injury and the hypercoagulable state of COVID-19. A diagnosis of  acroischemia is less likely, however, because the patient had no laboratory coagulation abnormalities, and histopathologic results did not show findings of thrombotic vasculopathy. Additionally, acroischemia typically involves additional acral sites beyond the ears.5 Ecthyma gangrenosum (EG) presents with gangrenous ulcers with an erythematous and edematous base and affects critically ill patients.Pseudomonas aeruginosaaccounts for 74% of cases of EG, but other gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria can cause EG.6Histopathologic findings would have demonstrated a vasculitis or vasculopathy, often with direct invasion of vessels by the causative organism. Because of the global COVID-19 pandemic, there has been a dramatic increase in the number of patients requiring prone positioning. Although it may be possible to alleviate and minimize this complication by frequent repositioning and protective padding, clinicians should be aware of the potential for this complication in patients with COVID-19 who require extended periods of ventilation support.

caption: A and B, After immersing both hands in water for 10 mins, there were symmetrical white papules, white hyperkeratosis spots, and excessive wrinkling on the thenar eminence, wrist flexure of both hands, and dorsum of fingers and hands. C and D, A skin biopsy taken from white papules after water immersion for 10 mins showed hyperkeratosis, dilated eccrine ducts in the epidermis and dermis, and hyperplasia of the eccrine sweat glanda (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: An otherwise healthy man in his 20s presented to the dermatology department with thickening and swelling of hands after immersion in water, accompanied by burning pruritus for 3 years. The lesions occurred as symmetrical white and transparent papules, white keratosis, excessive wrinkling on the dorsum of hands after water immersion and worsened in summer, and remitted in winter. He was treated with topical tretinoin ointment intermittently per a diagnosis of chronic eczema at the local clinic with little improvement. The lesions gradually aggravated, and the affected area dispersed to wrists and elbows during past the 1.5 years. He attributed these changes to the need for washing hands frequently in the period of the COVID-19 epidemic. He had no family history of similar skin problems and did not have a history of hyperhidrosis, cystic fibrosis, atopy, or trauma to the hands. Physical examination showed some changes emerged on both hands after water immersion contrasting with any other condition (Figure, A and B). We took a skin biopsy specimen from white papules on the right hand, and representative histopathologic features are shown in theFigure, C and D.
explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed remarkable compact orthohyperkeratosis in the epidermis, dilatation of intraepidermal eccrine ducts, and hyperplasia of the eccrine sweat glands. However, the patient’s clinical process was quite interesting. The lesions only appeared after immersion in water, disappeared about 30 minutes after drying, and no lesions occurred with the absence of water contact. This unusual phenomenon, named “hand in the bucket sign,” showed that multiple white and transparent papules, excessive wrinkling on an erythema base with a clear linear border alongside the immersed area appeared on the thenar eminence, dorsum of fingers and hands, and wrists flexure of both hands after water contact for several minutes. The diagnosis can be confirmed as aquagenic syringeal acrokeratoderma based on contact history, clinical manifestation, and histopathologic change. The patient was treated with topical hydrocortisone urea ointment and recommended to avoid unnecessary contact with water. The symptoms had greatly improved after 1 month, and he is still in follow-up as of this writing. Aquagenic syringeal acrokeratoderma (ASA) is a rare acquired skin disease that mostly occurs in female adolescents. Characteristic clinical manifestation is symmetrical, transparent-white papules and plagues. Aquagenic syringeal acrokeratoderma is also known as the hand in the bucket sign because it appears transiently and recurrently eruptions after immersion into water, and resolves in minutes to hours after drying.1The lesions are generally asymptomatic with occasional itching, stinging, burning, or even pain. Aquagenic syringeal acrokeratoderma mostly affects the bilateral palms, sometimes also on soles, and rarely involves the dorsum of fingers2and the medial heel according to previous reports.3In this case, the patient manifested unusual involvements of the dorsal areas of hands, wrists, elbows, with the palm areas spared, which, to our knowledge has previously not been reported. It is easy to misdiagnose ASA as eczema when the clinical features first appear without characteristic involvement. Furthermore, ASA is distinguished with progressive symmetric erythrokeratoderma that presents well-demarcated erythematous and keratotic plaques covered with thin scales initially on the bilateral palms, while not aggravating after water immersion. Another crucial differential diagnosis is hereditary papulotranslucent acrokeratoderma, which appears after puberty and persists for a lifetime. The clinical manifestation is persistent asymptomatic lesions, associated with fine-textured scalp hair and an atopic diathesis, whereas it presents pathologic findings of focal hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis, and normal eccrine ducts.4The diagnosis of ASA is mostly based on the contact history and clinical manifestations. Dermoscopic findings may assist in the diagnosis with deepened dermatoglyphics, hypertrophic stratum corneum, and dilatation of eccrine ostia—those forming a peculiar gruyere-like aspect.5The histopathologic study revealed no specific sign, but hyperkeratosis and dilatation of eccrine ducts after water immersion for several minutes. The etiology of ASA remains unclear. Clinical appearance may be related to abnormal sweat glands, hyperkeratosis, and impairment of stratum corneum resulting from increasing water-binding capability with excessive water absorption. Medications, like COX-2 inhibitors and spironolactone, might increase salt retention in the epidermal cells and promote water reabsorption.6In addition, some diseases, such as cystic fibrosis, asthma, allergic rhinitis, urticaria, palmar erythema, and malignant melanoma,7are closely associated with ASA. Topical therapy is the first choice for ASA. Medications like salicylic acid ointment, urea ointment, tazarotene gel, formalin, aluminum chloride, and botulinum toxin injections, have been reported to be effective in previous cases.8The condition relieves spontaneously by water escaping, hence it is vital for ASA to avoid contact with water in unnecessary situations. The COVID-19 pandemic outbreak has brought changes in lifestyle, including long-term glove wearing and frequent hand washing, causing longer duration of water contact.9,10So dermatologists should be more aware of the prevalence of ASA and help to prevent and diagnose this condition during the pandemic period.

caption: A, Millimetric erythematous to hyperpigmented monomorphic papules involving the trunk. B, Erythematous papules and symmetric annular brown erythematous plaques on the cheeks and temples. C and D, Punch biopsy results (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A teenaged boy presented to the outpatient clinic with a 1-year history of asymptomatic cutaneous lesions on the face that had progressively spread to the trunk and extremities. He also had asthenia and mild intermittent arthralgias. Physical examination revealed multiple millimetric erythematous to hyperpigmented monomorphic keratotic papules involving the head, trunk, and extremities. Symmetric annular brown erythematous plaques on the cheeks and temples were also seen. There were no vesicles or pustules (Figure, A and B). Laboratory investigations revealed a normal white blood cell count, mild anemia (hemoglobin level, 11.3 g/dL; normal level 12.50-15.50 g/dL; to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), hypocomplementemia, and moderate proteinuria. Autoimmune serology results showed raised levels of antinuclear antibodies (>1:160), anti-Smith antibodies, SSA/Ro antibodies, SSB/La antibodies, and anti-U1RNP antibodies. Anti-dsDNA antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, rheumatoid factor, IgG and IgM anticardiolipin antibody, and anti-β2 glycoprotein 1 antibody results were negative. A biopsy specimen obtained from an erythematous papule on the trunk and stained with hematoxylin-eosin is shown in theFigure, C and D.
explanation: A. Nonbullous neutrophilic lupus erythematosus Histopathological examination revealed a slightly atrophic epidermis with interface dermatitis, individual dyskeratotic keratinocytes, and a superficial perivascular and interstitial infiltrate of neutrophils, admixed with numerous mononuclear histiocytoid cells. Few eosinophils and leukocytoclastic debris were apparent, but there was no evidence of subepidermal blister formation or vasculitis. Immunohistochemical study results revealed that the mononuclear histiocytoid cells showed immunoreactivity for myeloperoxidase and CD68, suggesting myeloid lineage. Direct immunofluorescence showed negative results. The presence of a prominent infiltrate of neutrophils with leukocytoclasia, as well as an interface dermatitis, supported the diagnosis of nonbullous neutrophilic lupus erythematosus (NBNLE) in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).1The patient was treated with oral prednisone and hydroxychloroquine with partial resolution of the lesions. Nonbullous neutrophilic lupus erythematosus,2,3also known as SLE-associated neutrophilic dermatosis3or Sweet-like neutrophilic dermatosis,4is a newly recognized clinicopathological variant of cutaneous lupus erythematosus characterized by the presence of a dermal and/or subcutaneous infiltrate of neutrophils and variable degrees of interface dermatitis.2,3,5The disease predominantly affects women and is clinically manifested by multiple, usually nonpruritic, urticarial papules and nodules occurring in a wide distribution.2,3Lesions most commonly develop in patients with SLE, especially in those receiving immunosuppressive therapy. However, they can also be the presenting manifestation of the disease.3Histologically, NBNLE is characterized by a perivascular and interstitial infiltrate of neutrophils with prominent leukocytoclasia and variable degrees of vacuolar degeneration of the dermoepidermal junction. The neutrophilic infiltrate is usually superficial but can extend into the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue.3,6There is no evidence of vasculitis, necrobiosis, or prominent dermal edema, and direct immunofluorescence study results show complement and/or immunoglobulin deposition along the basement membrane zone in about half of cases. Exceptionally, a dermal infiltrate primarily composed of histiocyte-like immature myeloid cells has also been described.7,8The differential diagnosis of NBNLE includes other conditions associated with SLE, such as acute lupus erythematosus, Sweet syndrome, hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis, and palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis. In the rare cases of NBNLE with histiocyte-like immature myeloid cells, histiocytoid Sweet syndrome can be considered. Nonbullous neutrophilic lupus erythematosus can be distinguished from acute lupus erythematosus by its more persistent and widespread distribution of cutaneous lesions and more pronounced dermal neutrophilic infiltrate. Sweet and histiocytoid Sweet syndrome lack vacuolar degeneration of the dermoepidermal junction and show a denser infiltrate of neutrophils with prominent papillary dermal edema. Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis show cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis, and palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis show variable degrees of degenerated collagen and palisaded histiocytes. The pathogenesis of NBNLE is still unknown and seems to be complex. The combination of interface dermatitis and neutrophilic infiltrates suggests that both the innate and adaptive immune system may be involved. The prognosis of NBNLE is usually good but depends on the severity of the associated SLE. Lesions usually respond promptly to systemic corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine, or dapsone.9,10In case of persistence, mycophenolate mofetil and azathioprine have also been used with good response.2,3The present case highlights the wide range of clinicopathological features of cutaneous lupus erythematosus. Increased awareness of this peculiar variant is important, as it may be the first clinical manifestation of SLE.

caption: A, Numerous, submillimeter, skin-colored spiny projections over left foot web spaces were present. B, Close-up photograph over the left scapular area showed lesions of similar morphologic characteristics. C, Histologic results showed a parakeratotic column overlying a mildly acanthotic epidermis with a normal granular layer and keratinocyte maturation. A sparse superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate was present (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A patient in their 50s presented with asymptomatic keratotic papules, first noticed on the left middle and ring fingers and left toe web spaces more than 10 years earlier. The papules progressed proximally over the subsequent decade to involve the forearm, arm, scapular area, ankle, shin, and thigh, but only affected the left side of the body. The patient’s face, palms, soles, and entire right side of the body were spared. The patient has a history of rosacea being treated with topical metronidazole gel for flares but was otherwise asymptomatic. The patient did not have any alopecia, night blindness, or dry eyes or skin. There was no history of any exposure to radiation or arsenic, nutritional deficiency, inflammatory skin disease, or malignant neoplasm. There was no family history of a similar condition. Examination revealed multiple, submillimeter, skin-colored to yellowish keratotic spiny projections over the aforementioned areas, only on the left side of the body (Figure, A and B). Punch biopsy from a lesion showed orthokeratosis with parakeratotic columns emerging from an epidermal invagination. The epidermis was mildly acanthotic and with a normal granular layer. There was a sparse superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. Adjacent hair follicles were unaffected (Figure, C).
explanation: B. Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis (MMDH) is a rare disorder of keratinization, first coined by Goldstein in 1967.1To our knowledge, only 27 female and 11 male cases of MMDH have been reported worldwide, with age at onset ranging from 4 months to 83 years, including this case.2,3Several synonymous terms for MMDH exist in the medical literature (eg, familial disseminated piliform hyperkeratosis, disseminated spiked hyperkeratosis, minute aggregate keratosis).4 Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis is characterized by multiple submillimeter spiky projections or spicules, usually located on the trunk and limbs in a symmetrical nonfollicular distribution, classically sparing the face and palmoplantar surfaces.4They are often asymptomatic. The lesions can also be dome-shaped, flat-topped, or crateriform papules. White, yellowish, brown, or skin-colored variants have been described too. Typical histological features include focal columns of orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis arising from a tented epidermis, but there are cases of parakeratosis and epidermal invagination. The stratum granulosum is usually prominent but may be of variable thickness. Electron microscopy shows focally reduced number of keratohyalin granules and normal to increased number of lamellar (Odland) bodies.5 The pathogenesis of MMDH remains unknown. It can be sporadic, familial (autosomal dominant trait inheritance), or drug induced (cyclosporine, etretinate, simvastatin, antifungal).6,7A postinflammatory form associated with radiotherapy and solar irradiation has also been described. Late-onset forms of sporadic MMDH present after the fourth decade of life and most cases are idiopathic, but there are reports of concomitant cancer or inflammatory disease.5A review of 32 previously reported cases of MMDH found only 2 cases associated with internal malignant neoplasm: cervical carcinoma and breast cancer.7Hence, given the rarity of MMDH and the absence of cancer history in this case, we are inclined to support previous reports that the association between MMDH and concomitant malignant neoplasm was likely coincidental. Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis should be differentiated from other causes of digitate hyperkeratosis. It is a nonfollicular digitate keratosis, whereas lichen spinulosus is a follicular digitate keratosis affecting the trunk and limbs. Lichen spinulosus occurs mostly in children and adolescents, where it presents as plaques of follicular spines. Porokeratosis lesions have characteristic ridges on the border (cornoid lamella) and a central furrow. Histologic findings show parakeratotic columns overlying a vertical zone of dyskeratotic and vacuolated cells within the epidermis. Viral warts present as solitary or multiple verrucous papules, usually larger than the submillimeter lesions seen in MMDH. Histologic findings also demonstrate a hypergranulomatosis papillomatous epidermis with overlying tiers of parakeratosis. Other differential diagnoses should be excluded too. Phrynoderma is another type of follicular digitate keratosis, associated with xerosis and nutritional deficiencies (eg, vitamin A). Spiny keratoderma presents with discrete keratotic plugs on the palms, soles, or both. The predilection of acral sites in spiny keratoderma is typically not seen in MMDH. Arsenical keratoses present in the palms and soles of those exposed to arsenic, either from water (medicinal) or occupational. An approach algorithm to digitate hyperkeratosis has been published by Caccetta et al.4Other nondigitate keratinization disorders, such as keratosis pilaris and pityriasis rubra pilaris, are considered separately. Our case outlined a patient with the characteristic nonfollicular, digitate keratosis of MMDH but was atypical in that the lesions were unilateral. Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis usually presents in a bilateral symmetrical distribution, unlike this case. To the best of our knowledge, there has only been 1 other reported case of unilateral MMDH.7 The patient in the present case began treatment with tretinoin cream, 0.05%, and urea cream, and will be reviewed for outcome. Treatment of MMDH with systemic or topical retinoids and other topical keratolytic agents is often unsuccessful or at best temporary, with the lesions recurring quickly after cessation of therapy. Patient education and reassurance remain the best strategy.2Although rare, the diagnosis of this benign entity remains clinically important to avoid unnecessary treatment, investigations, and complications.

caption: A, Clinical image showing indurated and mobile subcutaneous nodule on the anterior surface of the arm. Arrowheads highlight a subtle linear plaque adjacent to the nodule. B, Histopathologic image showing dilated and thrombosed lymphatic vessels in subcutaneous tissue with recanalization (hematoxylin-eosin). C, Histopathologic image of partially thrombosed vessels. D, Immunohistochemistry finding was positive for D2-40 (podoplanin).
scenario: A woman in her 40s with a medical history of multiple sclerosis consulted for the sudden development of 2 adjacent nodules on the left arm. An excision with 1-cm margins of the left arm demonstrated desmoplastic melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 1 mm, and a left axillary sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) had been performed 3 weeks before under general anesthesia. The patient was also being treated with subcutaneous interferon beta 1a for the multiple sclerosis. Physical examination revealed 2 indurated and mobile subcutaneous nodules on the anterior surface of the arm 5 cm distal to the surgical scar, the larger of them measuring 15 mm in diameter (Figure, A) and the smaller of them measuring 4 mm. When the arm was abducted to 90°, the patient denied pain but described a subtle tightness sensation on the arm. An excisional biopsy from the larger lesion was performed (Figure, B-D).
explanation: Associated with the clinical findings, a subtle cord that projected from the largest nodule to the axillary region could be seen in physical examination (Figure, A). An excisional biopsy of the larger lesion showed the presence of dilated and thrombosed vessels in the subcutaneous tissue, with signs of recanalization. Other features present were edema, areas of acute hemorrhage, recent fibrosis, and focal steatonecrosis, without evidence of malignant melanoma (Figure, B). An immunohistochemical study confirmed the lymphatic vascular origin of the lesion, with expression for CD31, ERG and D2-40 (podoplanin) antibodies. Human herpesvirus 8 test results were  negative. In this setting, a Sox10 staining was also performed, ruling out a metastasis of melanoma. The medical history of a left axillary SLNB associated with the clinical, pathological, and special staining findings confirmed the diagnosis of axillary web syndrome (AWS). Axillary web syndrome is a frequently described complication in breast cancer SLNB surgical procedures, and a few cases have also been reported after SLNB for cutaneous malignant melanoma. Axillary web syndrome commonly appears within the 12 weeks after the surgical procedure.1,2It is clinically characterized by palpable tight cords in the axilla that can extend to the arm, antecubital space, and forearm, associated with pain and movement restriction of the affected segment.2Rarely, AWS can present as painless, mobile subcutaneous nodules in the ipsilateral arm of the SLNB, as observed in this patient.3The possible mechanism of the cord formation is the disruption of superficial lymphatics and vessels of the arm during SLNB surgery that cause thrombosis.3,4The histopathology of AWS is characterized by dilated and thrombosed superficial veins, lymphatics, or both.2,3The characteristic positivity of D2-40 stain in AWS strongly suggests its lymphatic origin.5A wide spectrum of differential diagnoses must be considered for sudden nodules appearing in a  postoperative patient with melanoma. Masson tumor (intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia) is a rare vascular tumor characterized by intravascular proliferation of endothelial cells that presents more frequently in female patients as a painless, slow-growing tumor in head and neck and rarely in upper extremities. It is characterized by intravascular proliferation of endothelial cells with papillary formations, almost always associated with some thrombus. Each papillary frond is covered by plump endothelial cells.6These tumors are commonly D2-40 negative and CD31, CD34, alpha smooth muscle actin, and factor VIII–related antigen positive in cells lining the papillae of Masson tumor.6,7 Melanoma is an aggressive tumor with a high ability to metastasize. Melanoma metastases typically show proliferation of atypical melanocytes and, in challenging cases, immunohistochemical markers such as Sox-10, HMB-45, Melan A, andMITFwill reveal a melanocytic differentiation.8 Pseudo-aneurysms of the brachial artery are infrequent lesions caused by trauma or iatrogenic damage after surgical interventions. They appear as growing, painful, pulsatile masses associated with tenderness and swelling under the traumatic/scar area. The walls of the pseudo-aneurysm contain variable amounts of laminated clot, surrounded by dense fibrous tissue reaction, marked accumulation of endothelial and muscle cells and deposition of proteoglycans.9The D2-40 immunohistochemical marker result is also negative. The diagnosis of AWS must be considered in patients who have undergone a recent SLNB procedure for cutaneous melanoma and develop sudden subcutaneous nodules near surgical scars. The detection of a palpable cord, frequently subtle, adjacent to the nodule, may help confirm the diagnosis of AWS rather than other less favorable diagnoses, such as melanoma metastases.

caption: A and B, Papules, plaques, and nodules on the skin surface of the right cheek (A, B), forehead (B), intercilium (B), and jaw (B). White arrowhead indicates the biopsy site (B). C and D, Composition of hair follicles. Presence of sebaceous glands and the perifollicular fibrous sheath within a fibrotic stroma can be clearly seen (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A male in his late teens presented with asymptomatic congenital papules, plaques, and nodules in a linear bilateral distribution following Blaschko lines on the scalp and face region. The papules and nodules appeared to grow as the boy grew, and some pedunculated lesions tended to fall off spontaneously. He had not received any prior treatment. The patient had no other significant medical history and denied having a family history of similar lesions. Clinical examination findings revealed multiple skin-colored, nontender soft papules of varying sizes protruding from the skin surface on the right cheek, forehead, and jaw, as well as on the anterior surface of the scalp, distributed along Blaschko lines, with sparse vellus hairs and multiple hair follicles on the lesions (Figure, A and B). However, no hair was observed on the lesion because the patient had shaved the hair on his face. An incisional biopsy of a pedunculated lesion above the left eyebrow was performed (Figure, B).
explanation: Histological examination findings revealed densely populated well-formed vellus hairs with sebaceous glands and accentuation of the perifollicular fibrous sheath embedded in a fibrotic stroma (Figure, C and D). However, examination of multiple deeper sections did not reveal any additional components, such as cystic follicular structures, prominent adipose tissue, or cartilage (Figure, C and D). Hence, the lesion was diagnosed as a hair follicle nevus. Hair follicle nevus is an extremely rare adnexal hamartoma with follicular differentiation.1It is typically congenital and located on the face.1Hamartomas are usually benign malformations composed of tissue elements normally found at that site, but grow in a disorganized fashion. However, some studies have shown that these lesions may occasionally undergo malignant degeneration. In fact, several chromosomal and genetic defects have been identified in benign neoplasms, hamartomas, and malignant tumors.2-4 Most cases of hair follicle nevi present as solitary lesions. However, this patient had multiple craniofacial lesions distributed bilaterally along Blaschko lines in a segmental pattern, probably owing to a somatic point sequence variation. Germain and Smith5also reported multiple papular and nodular lesions on the right side of the nose along Blaschko lines in a 6-month-old infant. The pattern of the lesions also implies that the hamartoma may be caused by a sequence variation in the early stage of gestation.5 Clinical differential diagnosis includes sebaceous nevus, connective tissue nevus, and trichofolliculoma. A sebaceous nevus is usually a hairless macular lesion, unlike papular/nodular hair follicle nevi at birth.5In addition, a sebaceous nevus has dilated apocrine glands and well-developed sebaceous glands; however, it does not have any vellus hairs.5Connective tissue nevus appears as yellow or brown-yellow papules or plaques along the long axis of the limb and is distributed linearly. Although the morphologic characteristics of the lesions in a hair follicle nevus were similar to that of the connective tissue nevus, histopathological findings can easily differentiate between these 2 types of nevi. The connective tissue nevus is characterized by substantial increase of collagen fibers in the dermal reticular layer and variable morphological changes of elastic tissue. Its lesions can also appear in newborns as fibrotic papules and nodules with a diameter of 1.0 to 10 cm, usually resulting in a peau d’orange texture to the skin.6Moreover, these collagen bundles are thick, homogenized, and disordered, which are completely different from hair follicle nevi. Trichofolliculoma is histologically characterized by a central follicular cyst connecting to the peripheral hair follicles. It is the most difficult to distinguish in differential diagnosis of hair follicle nevus because of the overlapping histological features with other tumors arising from the folliculosebaceous apparatus, which can give rise to numerous benign and occasionally malignant tumors.7-9Hair follicle nevus may be differentiated from trichofolliculomas by cytokeratin 19 staining in hair follicles, with results being partially positive in hair follicle nevus while negative in trichofolliculomas.9Hair follicle nevus is differentiated from accessory tragi based on the presence of a lesser amount of subcutaneous fat, rather than from trichofolliculomas, the central cyst from which the hair follicles radiate.10 We could not remove the lesions from the present patient in totality because the lesions affected a large portion of the facial area. However, Germain and Smith5successfully removed all nodules from their infant patient at 6 months. Hence, the awareness about this condition should be increased because these lesions may be more operable at a younger age. As the patients become older, the lesions grow as well, which can eventually be surgically challenging, as in the case of this patient.

caption: A, Pustular eruption of the face characterized by monomorphous 1- to 2-mm pustules over background erythema on the cheeks, chin, and nose appearing less than 24 hours after sun exposure. Punch biopsy of skin demonstrated intrafollicular (B and C) and subcorneal (B and D) pustule formation (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A woman in her 20s was referred for evaluation of a 4-year history of recurrent pustular eruptions on her face, which initially presented while she was vacationing in Florida. She noted mild associated pruritus but denied burning sensation. The eruptions occurred intermittently, appearing as erythematous papules with prominent pustules, and were exacerbated by sunlight. On average, her lesions would resolve in 3 to 4 days with only mild background erythema by 5 to 7 days. Even mild sun exposure would induce the eruption, leading to frequent recurrences in summer months but long periods of remission in the fall through spring. Trials with various broad-spectrum sunscreens in combination with topical and oral antibiotics and topical ivermectin did not prevent flares or mitigate severity of eruptions when they occurred. She denied joint pain, fever, fatigue, changes in urine color, use of other topical or systemic medications, or presence of rashes elsewhere. She was otherwise healthy without other medical history. On physical examination, she was well appearing with numerous 1- to 2-mm monomorphous pustules over background erythema on the medial cheeks, chin, and nose (Figure, A). No nail fold capillary changes or mucosal lesions were observed. Serum analysis results for antinuclear, anti-SSA/Ro, and anti-SSB/La antibodies were negative. A 4-mm punch biopsy was taken from a representative lesion along the right jawline (Figure, B-D).
explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed subcorneal and follicular pustules (Figure, B-D). Periodic acid–Schiff and Grocott methenamine silver stain results were negative for fungal organisms. Bacterial swab results from malar lesions were negative for growth. Considering failure of multiple treatments effective for papulopustular rosacea and acne vulgaris and the episodic and photo-aggravated nature of the eruptions, a diagnosis of actinic folliculitis was rendered. Phototesting was not performed owing to patient preference. Despite this, the clinical and histopathologic findings were considered sufficiently diagnostic. The patient initiated treatment with adapalene gel, 0.3%, and reported decreased severity of eruptions with fewer pustules and faster resolution. She was able to prevent recurrences with strict use of a solar umbrella in summer months. The treatment responses further supported the diagnosis. Actinic folliculitis is a monomorphic pustular dermatitis that presents on the face, with possible involvement of the arms and upper chest. The eruption normally occurs within 4 to 14 hours of sunlight exposure and resolves over 7 to 10 days.1,2This entity encompasses 2 previously separate disorders, acne aestivalis and actinic superficial folliculitis.1,3Acne aestivalis was previously described as a pruritic, papular eruption of the face induced by sunlight. Actinic superficial folliculitis is characterized by pustules distributed over the shoulders, upper trunk, and arms that typically appear 24 to 36 hours after sun exposure.1,3 Current case reports of actinic folliculitis in the literature describe patients between the ages of 17 and 42 years, but analysis regarding the average age at onset is lacking. The pathogenesis of the disease remains undetermined. However, some have hypothesized that epidermal thickening induced by UV radiation causes follicular infundibular occlusion, inflammation, and lesion development.2Histopathological descriptions in the literature include perifollicular mixed inflammatory infiltrate, perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, and subcorneal pustulosis.1,3,4 The differential diagnosis of actinic folliculitis includes papulopustular rosacea, pinpoint papular light eruption, acute localized exanthematous pustulosis, acne vulgaris, and photoallergy. Papulopustular rosacea presents with papules and pustules overlying erythema in a central facial distribution. Biopsy results are often nonspecific and unnecessary for diagnosis, but characteristic histopathology includes mixed perivascular and perifollicular infiltrates in the superficial and mid-dermis with accumulation of neutrophils beyond the follicle.5Papulopustular rosacea was considered unlikely given the failed response to established rosacea treatment regimens. Pinpoint papular light eruption is a clinical variant of polymorphous light eruption characterized by pinpoint papules and vesicles 30 minutes to 3 days after UV light exposure, most commonly in dark-skinned individuals.6Histopathologic findings correspond to clinical course. Acute lesions are similar to those of classical polymorphous light eruption and show spongiosis, edema, and superficial and deep perivascular infiltrates. Subacute lesions consist of an atrophic epidermis with claw-like extension of epidermal rete around a well-circumscribed lichenoid infiltrate, mimicking lichen nitidus. Pustules are not a typical morphologic characteristic of pinpoint papular light eruption clinically or histologically, arguing against this diagnosis in this patient. Acute localized exanthematous pustulosis consists of acute-onset nonfollicular, sterile pustules on an erythematous background affecting the face, neck, and chest.7Most cases have been linked to drug hypersensitivity, but some reports describe associations with viral infection or insect bites.7These lesions are often accompanied by fever and neutrophilic leukocytosis. Histologically, acute localized exanthematous pustulosis presents as sterile subcorneal pustules with an edematous papillary dermis and mixed perivascular infiltrates. This patient’s history was negative for recent illness, systemic medications, or fever, rendering this diagnosis unlikely. Several treatment strategies have been proposed for actinic folliculitis. Adapalene, a topical retinoid, has been successful in preventing flares with application beginning a few weeks before sun exposure.2Other reports have described success with isotretinoin, including complete clearance and extended periods of remission.8Newer reports have explored the role of narrowband UV-B phototherapy, but more research is needed to determine its utility.9

caption: A, Lacy, white erosive lesions on the tongue. B, Epidermis with acanthosis, parakeratosis, necrotic keratinocytes, and dermal band lymphocytic infiltrate with effacement of the dermoepidermal junction (hematoxylin-eosin). C, Fibrogen deposition along the basement membrane. D, Hypercapturing, heterogeneous mass in the right anterior hemithorax.
scenario: A White man in his 50s with a clinical history of recurrent respiratory infections and diarrhea presented with painful oral erosions that began 2 years before. Results of a previous intestinal biopsy had shown unspecific findings and absence of apoptosis. He reported a 5-kg weight loss that he attributed to impaired intake owing to the oral lesions. He was also being evaluated for a mediastinal mass detected in radiography of the chest performed for pneumonia. Physical examination revealed whitish edematous lacy patches with erosions on the dorsal and lateral aspects of the tongue and buccal mucosa (Figure, A); skin and nails were not involved. A lingual biopsy specimen was obtained for pathologic evaluation and direct immunofluorescence (DIF;Figure, B and C). The result of indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) testing, using monkey esophagus, salt-skin split, and rat bladder as substrates, was negative. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and immunoblot analysis did not detect any desmoglein-1 or -3, bullous pemphigoid-180 or -230, collagen VII, desmocollin-1 to -3, laminin-332, envoplakin, or periplakin antibodies. Results were normal for liver function; negative for hepatitis B and C; indicative of hypogammaglobulinemia, with a decreased immunoglobulin (Ig) G serum level of 465 mg/dL (normal, 750-1600 g/L; for g/L, multiply by 0.01); and normal for IgA and IgM levels. Positron emission tomography revealed a 10-cm hypercapturing extrapulmonary mass (Figure, D). Surgical excision of the mediastinal mass was performed; its histopathologic features were consistent with a type AB thymoma, Masaoka-Koga stage 2A.
explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed epidermal acanthosis with scattered necrotic keratinocytes, basal-layer vacuolation, and a band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the papillary dermis. Direct immunofluorescence examination showed shaggy fibrinogen deposition along the dermoepidermal junction. Because of the findings of thymoma, hypogammaglobulinemia, lichenoid oral lesions, and diarrhea, Good syndrome was suspected. A study of the lymphocyte populations revealed a decrease in the total B lymphocyte count and an increase in CD8+T count, with an inverted CD4:CD8 ratio. These data supported the diagnosis of Good syndrome. After a thymectomy was performed, the patient’s diarrheal episodes showed a transitory improvement; however, the oral lichenoid lesions persisted. Replacement therapy with immunoglobulins was initiated along with 0.4% tacrolimus oral rinses. After 2 years of follow-up, the lichenoid lesions remained unchanged. Nevertheless, the patient did not experience any new infectious episodes since initiation of treatment with immunoglobulins. First described by Robert Good in 1954, Good syndrome is a rare, primary, acquired, adult-onset immunodeficiency characterized by hypogammaglobulinemia, low or absent B lymphocytes, and CD4+cell lymphopenia with an inverted CD4:CD8 ratio, occurring in the context of previous or simultaneous thymoma.1Good syndrome is correlated with poor survival associated with severe infections2and autoimmune-associated diseases that occur in 59% of cases, which often require immunosuppressive therapy.3Diarrhea is present in 50% of patients and lichen planus (LP), in 12%.4,5All of the reported cases of Good syndrome-associated LP, patients presented with erosive lesions; skin involvement was only described in approximately 50%. Associated autoimmune diseases do not always improve after thymectomy—hypogammaglobulinemia usually persists, and substitutive treatment with immunoglobulins becomes mandatory to prevent infections. Thymoma-associated multiorgan autoimmunity (TAMA) is a disease of the skin, liver, or intestine similar to graft-vs-host disease on histopathologic examination in the setting of thymoma and no prior hematopoietic stem cell transplantation or transfusions.6About 30 cases of TAMA with cutaneous involvement have been described, some associated with hypogammaglobulinemia and/or B-cell lymphopenia. Most patients with TAMA presented with a maculopapular scaly eruption or erythroderma; oral involvement was described in fewer than 30%. Paraneoplastic autoimmune multiorgan syndrome (PAMS), initially described by Anhalt7as paraneoplastic pemphigus, is defined by 5 main features: (1) painful mucosal erosions and polymorphic cutaneous lesions occurring in patients with an underlying cancer; (2) histologic findings of epidermal acantholysis and vacuolar interface dermatitis; (3) DIF with IgG and complement deposition in the epidermal intercellular spaces and along the basement membrane zone; (4) IIF with intercellular IgG deposition on both the epithelial and non-epithelial substrates; and (5) humoral immunity against plakin proteins. Because the autoimmune response may involve different organs, the broad term PAMS was proposed.8Thymoma is associated with PAMS in 5.5% of cases. Reported as a paraneoplastic disorder, LP usually occurs in conjunction with thymoma or lymphoma.9The diagnosis is based on characteristic pathologic and DIF findings with negative serologic tests. Lichenoid or graft-vs-host disease–like skin and mucocutaneous lesions can arise in any of the 4 diagnoses proposed, without a clear-cut distinction between them. For this reason, it is imperative to perform a complete evaluation (ie, immunoblot or ELISA, DIF, IIF, gammaglobulin levels, and diagnostic imaging) to diagnose a neoplasm (eg, thymoma or other) or to initiate replacement treatment for hypogammaglobulinemia. Even after successful treatment of the malignant neoplasm, lichenoid lesions may persist, especially those associated with oral mucosa. Because infections are frequently associated with death in patients with hypogammaglobulinemia, an immunoglobulins replacement program must be established as early as possible.

B, Clinical image of the bandlike grooved alopecic lesion on the left side of the frontal scalp and vertex. C, Scanning view shows predominant lymphocytic infiltrates in perifollicular and periappendageal regions of the dermis and lobular panniculitis (hematoxylin-eosin staining). D, High-power view shows inflammatory infiltrates between adipocytes with hyaline fat necrosis in the subcutis (hematoxylin-eosin staining).
scenario: A man in his 50s presented to our dermatology department with an asymptomatic, arc-shaped, depressed skin groove on the left side of his forehead, frontal scalp, and vertex area. Localized linear hair loss and hair thinning on the left scalp area were observed. The patient reported that when the lesion had begun to appear, approximately 10 years earlier, he had received 2 doses of intralesional steroid via injection on a small bald patch on the vertex. Thereafter, the lesion gradually progressed to the frontal scalp and eventually made a linear furrow on the left side of his forehead. Physical examination revealed 2 long, curved-line, depressed, alopecic patches on the left side of the vertex and frontal scalp area extending to the left eyebrow (Figure, A and B). The lesions measured (length × width) 7 × 2 cm and 6 × 1 cm, respectively. Dermoscopic examination of the alopecic area revealed several short vellus hairs, yellow dots, and honeycomb hyperpigmentation; however, broken hairs were not seen. The result of a hair pull test was negative. The patient denied any trauma history and had no history of connective tissue disease nor any evidence of systemic involvement, such as arthralgia, photosensitivity, or skin rashes. Skin biopsies were performed on the left side of the vertex and the forehead. Histopathologic findings of the 2 biopsy specimens were identical (Figure, C and D).

options.C: Linear or annular lupus erythematosus panniculitis of the scalp

answer: Linear or annular lupus erythematosus panniculitis of the scalp
explanation: C. Linear or annular lupus erythematosus panniculitis of the scalp Histopathologic examination revealed prominent lymphocytic infiltration around the hair follicles and appendages in the dermis, and vacuolar degeneration in the basal layer of the hair follicles without epidermal involvement. In the subcutaneous tissue layer, a lobular lymphocytic infiltrate was present with associated hyaline fat necrosis (Figure, C and D). Abundant mucin deposition in the deep dermis and subcutaneous fat layer were highlighted by Alcian blue staining. Direct immunofluorescence results were positive, with granular deposition of immunoglobulin (Ig) G, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, and fibrinogen in the dermal blood vessels. All laboratory test findings were normal, including negativity for antinuclear antibody and antidouble-stranded DNA antibody. A diagnosis of lupus erythematosus panniculitis (LEP), specifically linear or annular lupus erythematosus panniculitis of the scalp (LALPS), was made. Slight improvement of the depressed skin lesion was observed with oral hydroxychloroquine (400 mg/d) and topical corticosteroid for 3 months. A unique clinical subtype of LEP, LALPS involves the deep dermis and subcutaneous fat layer of the skin.1,2Classically, LEP presents as deep subcutaneous nodules or plaques, sometimes occurring in crops.1,2Typically, it has predilection for the face and proximal extremities.1When LEP occurs on the scalp along the Blaschko lines, it is termed LALPS,2a condition first reported by Nagai and colleagues3in 2003 and renamed by Mitxelena and colleagues in 2013.4 Because LALPS is known to have a low rate of progression to systemic disease and spares the upper segment of hair follicles, it has a good prognosis.5Compared with classic LEP, LALPS has a discriminative feature: its nonscarring nature and distribution follows the Blaschko lines of the scalp.2Nevertheless, the extent of inflammation varies and may affect the scarring process of alopecia and the overall prognosis. When the inflammation is confined to the subcutaneous layer, the upper segments of the hair follicles and the stem cells in the hair bulge area are relatively well preserved; however, the contrary may lead to subsequent scarring alopecia.2,6Therefore, early diagnosis and proper management are crucial. The predilection of LALPS for the Blaschko lines is not fully understood; however, it has been hypothesized that during early embryogenesis, aberrant genetically programmed cloning of cells may give rise to cells along the Blaschko lines that are highly susceptible to disease.7 This case report describes an interesting presentation of LALPS, a condition that may be misdiagnosed as linear atrophoderma of Moulin, linear discoid lupus erythematosus, localized lipodystrophy, or en coup de sabre. Linear atrophoderma of Moulin is a rare clinical entity that follows the Blaschko lines. Its predilection for trunk or extremities and its histopathologic features, including basal hyperpigmentation and mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltrations preserving skin appendages, are helpful for differential diagnosis.8Linear discoid lupus erythematosus is usually accompanied by epidermal changes such as scleroatrophy, hyperpigmentation, and follicular hyperkeratosis.9Accordingly, compared with LALPS on histologic examination, LDLE more commonly involves the epidermal layer and has less involvement of the subcutaneous layer. Localized lipodystrophy may appear as an annular or semicircular subtype; however, its histopathologic features are generally noninflammatory.10In en coup de sabre,linear morphea on the frontoparietal scalp and forehead appears as a paramedian band resembling a “sword’s stroke.”7Morphea exhibits histopathologic features of dermal sclerosis with eosinophilic swollen collagen fibers. Previous reports of LALPS cases have shown that treatment with hydroxychloroquine, corticosteroids (systemic, intralesional, or topical), methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, dapsone, thalidomide, gold therapy, or topical minoxidil has been effective.5,6,9Although the prognosis of LALPS is favorable, diagnostic delay and progression to scarring alopecia may leave lipoatrophic scars and cosmetic problems. Although little information is available on LALPS, it should be considered as a differential diagnosis of linear and annular alopecia or furrowed skin lesion on the scalp.

B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain of skin biopsy specimen showing inflammatory infiltrate composed of giant cells in the deeper dermis extending into the subcutaneous fat. C, High-power view showing epithelioid cell granulomas and fungal profiles within giant cells (arrowheads). D, Periodic acid–Schiff stain highlighting septate fungal hyphae with acute-angled branching within giant cells.
scenario: A man in his 30s, employed as a painter, presented with multiple painless nodules on his right cheek of 4 years’ duration. He reported episodic breathlessness, cough, and wheezing with expectoration of brownish sputum, exacerbated with exposure to hay dust, in the past 5 years. He also reported recent-onset headache while reading. Physical examination revealed a depressed plaque measuring 6 × 4 cm in the right infraorbital region, surrounded by multiple nodules of sizes ranging from 1 × 1 cm to 5 × 1 cm (Figure, A). The nodules were firm, mobile, and nontender on palpation. Local temperature was normal. There was proptosis of the right eye with mild restriction of extraocular movements on lateral gaze. Examination of the oral cavity revealed dental caries, while gingivolabial sulcus was free on bidigital examination. Nasal mucosa was normal. Respiratory system examination revealed occasional polyphonic wheeze. Chest radiography imaging showed nodular opacities in right upper zone and bronchiectasis. Punch biopsy from 1 nodule was sent for histopathological and microbiological examination (Figure, B and C).
explanation: Histopathological examination with hematoxylin-eosin staining showed a granulomatous dermatitis with lymphohistiocytic infiltrate and variable presence of fungal elements (Figure, B and C). Gomori methenamine silver stain and periodic acid–Schiff stain highlighted acute-angled septate hyphae inside some of the giant cells (Figure, D). Fungal culture results revealed yellow-green velvety colonies characteristic ofAspergillus flavusspecies. Noncontrast computed tomography imaging of the chest showed mass-like consolidation in the right upper lobe anterior segment, while that of the head and neck demonstrated a soft tissue mass in the subcutaneous plane extending superiorly up to the intraconal compartment of the right orbit. On further evaluation, total immunoglobulin E level,Aspergillus-specific immunoglobulin E level, and absolute eosinophil count (1440/μL; to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001) were elevated. Spirometry revealed moderate obstruction. Based on these features, a diagnosis of primary cutaneous aspergillosis, granulomatous invasive subtype with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, was concluded, the latter probably acquired from his occupational environment. An extensive workup to rule out underlying immunosuppression, including CD4 counts, immunoglobulin levels, nitroblue tetrazolium test, HIV serology, fasting blood glucose, glycosylated hemoglobin level, and complete blood cell count with differential count and peripheral smear, was performed and revealed no abnormality. Cutaneous aspergillosis occurs relatively less frequently than its pulmonary and paranasal sinuses counterparts.1The most common cutaneous presentation is that of destructive plaques and nodules, in contiguity to underlying cavities, such as paranasal sinuses or orbit.2Primary cutaneous aspergillosis in an immunocompetent individual is extremely rare and is typically acquired as a result of traumatic inoculation. Only a handful of reports of cutaneous granulomatous invasive aspergillosis in immunocompetent individuals have been reported, mostly from India and Sudan.3The granulomatous variant of primary cutaneous aspergillosis seen in the present case may be analogous to granulomatous aspergillus sinusitis, which also presents in immunocompetent individuals.3 Presumptive diagnosis of cutaneous aspergillosis can be made by a KOH (potassium hydroxide) mount, though definitive diagnosis requires histopathology and culture. Histopathologically, granulomatous invasive aspergillosis is characterized by a granulomatous histopathology and has an indolent course.4Further evaluation should include assessment of risk factors such as neutropenia, recent or concurrent presence of a central venous catheter access, adhesive or occlusive tapes, or skin trauma. Special attention should be given to pulmonary symptoms, and if indicated, radiological evaluation is pertinent to rule out pulmonary foci. Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection may present with erythematous subcutaneous nodules, with or without suppuration. Histopathology findings reveal mixed inflammatory infiltrate with noncaseating granulomas and acid-fast bacilli can be highlighted with Fite stain. Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection in addition can have cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, dyspnea, and lymphadenopathy. However, wheeze, obstructive spirometry, and eosinophilia are generally not seen. Phaeohyphomycosis classically presents as a unilocular or multilocular intradermal cyst over exposed sites. Direct microscopy and histopathological examination reveal brown-walled (pigmented) acute-angled hyphae with constrictions around their septa, causing them to resemble pseudohyphae or yeast forms.5Entomophthoromycosis (conidiobolomycosis) presents with nasal discharge, epistaxis, nasal obstruction, and smooth, sharply demarcated woody hard nodules over the central face. Characteristically, the examiner’s fingers can be insinuated below the swelling. Short, thick hyphae with absent or few septa surrounded by eosinophilic granular material (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) are seen on histopathological examination. Pulmonary involvement is extremely rare in phaeohyphomycosis and conidiobolomycosis and is seen almost exclusively in immunocompromised patients.5,6Indolent destructive plaques and nodules, associated symptoms suggestive of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, and granulomatous inflammation with acute-angled septate hyphae point toward the diagnosis of granulomatous invasive aspergillosis in the present case. Azoles are preferred for both treatment and prevention of invasive aspergillosis, while polyenes and echinocandins are reserved as salvage therapy.7The present patient was treated with itraconazole, 400 mg daily, along with a steroid inhaler. There was softening and decrease in size of nodules after 4 weeks of treatment, in addition to improvement in visual and respiratory symptoms.

caption: A, Violaceous papules, plaques, and nodules on the left lower shin. B, Proliferation of superficial and deep vessels, with thickening of the endothelium (hematoxylin-eosin). C, Magnetic resonance angiogram demonstrating hypervascular soft tissue mass in the left lower extremity.
scenario: A young man presented to the clinic with large, purple plaques on the left lower extremity. The plaques had been present for years, but the patient noted enlargement and darkening for the past 5 years. The lesions were asymptomatic with no associated pruritus, bleeding, or pain. No treatments or diagnostic workup had been attempted prior to presentation. The patient was otherwise healthy and was a never-smoker with no history of hypertension, atherosclerotic disease, or HIV. Physical examination revealed dark violaceous plaques, scattered subcutaneous nodules, and swelling to the mid-shin of the left lower extremity (Figure, A). There was mild warmth noted, but no palpable bruits. Complete metabolic panel, complete blood cell count, prothrombin, and serology were negative or within normal limits. A punch biopsy was performed and submitted for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B).
explanation: Biopsy revealed a superficial lobular capillary proliferation with extravasated red blood cells, hemosiderin deposition, and ectatic muscular deep vessels (Figure, B). Immunostain for human herpesvirus-8 was negative. Verhoeff-van Gieson elastic tissue and Perls iron stains highlighted the presence of malformed vessel walls and hemosiderin deposition, respectively. Duplex ultrasonography of the left lower extremity did not show evidence of deep or superficial venous thrombosis or arteriovenous malformations (AVMs). Owing to high clinical suspicion, a magnetic resonance angiogram with contrast was obtained, which revealed hypervascular soft tissue lesions centered in the lower anterior compartment of the left lower leg and medial malleolar region (Figure, C). These lesions had the angiographic appearance suggestive of vascular malformations with multiple tortuous and ectatic vessels, suggestive of an AVM. Subsequent interventional radiologic angiography confirmed the presence of prominent AVMs without high-flow arteriovenous shunting; thus, interventional radiologic embolization was deferred and the patient was treated supportively. Acroangiodermatitis, also known as pseudo-Kaposi sarcoma, is a group of angioproliferative disorders that present clinically and histologically similar to Kaposi sarcoma. Patients often present in the second decade of life with brown macules, violaceous nodules, or verrucous and ulcerative plaques of the lower extremity.1These lesions may present as either of 2 subtypes: Stewart-Bluefarb syndrome, which occurs in the setting of congenital or sporadic AVM in a younger patient; or acroangiodermatitis of Mali, which results from chronic venous insufficiency in older patients.2,3Owing to their etiologies, Stewart-Bluefarb tends to occur unilaterally when compared with the Mali type, which can occur bilaterally.1,3 The workup for acroangiodermatitis involves ruling out its mimickers while performing imaging and biopsy for confirmation of diagnosis. Palpable thrills, auscultation of a bruit, or detection of asymmetrical arterial pulses are strong clues for AVMs. Biopsy reveals capillary proliferation in the dermis, extravasated red blood cells, tortuous vessels, and hemosiderin deposits.4,5Further staining with Verhoeff-van Gieson elastin and Perls iron stain can demonstrate thickened endothelial walls and hemosiderin deposition supporting abnormal vascular neoproliferation and shunting of blood, as seen in our patient; however, this step is not diagnostically necessary. Duplex ultrasonography is a noninvasive, highly sensitive test for the detection of suspected AVMs. Nonetheless, lesions without high-grade arteriovenous shunting may not always be identified. A high clinical suspicion of an AVM may warrant additional confirmation with magnetic resonance angiography, as this technique is currently the criterion standard for evaluating AVMs.1,6Furthermore, both forms of acroangiodermatitis can be mistaken for Kaposi sarcoma. An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay screening test for HIV and immunostain for human herpesvirus-8 are useful in ruling out Kaposi sarcoma. Pseudo-Kaposi sarcoma is thought to be induced by vascular endothelial growth factor–induced endothelial and perivascular cell proliferation.7Thus, histopathology reveals hyperplasia and reactive proliferation of pre-existing, normal-appearing vessels in the dermis as opposed to neoplastic spindle cell proliferation seen in Kaposi sarcoma.7,8Neither pseudo-Kaposi sarcoma/acroangiodermatitis nor Stewart-Bluefarb are designated syndromes in the latest International Society for the Study of Vascular Anomalies classification, as they are simply considered clinical manifestations of AVM. Finally, the absence of classic sawtooth acanthosis and lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrates on biopsy is significant for excluding lichen planus.9 Diagnostic precision of Stewart-Bluefarb syndrome is essential, as untreated cases have been associated with bone demineralization, destruction of soft tissue structures, hemorrhage, wound infection, and, in rare cases, heart failure. Conservative management in the form of bed rest, leg elevation, compression bandages, and topical steroids is recommended.1Supportive treatment is recommended for patients with multiple small AVMs or asymptomatic lesions. If conservative treatment fails or if lesions are complicated by refractory pain, recurrent infection, and/or bleeding, then the option of surgical embolization or ligation may be explored.1,8Unfortunately, both conservative and aggressive treatments have demonstrated varying success, and recurrence of the condition is common.
