scenario: A woman in her 50s with a history of nasal-type natural killer (NK)/T-cell lymphoma (diagnosed 2 years prior; treated with pembrolizumab and methotrexate, ifosfamide, etoposide, dexamethasone, and pegaspargase) and chronic pulmonary coccidiomycosis being treated with fluconazole was admitted for fever, hypotension, and rash. Three months prior, pembrolizumab treatment was stopped because of a widespread morbilliform reaction, which had resolved completely 6 to 8 weeks before admission. The new widespread, asymptomatic skin eruption had been ongoing for 1 to 2 weeks and appeared different from her pembrolizumab reaction. A complete blood cell count was notable for a normal white blood cell count of 4100/μL, normal absolute neutrophil count of 2940/μL, chronic normocytic anemia (hemoglobin level of 8.2 g/dL), and chronic thrombocytopenia (platelet count of 62 ×103/μL). Blood culture results showed no growth at 1 week. Serum β-D-glucan, galactomannan,Coccidioidesantibody by complement fixation, and immunodiffusion results were negative. Respiratory viral panel and SARS-CoV-2 test results were negative. Total body skin examination findings were notable for widespread, nontender, erythematous patches and thin plaques, some with prominent overlying telangiectases and hyperpigmentation (Figure, A). A punch biopsy of a representative lesion was performed (Figure, B-D).
explanation: B. Intravascular involvement by NK/T-cell lymphoma In addition to large CD3+/CD56+perivascular lymphocytes in the dermis, there were vessels in the subcutaneous fat with intravascular lymphocytes, with a CD3+/CD56+immunophenotype. A diagnosis of intravascular NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, was made; an Epstein-Barr virus–encoded RNA in situ hybridization study had been performed on a prior biopsy, and the result was positive. Results of CD30 immunostaining were negative. Patients with lymphoma may experience fevers owing to common or atypical infections, drugs, or as a direct consequence of lymphoma. Accordingly, a careful drug review and an extensive infectious workup were undertaken. Special stains (Fite, PAS-D, Brown-Brenn) and tissue cultures were performed and results were negative, as the clinical presentation was of fever of unknown origin. Brain magnetic resonance imaging did not reveal involvement of the central nervous system by lymphoma. Lumbar puncture did not reveal malignant cells in cerebrospinal fluid. Bone marrow biopsy results showed involvement of bone marrow by NK/T-cell lymphoma. Treatment was initiated with pegaspargase, gemcitabine, and oxaliplatin, with an initial favorable response. Intravascular lymphoma (IVL) is a rare phenomenon characterized by lymphoma cells occupying and filling lumens of blood vessels, including cutaneous vessels, usually seen in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Rare cases of NK/T-cell lymphoma manifesting as IVL have been described. In this case, the diagnosis of intravascular involvement by NK/T-cell lymphoma was suspected because of a known history of nasal-type NK/T-cell lymphoma. Positive staining for CD3 and CD56 helped confirm this diagnosis. In NK/T-cell lymphoma, angiotropism or angiocentrism should be distinguished from true IVL. Angiotropism is characterized by often large clusters of tumor cells primarily aligned along the external surface of blood vessels. By contrast, intravascular involvement is characterized by occlusion of blood vessel lumens with tumor cells. Angiotropism (seen in the dermis of this biopsy) is a diagnostic feature seen in many NK/T-cell lymphomas. True intravascular involvement (seen in the subcutaneous fat of this biopsy) is rare. Intravascular lymphoma, regardless of immunophenotype, can present with erythematous plaques, nodules, and peau d’orange–like changes, but skin changes are not always present.1Prominent telangiectases may be seen in about 20% of cases.2The diagnosis of IVL may be suspected in a patient with fever without source, unusual neurological symptoms, hypoxia, elevated lactate dehydrogenase level, and/or hematologic abnormalities.3 Inpatient dermatologists play an important role in the diagnosis of IVL even when cutaneous findings are absent. Random biopsy of apparently normal skin can help establish this diagnosis.3-5Because IVL may “colonize” benign vascular neoplasms, such as cherry hemangiomas, biopsies should target these.6,7 Vasculitis and infections were on our differential diagnosis when considering this patient’s clinical presentation. Although microscopic polyangiitis has been reported in association with malignant neoplasms, including lymphomas, this patient lacks livedo, ulceration, or other common features of microscopic polyangiitis. Sections of this patient’s biopsy did not show features of vasculitis, such as perivascular neutrophils, leukocytoclasia, or fibrin deposition. Cutaneous coccidiomycosis may present as erythematous plaques studded with pustules. The characteristic pathologic finding is endospore-containing fungal spherules. Such features were not seen in this case. Erythema nodosum was also not a good fit because the patient’s lesions lacked tenderness and were distributed on the upper body, and biopsy results did not show septal panniculitis. Treatment of intravascular NK/T-cell lymphoma is not well defined owing to its rarity. Cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone therapy has been referenced in older case reports. Dexamethasone, methotrexate, ifosfamide, L-asparaginase, and etoposide therapy has been used for NK/T-cell lymphoma in patients with and without intravascular involvement.8Brentuximab may be useful for the 20% to 50% of NK/T-cell lymphomas that express CD30.9An intensive regimen involving pegaspargase, gemcitabine, and oxaliplatin, as used in this patient, has shown promising results in small studies of NK/T-cell lymphoma.10

scenario: A school-aged boy experienced generalized erythematous rashes for 4 years. Skin examination showed ichthyosiform brownish plaques on his lower extremities and multiple erythematous confluent papules and plaques on his trunk and face (Figure, A and B). Topical steroid and pimecrolimus were administered, but their effects were limited. In addition, painful distal and proximal interphalangeal joints were noted for 2 years, and the patient could not clench his fists. Uveitis in both eyes was also diagnosed by an ophthalmologist. Microscopic examination of his hair showed no trichorrhexis invaginata or trichorrhexis nodosa. A skin biopsy specimen was obtained and submitted for further histopathologic analysis (Figure, C and D).
explanation: A skin biopsy from the ichthyosiform rash on the right arm showed small noncaseating granulomas, multinucleated giant cells, and neutrophil infiltration in the dermis and subcutis. Acid-fast staining, Gomori methenamine-silver staining, and modified Ziehl-Neelsen staining all showed an absence of microorganisms, and sarcoidosis was confirmed. Whole-exome sequencing revealed a heterozygous missense variation (Arg334Trp) inNOD2that has previously been detected in Blau syndrome.1Accordingly, the diagnosis of Blau syndrome was confirmed. Blau syndrome is an autosomal dominant inflammatory disease characterized by a triad of granulomatous dermatitis, uveitis, and systemic polyarthritis. Variations inNOD2/CARD15on chromosome 16q12 have been identified in patients with Blau syndrome.NOD2/CARD15is primarily expressed in monocytes, a cell type capable of differentiation into multinucleated giant cells and epithelioid cells.2It has been hypothesized thatNOD2/CARD15variation is associated with increased NF-kB activation, macrophage death, and granulomatous inflammation.2 Skin involvement is one of the early manifestations of Blau syndrome. Early cutaneous presentations include morbilliform and lichenoid papules that mimic granuloma annulare, whereas the late manifestations are more diverse and include ichthyosiform rash, erythema nodosum-like nodules, and granulomatous vasculitis.3 Ocular involvement is one of the most disabling complications of Blau syndrome, causing loss of vision that may progress to blindness if left untreated. The common form of ocular involvement includes granulomatous panuveitis, cataracts, band keratopathy, iritis, and secondary glaucoma.4Arthritis usually appears during the first decade of life, with the wrist, metacarpophalangeal, metatarsophalangeal, and proximal interphalangeal joints being the joints most commonly involved.5Plain radiography often shows joint space narrowing and deformities with periarticular swelling, but without bone erosion. Patients with Blau syndrome rarely present with pulmonary involvement, and bilateral hilar adenopathy is often absent.6 Currently, to our knowledge, there is still no standard treatment for Blau syndrome, although corticosteroids are generally the first line of treatment. Additional immunomodulant agents or biologics (including methotrexate, tumor necrosis factor [TNF]–α inhibitor, and interleukin 1 receptor antagonist) may be added.1The patient in this article was treated with oral prednisolone in addition to methotrexate, but his skin eruptions and arthritis were only mildly responsive to those treatments. Because elevated serum TNF-α (17.9 pg/mL) levels were still noted, TNF-α inhibitor with adalimumab was administered, and the patient’s skin, arthritis, and uveitis all had satisfactory responses after adalimumab treatment for 6 months. Ichthyosiform rash is usually a late presentation of Blau syndrome.7The differential diagnoses of ichthyosiform rash include ichthyosis vulgaris, Netherton syndrome, and pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP). Ichthyosis vulgaris is caused by variations inFLGand characterized by diffuse scaling of the skin since childhood, palmar hyperlinearity, and keratosis pilaris.8Ichthyosis vulgaris is associated with atopic dermatitis and typically manifests with early-onset chronic dry skin with severe pruritus. Histologically, ichthyosis vulgaris may present with a thin or absent granular cell layer. Netherton syndrome, which is caused by an autosomal recessive variation ofSPINK5, is often associated with atopic diathesis and other important clinical traits, such as ichthyosis, ichthyosis linearis circumflexa, and hair shaft abnormalities.9Histology shows psoriasiform rather than granulomatous dermatitis. However, ichthyosis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis are not associated with uveitis or arthritis. Pityriasis rubra pilaris may be characterized as inherited ichthyosiform rashes.10Atypical juvenile-onset PRP (type V) was found to be associated withCARD14variations, which function as an activator of NF-kB signaling. Because the involved signaling pathway is similar, PRP and Blau syndrome also share similar manifestations, such as ichthyosiform scaling on the lower extremities and scaly patches involving the cheeks, with sparing of the infralabial region. The histopathology of PRP shows the presence of alternating parakeratosis and hyperkeratosis in vertical and horizontal directions. The present case highlights the characteristic manifestations of Blau syndrome. Early recognition of the disease aids in its early diagnosis and treatment and can help to prevent subsequent ocular and articular complications.1

scenario: A woman in her 70s presented with a 3-month history of episodic fever and painless cutaneous lesions on her lower limbs. The patient otherwise felt well and denied malaise, weight loss, or any other symptoms. She did not have any known benign inflammatory conditions. Physical examination showed indurated plaques with multiple telangiectasias (Figure, A and B) on almost all the surface of the legs. Except for slightly elevated C-reactive protein levels, the results of other routine blood and urine tests were unremarkable. A skin biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathology examination (Figure, C and D).

options.D: Intralymphatic proliferation of T-cell lymphoid blasts

distractors: Intralymphatic proliferation of T-cell lymphoid blasts
explanation: C. Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma Histopathologic evaluation revealed large round cells with scant cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli proliferating within blood vessels. Immunohistochemical analysis showed positivity for CD20, B-cell lymphoma (Bcl) 2, Bcl-6, cellularMYC, and multiple myeloma 1. The Ki-67 staining index was about 90%. The endothelial cells of the involved vessels expressed CD34 and CD31 and were negative for D2-40. Positron emission tomography scan results revealed no lymphadenopathy or metastases. No evidence of bone marrow involvement was found. The diagnosis of intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (IVLBCL) cutaneous variant was made. The patient was treated with 6 cycles of rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) with a complete response. At her last follow-up, 1 year after treatment, she continued to be in remission. Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma is a rare subtype of extranodal lymphoma that is defined by an accumulation of large neoplastic B cells within the lumina of blood vessels.1Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma is separated into 3 variants based on the clinical presentation, organs involved, and prognosis.2The classical variant is the most common form. The skin and central nervous system are most frequently affected. Involvement of the lung, kidney, liver, and adrenal glands has also been reported.3The hemophagocytic syndrome–associated variant traditionally presents with fever, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly, and bone marrow involvement.2Finally, the cutaneous variant presents with 1 or more cutaneous lesions and negative workup results for additional sites of involvement. The cutaneous variant represents 25% of cases4and has much better outcomes and response to treatment than the other variants.3,5The most common cutaneous findings in patients with IVLBCL are telangiectasias and/or indurated erythematous or violaceous ill-defined plaques, which are preferentially located on the trunk and thighs. However, ulceration,peau d’orangeappearance, panniculitis-like lesions, palpable purpura, retiform purpura, and cherry angiomas have also been described.4,6 Histopathologic findings of IVLBCL show a proliferation of medium-sized to large lymphocytes, with scant cytoplasm and often with prominent nucleoli, filling dilated blood vessels within the dermis and subcutaneous tissues.7Endothelial cells are CD34- and CD31-positive and negative for D2-40.7Neoplastic lymphocytes express CD20 and CD79; Bcl-2, cellular MYC, and multiple myeloma 1, Bcl-6, and CD10 are often positive. Therapy for IVLBCL is not firmly established but, traditionally, the disease is treated as a high-grade B-cell lymphoma with R-CHOP. The treatment of the cutaneous variant of IVLBCL, given its rarity, is less clear, although many authors recommend R-CHOP.8 Histopathology is crucial in making a diagnosis in patients who present with telangiectatic or retiform indurated lesions. Generally, cell morphology, immunohistochemistry, and the type of vessels affected are key to differentiate IVLBCL from other conditions. In intralymphatic histiocytosis, a reactive phenomenon secondary to chronic cutaneous infections, connective tissue disorders, or surgical scars, clusters of histiocytoid cells (expressing CD68 and CD163) are floating within the lumina of dilated vessels.9The structures affected are lymphatic vessels (positive for CD31, CD34, and podoplanin). Reactive angioendotheliomatosis is a benign intravascular proliferation of endothelial cells9of unknown etiology that has been described in association with systemic infections, microvascular occlusive disorders, and rheumatoid arthritis. The histopathologic spectrum of reactive angioendotheliomatosis is quite broad. The main histopathologic finding is a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries in the dermis that is without significant cellular atypia. Other common features include fibrin microthrombi and reactive dermal alterations, such as diffuse dermal angiomatosis, and glomeruloid hemangioma-like or tufted angioma-like patterns.10Intralymphatic proliferation of T-cell lymphoid blasts or benign atypical intralymphatic CD30+T-cell proliferation can also mimic an intravascular lymphoma histologically. Intralymphatic proliferation of T-cell lymphoid blasts are a recently described rare entity that can be an incidental finding in other benign inflammatory conditions. It has been speculated that it could represent a population of activated CD30+T cells that migrate to the lymph nodes in response to an unknown antigen. Intralymphatic proliferation of T-cell lymphoid blasts are characterized by the presence of large, blastoid T lymphocytes within lymphatic vessels.9These lymphocytes often express CD30 and lack the monoclonal rearrangement of the T-cell receptor genes. This case of skin-limited IVLBCL highlights the role of histopathology in the diagnosis of intravascular proliferations. Initial assessment and evaluation for the involvement of other organs is very important in patients with IVLBCL because the skin-limited disease has much better outcomes.

scenario: A woman in her 70s was referred to the dermatology department by the rheumatology department with concerns for vasculitis of the bilateral lower legs. She had been healthy until 6 years earlier when she had suddenly developed peripheral neuropathy, with subsequent workup revealing a diagnosis of immunoglobulin M (IgM) monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. Her symptoms had rapidly progressed during the past few months. In addition to worsening neuropathy, she had developed fatigue, weight loss, and sudden altered mental status. An ischemic stroke was identified. The patient was hospitalized, and extensive diagnostic examinations and procedures were completed. A lymphoproliferative disorder with plasmocytic differentiation was detected in a bone marrow biopsy specimen, which together with the monoclonal IgM paraproteinemia was consistent with Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM). Weeks later, the patient developed an asymptomatic rash of her lower legs. A physical examination revealed several bright red, nonblanchable, pinpoint macules of the bilateral lower legs (Figure, A). An antinuclear antibody test result was positive (titer 1:320, diffuse pattern). Other laboratory testing procedures (ie, complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, anti-Sjogren syndrome [SS]-A and SS-B, anti–double-stranded DNA, complement [C]3 and C4, homocysteine, β-2-glycoprotein, anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and vitamin C) returned normal. A punch biopsy of the right lower leg was performed for further diagnostic evaluation (Figure, B-D).
explanation: Tests results of serum viscosity, cryoglobulins, and cold agglutinins returned normal. Histopathologic findings revealed many amorphous eosinophilic deposits strongly positive for periodic acid–Schiff stain (PAS) in the papillary dermis. Congo red stain result was negative, with no apple-green birefringence. Immunofluorescence showed strong reactivity for IgM and lambda chains. Overall, these findings were consistent with cutaneous macroglobulinosis (CM). Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma associated with IgM hypersecretion and invasion of neoplastic B cells in bone marrow and peripheral organs.1It most commonly affects people from 60 to 70 years of age. One-quarter of patients are asymptomatic at diagnosis; however, 40% of individuals will experience symptoms within 3 years.1The most commonly associated systemic manifestations include lymphadenopathy, anemia, and hepatosplenomegaly.1,2Neuropathy, which the patient in this case experienced, is present in as many as one-third of individuals. Interestingly, this prevalence seems higher in patients with CM.3,4 Cutaneous manifestations affect only 5% of patients with WM. They may be a presenting feature of WM. However, the onset of skin lesions may develop more than 1 decade later.5Most WM cutaneous manifestations are nonspecific, often being associated with hyperviscosity or cryoglobulinemia, both of which are poor prognostic factors.1There is substantial heterogeneity in presentation. Hyperviscosity may manifest with peripheral edema, mucosal bleeding, or acral bleeding. Cryoglobulinemia may manifest with livedo reticularis, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, cold urticaria, Raynaud phenomenon, or ulceration.6Purpura can be seen with either hyperviscosity or cryoglobulinemia.2 Specific findings of cutaneous WM are associated with direct IgM deposition in the skin, with fewer than 20 cases of cutaneous macroglobulinosis (CM) identifiable in the literature.3,5To our knowledge, all reports describe pink or flesh-colored papules and nodules, some of which are hemorrhagic or ulcerative, on the trunk or extensor surfaces. Purpura or petechiae have yet to be described as a specific manifestation of CM. Although 1 patient with WM developed petechiae of the lower extremities, there was no evidence of IgM deposition within the dermis, thereby making this prior case an example of a nonspecific manifestation of WM rather than true CM.7 The hallmark feature of CM is the histopathologic presence of pink, PAS-positive, IgM-positive material within the dermis, as seen in this case.6Direct immunofluorescence or immunohistochemistry for IgM should be performed. The microscopic differential diagnosis of CM includes other conditions with deposition of eosinophilic, amorphous material in the dermis. This includes amyloidosis, cryoglobulinemia, lipoid proteinosis, and adult colloid milium.6 Systemic amyloidosis is associated with plasma cell dyscrasias, including WM.8It may present with purpura and waxy papules and nodules on the skin.8Given that amyloidosis and CM share histologic features and an association with WM, Congo red stain and examination under polarized light are completed to differentiate these diagnoses microscopically.6Under polarized light, amyloid shows apple-green birefringence. Apple-green birefringence was not identified on the skin and abdominal fat biopsy specimens of this patient, making the diagnosis of amyloidosis unlikely. Amyloid deposits can also be highlighted by thioflavin-T, PAS, and crystal violet stains.8 Cryoglobulinemia should also be considered in patients with paraproteinemia or monoclonal gammopathy. Cryoglobulinemia type II and type III can manifest as vasculitis on the skin; however,  histopathologic findings should show perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate and fibrinoid necrosis, which were not seen in this case.9In contrast, type I cryoglobulinemia histologically mimics CM with PAS-positive material in the dermis, but it is classically vaso-occlusive.9Additionally, normal serum cryoglobulins and complements make this diagnosis unlikely. Although this patient’s initial clinical presentation was suggestive of PPD or capillaritis, PPD histologic findings reveal a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate and red blood cell extravasation, which were not seen in this case.10Notably, both cryoglobulinemia and capillaritis are examples of nonspecific cutaneous manifestations of WM. In conclusion, this patient developed a unique presentation of CM with bright red macules mimicking petechiae. Treatment with rituximab was initiated with limited success. Although purpura and petechiae can be seen in WM, results of this patient’s histopathologic testing did not reveal features of capillaritis, vasculitis, or other nonspecific findings of WM. Instead, the presence of IgM eosinophilic depositions within the dermis identified a unique presentation of CM.

scenario: A man in his late 70s with stage IV adenocarcinoma of the lung presented with acute onset of redness, pain, and swelling of both lower limbs. The patient had received 4 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin, pemetrexed, and pembrolizumab for progressive disease and was currently in maintenance with pemetrexed-pembrolizumab. The edema appeared 5 days after the patient’s 8th cycle of chemotherapy and evolved into sclerotic plaques. Physical examination revealed ill-defined, erythematoedematous plaques symmetrically distributed along the shins, with areas of induration (Figure, A). The patient remained afebrile and systemically well. Results of laboratory tests showed no elevation of inflammatory markers (normal white blood cell count and C-reactive protein level), with kidney, liver, and heart functions within the normal ranges. Results of venous Doppler ultrasonography imaging of the patient’s legs did not show evidence of deep vein thrombosis. A biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B and C).
explanation: C. Pemetrexed-induced inflammatory and sclerotic edema Histopathologic examination showed a normal-appearing epidermis with edema in papillary dermis and perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes. In reticular dermis, a marked thickening of collagen with activated fibroblasts was observed. No signs of eccrine squamous syringometaplasia (ESS) or neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis were detected (Figure, B and C). The patient was treated with a 7-day course of oral prednisone and topical clobetasol and showed substantial clinical improvement, including the disappearance of the lesions with only residual hyperpigmentation. Based on the findings and treatment response, the diagnosis was grade 3 pemetrexed-induced inflammatory and sclerotic edema. Pemetrexed treatment was subsequently discontinued, and the patient continued with pembrolizumab treatment alone. Pemetrexed-induced inflammatory and sclerotic edema is a rare but increasingly recognized cutaneous adverse reaction that can affect as many as 13% of patients.1Pemetrexed is an antifolate drug that inhibits the enzymes required for thymidine and purine nucleotide synthesis. It is approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for treatment, in combination with cisplatin, of malignant pleural mesothelioma and advanced nonsquamous non–small cell lung cancer. It is also used off label in the treatment of other malignant neoplasms, such as those of the breast, ovaries, and bladder, and in carcinoma of the head and neck.2,3 Pemetrexed-induced inflammatory and sclerotic edema has been described after 1 to 23 cycles (dose, 500 mg/m2), with a median of 6 cycles.4Clinically, the lesions begin with an edematous, indurated, and inflammatory phase called pseudocellulitis, which typically affects the lower extremities bilaterally, does not cause fever, and produces normal test results (white blood cell count, C-reactive protein, and kidney function). If misdiagnosed (eg, as cellulitis) or corticosteroid treatment is delayed, the condition can progress to the sclerotic phase, during which lesions evolve into hyperpigmented sclerotic plaques.5Because of this duality between the inflammatory and sclerotic phases, several names have been used in the literature to refer to this condition: pseudocellulitis, cutaneous sclerosis, scleroderma-like changes, and lipodermatosclerosis secondary to use of pemetrexed or pemetrexed-induced.4-7Histopathologic findings in the inflammatory phase are characterized by an interface dermatitis, while in the sclerotic phase, a thickening of the dermis and lymphocytic perivascular infiltration are predominant.6Another distinctive feature of this condition is its improvement with topical and oral steroids, and although it is not always necessary to discontinue pemetrexed, a prompt improvement of the lesions is observed with dose reduction or discontinuation.4 Toxic erythema of chemotherapy is also characterized by areas of painful erythema and oftentimes edema, both of which are frequently bilateral; however, the plaques are usually localized in acral regions (feet, hands, ears, and/or perineum) and in the pressure or contact areas—large folds and, to a lesser extent, elbows and knees. Toxic erythema of chemotherapy appears 2 days to 3 weeks after the administration of chemotherapeutic agents and is considered a toxic phenomenon and not an immune-mediated effect. Histologic findings are characterized by atypia and apoptosis of keratinocytes, loss of polarity of epidermal cells, vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer of the epidermis, dermal edema, and ESS.8The patient in this case had no involvement of the hands or feet, nor did he have intertrigo-like eruptions. Furthermore, the biopsy specimen showed no pathologic findings in the epidermis nor signs of ESS. Sclerosing panniculitis, also known as lipodermatosclerosis, should also be included in the differential diagnosis. This condition is a chronic panniculitis characterized by skin induration and hyperpigmentation of a single leg or both legs and often occurs in patients who have venous insufficiency. Clinically, it usually appears in the shape of an inverted bottle. This shape can also be observed in the sclerotic phase of pemetrexed-induced inflammatory and sclerotic edema (Figure, A). Histopathologic findings of sclerosing panniculitis show a mostly lobular panniculitis with fat necrosis and absence of vasculitis. Fully developed lesions show septal sclerosis and membranocystic changes. This is different from what is observed with pemetrexed-induced inflammatory and sclerotic edema, whose sclerotic phase is characterized by dermal fibrosis and lymphocytic perivascular infiltration.6 Wells syndrome can also be considered in the differential diagnoses, especially in its acute phase, but this condition is characterized by the presence of peripheral eosinophilia, eosinophilic dermal infiltrate, or flame figures. However, there are 2 published cases of pemetrexed-induced pseudocellulitis with a predominantly eosinophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy that point to a hypersensitivity reaction.3,5 Pembrolizumab is an antiprogrammed death-1 drug involved in cutaneous adverse reactions in as many as 42% of patients. Cutaneous sclerosis induced by this drug has been reported9; however, it is much more likely that in this case, the patient’s condition was associated with pemetrexed given the response to drug removal. Sclerotic edema of the lower limbs is not a specific effect of pemetrexed, and it has been described with other chemotherapeutics, such as gemcitabine or taxanes.10Eguia and colleagues1suggest that its pathophysiology is not owed to a specific cytotoxicity of antifolates but to a nonspecific systemic inflammation associated with capillary leakage. In conclusion, pemetrexed-induced inflammatory and sclerotic edema is a rare adverse effect that should be recognized by dermatologists and oncologists. Accurate diagnosis and treatment are essential to avoiding chronic sclerotic cutaneous changes and to improving the patient’s quality of life.

D, The stratum corneum is lifted off the stratum granulosum, with subtle portions from the granular zone still attached (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification x400).
scenario: An otherwise healthy Black woman in her 30s presented to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of hypopigmented, intermittently pruritic patches. Patches were confined to her face and neck and occurred intermittently after her last pregnancy approximately 10 years ago. She had no history of eczema, atopic skin conditions, or autoimmune conditions and denied family history of such. In previous evaluations, the areas were treated with petroleum-based creams, low- to medium-potency topical steroids, pimecrolimus, and topical antifungals, without consistent improvement. Physical examination identified multiple hypopigmented macules and subtle patches symmetrically distributed across the lower aspect of the forehead, cheeks, nasofacial sulci, and nasolabial folds; and along the jawline and neck (Figure, A and B). Many had a slight overlying scale that was tested with potassium hydroxide and was negative for hyphae. No hair or nail abnormalities were noted. A 4-mm punch biopsy of a hypopigmented patch on the right cheek was performed (Figure, C and D).
explanation: Biopsy revealed focal epidermal parakeratosis with minimal acanthosis. The stratum corneum was uniformly lifted off the granular layer, with subtle portions still attached. The dermis showed mild perivascular lymphocytes and melanin incontinence (Figure, C and D). Periodic acid-Schiff stain result was negative for fungus. Subsequent enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for antibodies against desmoglein (Dsg) 1 and 3 was positive against Dsg 1. Histology demonstrating a subcorneal blister and positive ELISA for antibodies to Dsg 1 supported the diagnosis of pemphigus foliaceus (PF). The patient began receiving a prednisone taper with transition to mycophenolate mofetil, resulting in improvement. Pemphigus foliaceus is a rare autoimmune blistering disease mediated by antibodies targeting the desmosomal adhesion protein Dsg 1, resulting in acantholysis and subcorneal blister formation. Sporadic PF is the second most common variety within the pemphigus group of blistering disorders, accounting for 10% to 30% of cases.1Sporadic PF typically manifests between the ages of 45 and 65 years, with rare pediatric cases.1Higher frequency in children and young adults, as well as familial cases, is noted within endemic PF, which is well described in Tunisia, as well as Brazil (fogo selvagem) and other South American countries.2Diagnosis is established when clinical presentation and histology of a lesion are consistent with PF, with positive direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin or serology detecting autoantibodies to epithelial surface antigens.3 The clinical spectrum of PF is diverse and can mimic many skin diseases. Classic PF is associated with erythematous papules or plaques with cornflake scaling and crusting distributed in seborrheic areas of the scalp, face, and upper region of the trunk.1Mucosal surfaces are spared. True blisters are uncommon because of the superficial nature of the subcorneal split. In a severe form, PF can present as a generalized exfoliative dermatitis and erythroderma.2A generalized psoriasiform dermatitis with pustular component has been described.4Milder forms can mimic seborrheic dermatitis and actinic keratoses. Pemphigus erythematosus, a localized variant of PF, favors photodistributed areas of the face and upper region of the trunk, resembling cutaneous lupus erythematosus.1Drug-induced PF has been reported most commonly with penicillamine and captopril.1Transient PF can develop in neonates from passive transfer of autoantibodies from a mother with PF.5 The tuberculoid spectrum of leprosy, representing a paucibacillary form of leprosy in patients with a robust TH1 cell–mediated immune response, presents with a few localized, hypopigmented, anesthetic macules or patches. These can be scaly and may have a raised border.6Seborrheic dermatitis favors the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and chest, with a yellow greasy scale and underlying erythema. However, in Black patients, hypopigmentation in a seborrheic pattern can be the predominant clinical finding.7Hypopigmented mycosis fungoides favors patients with darker skin tones and younger ages compared with classic mycosis fungoides. It typically manifests on the extremities, trunk, and buttocks, although rare cases of facial involvement have been reported.8 Recommendations regarding management of pemphigus have recently been published.3Treatment decisions should be made according to severity of the condition and effect on quality of life. First-line treatment is systemic corticosteroids. Recommended first-line steroid-sparing agents include mycophenolate mofetil and azathioprine. Rituximab, an anti-CD20 antibody, is recommended as a first-line treatment for moderate to severe disease or for individuals who do not improve with immunosuppressant adjuvants. Additional treatment options reported successful in some cases include intravenous immunoglobulin, dapsone, cyclophosphamide, and tetracycline antibiotics with oral niacinamide.9 This case of PF presented as subtle hypopigmentation of the face and neck that persisted intermittently for a decade. We illustrate the importance of considering biopsy in cases that are persistent and not responding as expected to therapy, and of expanding our differential beyond the common, even in cases appearing banal.

scenario: A man in his 50s presented with painful palmar and plantar purpura that lasted for 2 months (Figure, A). The lesions first appeared on the volar aspect of the left hand and resolved spontaneously within a few days. However, the purpura soon relapsed on the left plantar area. Oral administration of aspirin and limaprost alfadex was ineffective, and the purpura spread on the palms and feet, followed by onset of left hemiplegia with dysarthria. The patient had no history of arterial or coronary catheterization, hyperlipidemia, hepatitis, nor endocrine neoplasia. The patient’s body temperature and laboratory test results, including inflammatory markers, were slightly elevated. Autoimmune blood tests, including antinuclear antibody, anticardiolipin antibody, and lupus anticoagulant, were not detected. Lentiginosis was not evident. A skin biopsy of the purpura of the left plantar area was conducted (Figure, B).
explanation: A. Cutaneous embolization of cardiac myxoma The histological examination showed subcutaneous intracapillary occlusion (Figure, B). The obstruent was positively stained with Alcian blue (Figure, C) and calretinin (Figure, D). Computed tomography and echocardiography detected a right cerebral infarction and a 23-mm mass in the left atrium, respectively. Therefore, cardiac myxoma (CM) was suspected, and the tumor was surgically resected. The tumor was histopathologically composed of spindle- or star-shaped cells that were surrounded by an extracellular matrix. The tumor cells and extracellular matrix were positively stained with calretinin and Alcian blue, respectively. Collectively, a diagnosis of CM was made, and the painful palmar and plantar purpura was attributed to CM embolization. Cardiac myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor that manifests in women aged 30 to 60 years. Most CM originates from the fossa ovalis of the interatrial septum, thereby developing in the left atrium.1,2While CM is a benign tumor, serious systemic complications may occur, including intracardiac obstructions, such as dyspnea, palpitation, and orthopnea; extracardiac embolisms; and immunologic systemic symptoms that are caused by tumor-derived cytokines, such as fever, arthralgia, and myalgia.3Intracardiac obstructions occur in 67% of patients with left atrial CM.4Extracardiac embolisms are primarily developed in the central nervous system and also develop in other organs, such as the kidneys, spleen, and extremities.3Around 13% of patients with left atrial CM develop peripheral limb embolization by fragmentation or total CM, similar to this patient.4Cutaneous manifestations include erythematous or purpuric macules and patches, telangiectasia, petechiae, livedo reticularis, and digital cyanosis and necrosis.3Histopathologically, myxoma consists of myxoma cells and an abundant acid mucopolysaccharide myxoid matrix.3Myxoma cells are star- and spindle-shaped cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and are observed to form structures like rings, cords, and nests. One commonly used marker for myxoma cells is calretinin, and the myxoid matrix is positively stained with Alcian blue staining.5 Differential diagnosis of palpable purpura includes the Carney complex, Osler nodes, dermatologic manifestation of COVID-19, and collagen vascular diseases, including autoimmune vasculitis, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, and cryoglobulinemia. Cardiac myxoma is one of the major symptoms of the Carney complex, which is a rare, autosomal-dominant, multiple endocrine neoplasia, and lentiginosis syndrome, and is primarily caused by defects of thePRKAR1Agene, which encodes the regulatory subunit type 1α of protein kinase A.6The Carney complex is associated with the development of various mucocutaneous manifestations, such as mucocutaneous myxomas, lentiginosis, blue nevi, and café-au-lait spots.7Osler nodes, which are a major manifestation of infective endocarditis, occur as painful nodular lesions on the palmar and plantar areas that pathologically exhibit not only vascular occlusion but also necrotizing vasculitis.8The global COVID-19 pandemic began in 2020. Various skin manifestations, including urticarial rash, papulovesicular exanthem, or palpable purpura, have been reported. Retiform purpura that was observed in patients with COVID-19 was presumed to be caused by vascular thrombosis.9COVID-19 antigen or antibodies were not detected in this patient. Cryoglobulinemia, which is caused by circulating cryoglobulins in the serum, results in the development of systemic inflammatory symptoms, including fatigue, arthralgia, and purpura. Cryoglobulinemia pathologically exhibits small-to-medium sized vessel vasculitis that is caused by the development of immune complexes.10 The incidence of CM is low, and its cutaneous findings are nonspecific and diverse. Therefore, it is important to consider that cutaneous embolization of CM is a differential diagnosis of painful purpura on the extremities. A skin biopsy is indispensable for diagnosing CM. Conversely, it is possible to find CM by physical examination and skin biopsy. If CM is suspected, an echocardiography must be performed, and a total-body skin examination is recommended so as not to miss the cutaneous signs of a Carney complex.

Note the nail dystrophy in the left first toe. B, Detail of tense blisters and vesicles, erosions, and scar areas. C, Subepidermal blister with orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis and mild inflammatory infiltrate in the papillary dermis (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×20). D, Detail of the dermoepidermal detachment and the perivascular lymphohistiocytic inflammatory infiltrate. Some apoptotic keratinocytes are seen in the epidermis, possibly because it is a long-standing blister (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×100).
scenario: A man in his 50s presented with a history of pruritic lesions of the lower legs over the past 15 years that were unresponsive to topical corticosteroid therapy. On examination, he had multiple lichenified and ulcerated papules and nodules, some of them grouped in plaques located on the medial aspect of both shins (Figure, A). Occasional tense blisters were also seen (Figure, B). The patient’s family history was significant for similar cutaneous lesions in his father, brother, and cousin. Mild toenail dystrophy was also observed. A punch biopsy from the shin for histopathologic examination was performed (Figure, C and D).
explanation: Histopathologic examination showed dermoepidermal detachment and scarce lymphohistiocytic inflammatory infiltrate in perivascular distribution in papillary dermis. Given the clinicopathological suspicion of pretibial epidermolysis bullosa (PEB), a genetic study was requested, which confirmed a heterozygous pathogenic sequence variation in the protein p.Lys2562Asn from theCOL7A1gene (OMIM120120). The same variant was found in his 14-year-old son, who remains asymptomatic, while the rest of the family could not be reached. Pretibial epidermolysis bullosa is an uncommon variant of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa first described in 1946 by Kuske.1It is characterized by the presence of localized pretibial lesions, with blisters and erosions, scarring, and atrophic or lichenoid papules or plaques. This mechanobullous genodermatosis results from sequence variations occurring in theCOL7A1gene. The latter encodes type VII collagen, the main constituent of the anchoring fibrils, which participate in the adherence of the lamina densa to the epidermis. The exact pathophysiological mechanism of PEB remains unknown, but some in vitro studies found an association between the peculiar phenotype of PEB and increased endoplasmic reticulum stress in keratinocytes.2 MultipleCOL7A1variations have already been identified in patients with PEB, and approximately two-thirds show a dominant inheritance pattern.3The onset of cutaneous lesions is highly variable, occurring from early infancy to adulthood. In PEB, pretibial blisters, milia, atrophic scarring, and lichenoid papules and plaques are usually associated with dystrophic or absent toenails. Pruritus is a common manifestation, and there is an appreciable clinicopathological overlap with dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa pruriginosa, which usually shows more widespread distribution of prurigo nodularislike lesions, marked scarring, and an earlier age at onset.4 Histopathologically, subepidermal bulla formation with minimal inflammation is commonly seen, but lichenification and atrophy may be artifactual findings. Direct immunofluorescence is always negative for the deposit of immunoglobulins and complement. When the characteristic clinical features of PEB are present and skin biopsy findings support the diagnosis, genetic testing is recommended and can deliver a final diagnosis. Other techniques, such as immunofluorescence mapping or transmission electron microscopy, may frequently remain uninformative and useless in mild and localized subtypes of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa because of the lack of skin cleavage and the alteration of immunoreactivity.5 Delayed diagnoses are frequent because clinical features can mimic more common diseases. The main differential diagnosis includes lichen planus, lichen amyloidosis, and even dermatosis artefacta. Bullous lichen planus presents as bullae or vesicles associated with typical lichen planus papules that are mainly located on the lower extremities. Nail abnormalities, such as a thin nail plate, scarring, or complete loss of the nail, may also be present. In contrast to PEB, histopathologic examination demonstrates vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer, lymphocytic infiltration in the subepithelial layer, and necrosis of individual keratinocytes.6Lichen amyloidosis is a clinical manifestation of primary cutaneous amyloidosis, which presents as firm or hyperkeratotic papules, typically on the legs, and causes severe itching. The diagnosis is confirmed by histopathologic evidence of keratinocyte-derived amyloid deposits located predominantly in the papillary dermis.7Dermatitis artefacta should be present in the differential diagnosis of every chronic and recurrent dermatosis. As in PEB, the lower extremities are usually affected, and lichenified papules, erosions, or scarring are some of the lesions seen in dermatitis artefacta. The clinical presentation, including distribution and physical characteristics, are almost diagnostic in most cases, but some histologic findings, such as blistering with a mild inflammatory infiltrate, rupture of collagen fibers, or elongated and vertically aligned keratinocyte nuclei, may support the diagnosis of dermatitis artifacta.8 Current management of dystrophic PEB consists of minimizing further trauma and preventing secondary infection. Unresponsive pruritus can be a troublesome aspect in this disease, and treatment with oral antihistamines or phototherapy shows variable results. New therapeutic perspectives are focused on ways to enhance type VII collagen expression at the dermoepidermal junction, gene therapy, allogenic intradermal injections of fibroblast, and stem cell therapy.9

Sections show an unremarkable epidermis overlying diffuse transdermal edema and hemorrhage. A diffuse, patchy basophilic infiltrate with lymphohistiocytic inflammation and abundant infectious organisms are seen in the dermis. scenario: A man in his 80s with a history of asthma and bronchiectasis who was receiving immunosuppression therapy presented to an outside hospital with dyspnea and right arm swelling and tenderness 8 days before transfer to our center. The immunosuppression therapy consisted of methylprednisolone, 12 mg every other day, and the patient’s medical history included cerebrovascular accident, atrial flutter, and aortic stenosis. On initial evaluation, his vital signs were stable. On physical examination, the patient had edema of the right arm, hand, and fingers with overlying diffuse violaceous nonblanching and edematous nodules (Figure, A). Purpuric plaques were also noted on the right cheek, central chest, left arm, and left posterior shoulder. Laboratory findings were significant for a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL (reference range 13.5-17.5 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]). Results of blood cultures from the outside hospital showed “yeast” at the time of transfer. Computed tomography imaging of the chest showed diffusely scattered patchy lung infiltrates suspicious for inflammatory disease or infection, along with a small left pleural effusion. A skin biopsy specimen was obtained from a purpuric plaque (Figure, B, C, and D).
explanation: A frozen section skin biopsy specimen showed extensive lymphohistiocytic inflammation of the dermis and subcutis with hemorrhage as well as numerous intracellular organisms. Blood cultures subsequently grewPrototheca wickerhamii, and a diagnosis of disseminated protothecosis was made. Tissue cultures also grewProtothecaspecies. Treatment was transitioned from caspofungin acetate to amphotericin B and doxycycline hyclate forPrototheca,with ampicillin sodium added forEnterococcus faecalispresent in repeat blood cultures. Despite this therapy, the patient declined precipitously, requiring intubation and vasopressor medications. A family decision to transition to comfort care was made, and he died shortly thereafter. Protothecosis is a rare disease associated withPrototheca, a genus of unicellular algae that is ubiquitous in nature and most prevalent in humid climates and aqueous environments.1﻿Prototheca wickerhamiiis theProtothecavariant most commonly associated with human disease. The organism is typically introduced into the skin via trauma in contaminated water, with the trauma characteristically not recognized or remembered by the patient.2 The 3 most common presentations of humanProtothecainfection are (1) cutaneous disease localized to the skin, (2) olecranon bursitis, and (3) disseminated protothecosis. Cutaneous disease and olecranon bursitis typically is present in patients who are immunocompetent, whereas disseminated protothecosis with algaemia is exceedingly rare and usually affects only immunocompromised individuals.3The cutaneous lesions ofProtothecahave been previously reported as bullae, ulcers, papules, and nodules.3,4 Histopathologically,P wickerhamiican be observed extracellularly or within the cytoplasm of macrophages and multinucleated giant cells. On close inspection, the organisms appear as thick-walled nonbudding spherical bodies, which have been likened to soccer balls given the endospores’ morulalike forms. The organisms may be difficult to visualize with hematoxylin-eosin stain but can be enhanced with silver methenamine or periodic acid–Schiff stains.4 Differential diagnosis of disseminated protothecosis includes other fungal infections, such as coccidiomycosis, cryptococcosis, and aspergillosis. Clinical presentation of each of these entities is variable, making skin biopsy and tissue culture necessary to identify the source of the infection.2WhereasP wickerhamiitypically has the aforementioned spherical nonbudding sporangia with morulalike structures (3 to 30 microns in size),Coccidioides immitisclassically presents with larger spherules containing endospores (10 to 200 microns). Clinically, disseminated coccidiomycosis can appear on the skin as verrucous nodules, subcutaneous abscesses, or pink papules.5 Cryptococcus neoformansis characterized by spherical cells with a thick polysaccharide capsule (2 to 15 microns).2Cryptococcosis typically begins as a lung infection and can disseminate to the central nervous system and skin, with skin lesions most commonly occurring on the head and neck. Variable skin morphologies have been reported, with molluscum contagiosumlike lesions described classically in patients with HIV.5 Aspergillusappears in tissue as slender hyphae with acute angle branching.6On the skin, disseminated aspergillosis typically presents with red papules and plaques with progressive necrosis attributed toAspergilluswithin blood vessels. Systemic involvement often includes the lungs, with possible involvement of the kidneys and central nervous system.5,6 As in this case, results of blood cultures forProtothecamay initially show yeastlike organisms, which can confuse the clinical picture.7Thus, clinicians should keepProtothecaalgaemia in the differential diagnosis even when blood cultures show “yeast.” Skin biopsy is critical for establishing early diagnosis given possible delays in culture identification ofPrototheca. Treatment of disseminated protothecosis is challenging, with amphotericin B as the currently recommended first-line treatment. Other options include adding doxycycline to amphotericin B, as was done in this case, or antifungals, such as ketoconazole, itraconazole, or fluconazole.4Mortality remains high forProtothecaalgaemia even with treatment, with a mortality rate of 62.5% reported in 1 review.8
